en: The Kalki Purāṇa. First Part. First Chapter.

The hosts of gods led by Indra, the lords among sages, and the worlds together with their guardians— these supreme beings always worship day after day with devotion that Vighneśa, who is infinite, infallible, unborn, the omniscient refuge of all, for the sake of the perfect accomplishment of each of their respective tasks.
I bow to Nārāyaṇa, who is praised at the outset by various scriptures such as the Vedic and Tantric;
and having paid homage to Nara, the best of men, and to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then proclaim the word "Jaya. (1–2)

He whose body blazes with the flames of the gaping maw of the serpent-like staff of his arm, by whom kings who cause the earth to tremble are crushed like blades of grass by the staff of his excellent sword—
Kalki, born of a twice-born family, riding a horse from the Sindhu region, is the Supreme Self, Hari.
"May that Blessed One, who is fond of the manifestation of Dharma, protect us as he did at the beginning of the Satya Yuga.
Having heard these words of Sūta, the highly fortunate residents of the Naimiṣa forest, headed by Śaunaka, questioned him regarding this narrative.
"O Sūta, knower of all dharmas, son of Lomaharṣaṇa, knower of the three times and the Purāṇas, tell us the story of the Bhāgavata.
Who was Kali, and where was he born? Who is the Lord and Master of the worlds?"
"How could the destruction of the eternal Dharma have been wrought by Kali?
Having heard these words of theirs, the Sūta meditated upon the Lord Hari;
with all his limbs bristling with hair from joy, he spoke to those sages.
Sūta said:
Listen to this most wonderful narrative concerning the future, which was formerly narrated by Brahmā to Nārada when he questioned him. (8)
Nārada spoke it to the sage Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor;
he, Vyāsa, [spoke it] to his own son, the wise Brahmarāta;
and he, in turn, [spoke it] to Viṣṇurāta, the son of Abhimanyu, in the assembly.
He then proclaimed the eighteen thousand verses of the Bhāgavata-dharma.
When the king had met his end after seven days of questioning,
Śuka, having been questioned by Mārkaṇḍeya and others at the holy hermitage, spoke.
Having been authorized therein, I have heard those stories;
I shall now relate here the meritorious, auspicious, and divine narratives concerning the Bhagavān.
Listen to them, O highly fortunate ones, with concentrated minds and without ceasing.
When Kṛṣṇa had departed for his own abode,
Kali appeared like the world-creator Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, who at the end of the dissolution created from the back of his body a terrible and impure sin.
He is known as Adharma; by hearing or remembering the recitation of his lineage, the world is liberated from all sins.
Adharma’s beloved wife was the lovely Mithyā, who had eyes like those of a cat.
His son was Dambha, possessed of great splendor and extremely wrathful.
He begot Lobha as a son and Kanyaka as a daughter upon his sister Māyā;
Krodha became the son of those two.
He begot that Kali upon his sister Hiṃsā;
he held his lap with his left hand and had the luster of collyrium smeared with oil.
He was a serpent-bellied, fanged-mouthed, long-tongued, and terrifying being.
He produced a foul stench, gambling, intoxicants, women, and the pursuit of gold;
moreover, he begot fear upon his sister Durukī, as well as a son and a daughter,
and for those two, hell ensued.
In her sister Yātanā, she obtained ten million sons;
thus, many born in the Kali lineage became revilers of Dharma, destroyers of the Vedas and Tantras, and neglectors of sacrifice, study, and charity. (21)
Resorting to mental anguish, physical disease, old age, exhaustion, sorrow, grief, and fear, men followed the kings of the Kali age;
they moved about in groups as destroyers of the world, fallen from the right timing, transient, and lustful. ||22-23||
The twice-born will be hypocritical in conduct, ill-behaved, and harmful to their fathers and mothers; devoid of the Vedas, they will be wretched and constantly intent on serving Śūdras.
(24) Abounding in fallacious arguments and pride, these lowest of men will be sellers of dharma.
Those who sell the Vedas, the *vrātyas*, as well as those who sell liquids,
the cruel sellers of meat, those devoted to their genitals and bellies, those addicted to the wives of others, the intoxicated, and those who cause the intermixture of castes; ||25-26||
Short in stature, evil-natured, deceitful, and dwelling in monasteries;
having a lifespan of sixteen years, they will have their brothers-in-law as kinsmen and associate with the base.
Agitated by disputes and quarrels, they will adorn themselves with matted hair and fine headgear. (27)
In the Kali age, those of noble lineage will be wealthy, and Brahmins will be usurers;

renunciants will be attached to home life, while householders will be lacking in discernment; they will be intent on reviling their gurus, hypocritical regarding dharma, and deceivers of the virtuous. (28–29)

Śūdras delight in receiving gifts, take pleasure in seizing the property of others, consider marriage to be the mere acceptance of two people, regard friendship as a form of flattery, and display generosity only toward those who are dishonest; they possess forgiveness only when there is a return gift, and lack the capacity for dispassion even when possessing power. (30)
Fluency in speech is for the sake of scholarship, the practice of dharma is for the sake of fame;
wealth is for the sake of goodness, and the status of a sacred ford exists only in water far away.
One becomes a Brahmin by the mere thread [of the *yajñopavīta*], and a wandering mendicant by the mere staff. (31–32)
The earth yields little grain; women planted along the riverbanks have their minds abandoned by their own husbands, finding pleasure only in the talk of courtesans;
and Brahmins, greedy for the food of others, act as priests for the dwellings of outcasts.
Women will be devoid of widowhood and fond of acting according to their own whims;
the clouds will produce variegated rains, the earth will yield poor crops, kings will devour their subjects, and the people will be tormented by the oppression of taxes.
Placing their burdens upon their shoulders and taking their children with them, the distressed and unfortunate people will take refuge in mountain fastnesses and formidable forests,
sustaining their lives on food consisting of honey, meat, roots, and fruits. (36)
Thus, in the first quarter of the Kali age, there will be those who revile Kṛṣṇa;
in the second, those devoid of his name; in the third, those of mixed castes; and in the fourth, those of a single caste who have forgotten the true nature of Acyuta. ||37-38||
Deprived of Vedic recitation, the *svadhā*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, and *oṃ* syllables,
all the gods, being without food, went for refuge to Brahmā,
placing before him the Earth, who was emaciated, distressed, yet noble-minded. (39)
They beheld the world of Brahmā, resounding with the sound of the Vedas,
filled with the smoke of sacrifices, and frequented by the best of sages;
in the midst of its golden altar stood a brilliant conch-shell turning to the right.
The garden, marked by sacrificial posts of fire and endowed with flowers and fruits from its groves,
seemed to invite the guest with its lakes filled with cranes and swans;
it was further agitated by swarms of bees amidst the clusters of blossoms on creepers trembling in the wind.
With prostrations, invitations, honors, sweet conversation, and glances, the gods, together with their Lord, entered that abode of Brahmā with hearts full of devotion;
permitted by him, they entered to report their own business. ||43-44||
The gods, led by Brahmā, bowed down before the Lord of the three worlds, who was seated upon his throne, his lotus feet served by the Siddhas Sanaka, Sanandana, and Sanātana.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Kali Age," in the glorious *Kalki Purāṇa*, the subsequent *Bhāgavata* concerning the future.
The Second Chapter.
Sūta said:
Then, at the word of Brahmā, the gods sat down before him.
Out of respect, they spoke of the decline of dharma due to the defects of the Kali age.
Chapter Two:
Having heard those words of the gods, Brahmā spoke to them who were distressed.

"Having propitiated that Viṣṇu, I shall accomplish my desired goal. Thus addressed by the gods, Brahmā went to the dweller of Goloka, and after praising him, spoke before him the desire that was in the hearts of the gods.
Having heard that, the lotus-eyed one spoke this to Brahmā:
"O Lord, at your command, I shall manifest in the house of Viṣṇuyaśas in Śambhala, in my mother Sumati, who is a maiden;
O God, together with four brothers, I shall bring about the destruction of the Kali age."
"O lords, kinsmen, and gods, you shall descend with your own portions.
This beloved Lakṣmī of mine, lotus-eyed, will be born in Siṃhala as the daughter of King Bṛhadratha during the month of Kārttika."
"In my wife, she who is named Padmā shall give birth to this son.
Go now, O gods, intent upon descending with your own portions to the earth;
I myself shall establish Maru and Devakī as kings upon the earth."
"O Lord, having once again established the Kṛta Yuga and reinstated the dharmas as they were before,
and having cast out the serpent of the Kali age, I shall depart for my own abode.
Having heard these words spoken, Brahmā, surrounded by the hosts of gods, [responded].
He went to the abode of Brahmā, and the gods departed for the third heaven.
Having manifested his own greatness and exerted himself for his own birth, the Blessed One, whose nature is the Supreme Self, O brahmin-sage, entered the village of Śambhala.
Viṣṇuyaśas conceived in Sumati a Vaiṣṇava embryo, whose lotus feet were served by the planets, constellations, zodiac signs, and so forth;
[and by whom] the rivers, oceans, mountains, and the worlds, including all things stationary and moving, were sustained. (11)
When Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World, was born, the sages and gods were filled with joy;
all living beings experienced various forms of bliss.
The ancestors danced in delight, while the satisfied gods sang his praises.
The Gandharvas played musical instruments and the hosts of Apsarases danced.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Mādhava, the parents, their minds filled with joy, beheld their son Mādhava who had been born.
Dhātṛmātā, Mahāṣaṣṭhī, Nābhicchetrī, Ambikā, Gaṅgodakakledamokṣā, and Sāvitrī, intent on purification—
these sustain the milk and nectar of that infinite Viṣṇu, the supporter of the earth. (16)
On the day of Kṛṣṇa’s birth, Mātṛkā likewise spoke auspicious words.
Having understood that, Brahmā quickly said to his messenger, his own swift-moving servant:
"Go to the lying-in chamber and awaken Viṣṇu."
"O Lord, having abandoned this four-armed form which is difficult even for the gods to attain, assume a human-like form as you have deliberated.
Having heard these words of Brahmā, the fragrant wind blew pleasantly.
O King, Śiva spoke thus, honoring the word of Brahmā.
Having heard that, the lotus-eyed one became two-armed at that very moment;
then his parents, seeing this, were filled with wonder in their minds.
Due to his illusory power (*māyā*), they perceived it there as if it possessed the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of delusion;
consequently, in the village of Śambhala, all living beings were full of festive joy, abounding in auspicious rites, and free from the torment of sin.
Having obtained that son Viṣṇu, the victorious lord of the world, Sumati’s desires were fulfilled; she summoned the foremost of the brahmins and gave them a hundred cows.
With a pure heart, Hari performed the auspicious rites for Viṣṇuyaśas.
The foremost experts in the Sāman, Ṛg, and Yajur Vedas were intent upon performing his naming ceremony.
At that time, Rāma, Kṛpa, Vyāsa, and the son of Droṇa arrived in the form of mendicants to behold Hari who had attained childhood.

Beholding those four lords who had arrived, resplendent like the sun, the best of the twice-born, his hair standing on end with joy, performed their worship. Having been honored, they sat upon their own seats, resting in their own comfort.
All the embodied forms beheld Hari situated within his belly.
Having bowed to that child in human form, Viṣṇu, the lords of sages and the wise knew him to be Kalki, who had manifested for the sake of destroying all evil (kalka).
Then they gave him the name Kalki, which became widely renowned;
having performed the rites of consecration, they departed with joyful minds.
Thereafter, he grew up there, protected by Sumati.
In a short time, the enemy of Kaṃsa will be like the moon in the bright fortnight.
Kalki’s three heroic elder brothers— Kavi, Prājña, and Sumantraka—
will act for the pleasure of their father and mother, and they will be firmly established in their devotion to their gurus and brahmins.
The portions of Kalki were born previously as virtuous men devoted to dharma—
Gārgya, Bhargya, Viśāla, and others— who were his kinsmen and followed his path;
they were protected by King Viśākhayūpa and were free from all suffering.
Upon beholding Kalki, the Brahmins attained supreme joy.
Then Viṣṇuyaśas spoke to his son Kalki—the steadfast one, the source of all virtues, lotus-petal-eyed, and devoted to recitation—saying: 33–34.
"Dear father, I shall cause you to recite the Sāvitrī— the unsurpassed sacrificial thread that constitutes the Vedic initiation— and thereafter you shall study the Vedas.
Kalki said:
"What is the Veda? What is the Sāvitrī? By which Sūtra were they consecrated?
O father, tell me the truth regarding that which was known by Brahmā in this world.
The father replied: The father said:
The Veda is the speech of Hari; Sāvitrī is established as the Mother of the Vedas.
The three-stranded thread consists of the three qualities (guṇas); by means of it, the Brahmins are established.
Those Brāhmaṇas who are consecrated by the ten sacrifices are exponents of the Brahman.
In this regard, the Vedas are the sustainers of the three worlds here;
through sacrifices, study, charity, and other forms of austerity, as well as self-study and self-restraint, they please Hari with devotion according to the ordinances of the Vedic tantras. ||38-39||
"Therefore, O auspicious one, I desire that you be consecrated by me along with the twice-born and our kinsmen on an auspicious day, following the rite of initiation (upanayana).
The son said:
"And what are those ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) established among the Brahmins?
Or by what means do the Brahmins worship Viṣṇu according to the prescribed rule?
The father said:

Born of a Brāhmaṇa father from a Brāhmaṇa mother, consecrated by the sacraments beginning with *garbhādhāna*, devoted to the three daily junctures (*saṃdhyā*), the worship and recitation of the *Sāvitrī*,
ascetic, truthful in speech, steadfast, and righteous in soul— he delivers one from the cycle of worldly existence.
"Having understood this worship of Viṣṇu, the twice-born one became eternally filled with bliss.
The son said:
"Where is that twice-born man who saves the entire world?"
Pleasing Hari by the path of the righteous, he was the granter of desires throughout the three worlds.
His father said:
"By the powerful Kali, the destroyer of dharma and slayer of the twice-born..."
Those who delight in the Dharma have been cast out and have gone to other regions. Those Brahmins who possess only slight austerity remain within the Kali Yuga;
they are devoted to unrighteousness, intent on nourishing their genitals and bellies, and have desisted from sacred rites. ||45-46||
"Those whose essence is sin, who are of wicked conduct, devoid of luster, and unskilled in the arts— these servants of the Śūdra are utterly unable to protect themselves.
Having heard these words of Janaka, Kalki, born with the desire to destroy the race of Kali, [proceeded].
Then, brought there by the words of the twice-born and his own kin, the Lord of the Righteous dwelt in residence at the teacher’s house.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Birth and Initiation of Kalki," in the glorious *Anubhāgavata*, the future *Kalki Purāṇa*.
Chapter Three.
Sūta said:
Then, seeing Kalki departing for the preceptor’s hermitage to dwell there,
the lord Rāma, staying on Mount Mahendra, brought him back to his own hermitage.
He said to you, "Know me to be your preceptor according to the Dharma;
know me as the great lord Jamadagnya, born of the lineage of Bhṛgu,
who knows the truth of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas and is an expert in the science of archery."
Having rid the earth of the Kṣatriyas and given sacrificial fees to the Brahmins,
O son of a twice-born, I have come to Mount Mahendra to perform austerities;
you, meanwhile, should study here your own Veda and whatever other supreme scripture there may be.
Having heard those words, Kalki’s hair stood on end with joy; bowing before him, he then became a student of the Vedas,
including the auxiliary branches (*aṅgas*) and the sixty-four arts, as well as the science of archery (*dhanurveda*) and so forth.
Having completed his studies under Jāmadagnya, Kalki spoke with palms joined in reverence:
"O Lord, request a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) that may be given in your presence—
one by which I may attain all perfections and which shall bring you satisfaction."
Rāma said:
O Infinite One, at the request of Brahmā for the purpose of suppressing Kali, you—the perfect Viṣṇu, the refuge of all—were born in Śambhala. 8.
Having received from Śiva the knowledge and the weapon consisting of the Vedas, you shall establish the Dharma in Siṃhala and your beloved Padmā,
and then, during your conquest of the quarters, [subdue] those kings who are devoid of dharma and fond of the Kali age.
Having subdued the Buddhists, you shall establish Devāpi and Maru.
We, however, being satisfied by these virtuous deeds and accompanied by sacrificial fees, shall perform sacrifice, charity, austerity, and ritual action as is appropriate.
Having heard these words, and having paid homage to the sage and teacher,
he went to the god Bilvodakeśvara and praised Śaṅkara;
having worshipped the peaceful Maheśvara, Śiva, according to the prescribed rule.
Having prostrated before him who is easily pleased and having meditated upon him who resides within the heart,
Kalki spoke: "To Gaurīnātha, the Lord of the Universe, the Refuge..."
I bow to the ancient primordial deity, the abode of all beings, whose neck is adorned by Vāsuki, who possesses three eyes and five faces, and who is capable of bestowing a mass of intense bliss. 14.
The Lord of Yoga, the destroyer of desire, the formidable one whose head is moistened by contact with the Gaṅgā,
the Lord whose being is encompassed by the mass of his matted locks.
I bow to Mahākāla, who has the moon upon his forehead (Candrabhāla),
who dwells in the cremation ground, is accompanied by spirits and vetālas,
and is armed with various weapons such as swords, spears, and the like. ||15||
His arms, fierce and exceedingly terrible, cause the destruction of the world; by his wrath, the world is shaken and goes to its end.
He is the source of all beings, desiring to create through the five elements.

I bow to that Lord who, having struck down this world through time, karma, and inherent nature— which are themselves composed of the subtle elements— attains the state of the individual soul and rejoices in the bliss of Brahman. 17.
In the state of maintenance, Viṣṇu, the all-conquering soul of the gods,
who possesses the nature of the qualities and the sense of ego within the portion of Brahmā and others, sustains the worlds, the virtuous, and the bridges of dharma.
I bow to that Supreme Lord, whose limbs are sound and the rest,
by whose command the winds blow in the world,
the fire blazes, and the sun moves along, scorching with heat.
The cool-rayed moon moves in the sky along with the planets and the Nārakas; I take refuge in that Supreme Lord, by whose breath the earth, the sustainer of all, exists. 19.19
The god rains water at the proper time; he is the measurer and the sustainer of the worlds in their midst—to that Īśāna, whose form is the universe, I bow. 20.
Having heard this hymn of Kalki, Śiva, who perceives the Self in all,
spoke directly and laughingly at night before Pārvatī,
joyfully touching every limb of Kalki with his hand.
He said to him: "Choose, O dearest one, whatever boon you desire.
For those people on earth who recite this hymn composed by you, there shall be the accomplishment of all their aims, both in this world and in the next."
A seeker of knowledge shall obtain knowledge, a seeker of dharma shall obtain dharma,

and one who desires objects of desire shall attain them, simply by reading or even hearing this. You [shall receive] this Gāruḍa [mantra], as well as a horse that moves at will and assumes many forms.
"O sir, accept this parrot, who has been given by me; he is omniscient.
Men shall call you a destroyer of all scriptures and weapons, one who has reached the further shore of the meaning of all Vedas, and a conqueror of all beings. (25-26)
"Take this sword with its jewel-encrusted hilt, formidable and of great luster, which shall serve to relieve the heavy burden of the earth.
Having heard these words and having paid homage to Maheśvara, [he took it].
He went to the village of Śambhala on horseback with great haste.
Having paid homage to his father, mother, and brothers according to the prescribed rites, he related everything that the son of Jamadagni had said. ||28-29||
Having related the granting of boons by Śiva and other auspicious stories, the supremely radiant Kalki joyfully spoke to his kinsmen;
Gārgya, Bhargya, Viśāla, and the others, having heard that, remained there filled with delight.
A conversation arose among the inhabitants of the village of Śambhala.
Having heard their speech, King Viśākhayūpa considered the manifestation of Hari to be the means for the suppression of the Kali age.
Seeing that in his own city of Māhiṣmatī, even the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras were dear to Hari and devoted to their own duties through sacrifices, gifts, austerities, and vows,
the king himself became most righteous.
Because of the manifestation of the Lord of Śrī, the protector of subjects became pure-minded;
seeing those people devoted to righteous deeds, the descendants of unrighteousness—greed, falsehood, and the rest—departed from that land, afflicted by sorrow and fear. (34–35)
Having mounted his victorious steed and taken up his sword of stainless luster,
as well as his bow with arrows,
King Viśākhayūpa— beloved by virtuous people— went forth from the city, fully armored. (36)
Accompanied by the wise and learned Sumantu, and preceded by the highly effulgent Kavi, he went to see Kalki— the portion of Hari manifested in Śambhala—
surrounded by his kinsmen, Gārgya, Bhargya, and Viśāla.
Viśākha-yūpa beheld Candra outside the city, like Indra being gazed upon by the gods from afar, while Uccaiḥśravas stood nearby;
Viśākha-yūpa bowed down, his hair standing on end with joy. (39)
Upon seeing Kalki, he immediately became a Vaiṣṇava whose self was perfected.
Dwelling together with the king, Kalki proclaimed the duties previously mentioned for the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, as well as for the stages of life (āśramas), in brief.
"Perform the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices with a concentrated mind, worshipping me as those portions of mine that have been lost in the Kali age and are now united through my incarnation.
I alone am the supreme in the world, and I am the eternal Dharma."
Time, inherent nature, and the formative forces are my followers of karma.
Having established Devāpi and Maru, born in the lineages of the Moon and the Sun, and having brought about the Kṛta Yuga, I shall go to the state of eternal bliss.
Having heard those words, King Kalki bowed down to the Lord Hari and spoke of the Vaiṣṇava truths of the true dharma that were desired by his mind.
(45) Having heard these words of the king, Kalki— the incarnation whose latent purpose was the destruction of the Kali age— [proceeded].
Delighting his own assembly with sweet words, he spoke of the excellent dharmas.
(46) Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Attainment of the Boon from Kalki," in the glorious *Kalki Purāṇa*, within the section concerning the future.
Chapter Four.
Sūta said:
Then Kalki, shining like the sun in the midst of the assembly,
spoke to that king about the duties dear to the twice-born, being himself the embodiment of dharma.
Kalki said:
"At the time of the dissolution of Brahmā at the end of the aeon, all things were merged into me;
I alone existed in the beginning, and this entire creation was not other than myself. (2)
When the world-machine was fast asleep and the Self was devoid of duality, at the end of the great night, the Lord Virāṭ arose from me to sport;
he is the Puruṣa with a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet.
From that [portion] was born Brahmā, the great lord, whose mouth is the Veda;

he is the embodiment of Brahman, omniscient, and governed by my speech, the Veda, through my own portion as the limiting adjunct of the individual soul (jīva) and by means of my own nature, Māyā. ||4-5||
Through the conjunction of time, *māyā*, and his own portions (*aṃśa*), the Lord emitted the various classes of living beings—
the gods, the Manus and others, the worlds, and the Prajāpatis.
By means of *māyā*, which possesses qualities (*guṇinī*), he created my portions within various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
These worlds, along with their conditions, the gods, and all things stationary and moving,
are portions of me created by my *māyā*, since they enter into me at the time of dissolution.
Those Brahmins who are of this nature are my body and have me as their self.
In this world, sacrifices, Vedic study, and virtuous deeds uplift me;
here, penance, charity, and ritual acts serve me and praise me.
They remember me and indeed gladden me; other gods and such beings do not act in this way.
The Brahmins are the speakers of the Vedas; the Vedas are my supreme forms.
Therefore, these people born as Brahmins nourish the inhabitants of the three worlds.
The worlds are my bodies; thus, the maintenance of the Brahmins is the highest boon for Brahmā.
Therefore, I, who am the refuge of the qualities of pure beings, pay homage to them;
consequently, all those who take refuge in me first serve me, who am composed of the universe.
Viśākhayūpa said:
"Tell me the characteristics of a Brahmin, and what constitutes devotion to you, by which [devotion] the Brahmins were made into word-arrows through your grace. Kalki said:
The Vedas declare me to be the Lord, unmanifest yet possessing manifestation, supreme; those Vedas have been revealed through various duties in the mouths of the Brāhmaṇas.
Indeed, that which is the duty of the Brāhmaṇas is my abundant devotion.
Pleased by her, I, the Lord of Śrī, manifest in age after age.
The wise know the sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*) to be that which has three strands wound upwards, slowly fashioned by a virtuous woman, with three threads coiled downwards. ||15-16||

It should be triple-stranded, provided with knots, and measured according to the excellence of the Vedas; it should extend from the neck to the middle of the navel, with its length equal to half the back.
For those who know the Yajurveda, it is measured to the navel; this is the rule for the chanters of the Sāmaveda.
The sacred thread (*yajñasūtra*) held over the left shoulder bestows strength.

A twice-born man should apply a *tilaka* with clay, ashes, sandalwood, and so forth; on his forehead, he should bear the bright triple-mark (*tripuṇḍra*), which is an integral part of ritual action and extends to the hairline.
The *puṇḍra* is the measure of a finger; that triple *puṇḍra* is divided into three parts.
It is the abode of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, and it destroys sins merely by being seen.
(20) For Brahmins, heaven is in their hands, the Vedas are in their hands, and Hari is in their hands.
The sacred fords (*tīrtha*) are on the limbs, the passions (*rāga*) are in the channels (*nāḍī*), and the threefold primordial nature (*prakṛti*) resides there.
*Sāvitrī* is in the hollow of the throat, and the heart is known as *Brahman*.
Between their breasts is *Dharma*, and *Adharma* is proclaimed to be on the back.
O King, the earthly gods, the Brahmins, are worthy of worship and salutation with well-spoken words; they are skilled in the four stages of life and are the promoters of my dharma.
Even those who are young, yet matured in knowledge and matured in austerity, are dear to me.
In order to fulfill their word, I have taken incarnations.
Having heard this great glory of the Brahmins— which destroys all sins and removes the defects of the Kali age— one is liberated from every fear.
Having heard these words of Kalki, which destroy the defects of the Kali age,
that leader of the Vaiṣṇavas, with a pure mind, bowed to him and departed.
When the king had gone, at twilight, the wise Śivadattaśuka—
Having wandered about and offered praise before Kalki, he stood before him. Then Kalki spoke with a smile to that parrot who had recited the hymn:
"Welcome! From which country have you come, and what did you eat there?"
Śuka said:
Listen, O Lord, to my words filled with curiosity;
I went into the midst of the ocean to the place known as Siṃhala. (29)

This wonderful account of King Bṛhadratha’s daughter, as it actually occurred on the island, is pleasing to the ear— an ambrosial narrative that destroys the sins of the worlds when heard during the Kaumudī festival. 30.130
The life story [took place] on the island of Siṃhala, which was filled with people of the four castes, resplendent with rows of cities, palaces, mansions, and dwellings,
and adorned with golden creepers upon walls made of jewels and crystal. ||31-32||
It was surrounded by lakes filled with women of exquisite attire who were like lotus-ponds,
their waters crowded near the banks by cranes and swans; it was rich with the activity of bees and abounded in lotuses, white water-lilies, and jasmine flowers.
In a region adorned with various groves of lotus-stalks and forest parks,
there was a king named Bṛhadratha, possessed of great strength and prowess;
his daughter, the fortunate and illustrious Padmāvatī, shone forth.

In this world, she is difficult to find; peerless in the universe, a woman of excellent complexion, she who deludes with passion, of beautiful conduct, and fashioned like a wondrous creation—Gaurī, devoted to the service of Śiva, is as worthy of worship and highly esteemed. (36)
Engaged in silent recitation and meditation along with her female friends and maidens, she perceived that Lakṣmī of Hari had become an excellent woman;
then Hara, together with Pārvatī, appeared visibly before her, filled with joy. ||37-38||

Beholding Śiva, the bestower of boons, accompanied by Gaurī, she stood before him with her face slightly cast down in modesty and said nothing. Hara said to her: "O blessed one, Nārāyaṇa is your husband."
No other prince in the world is as worthy as he to take her hand with joy.
Furthermore, those men in the world who behold you with amorous intent shall instantly become women at that very same age.
It is said that the gods, asuras, nāgas, gandharvas, cāraṇas,
and others shall at the proper time have women with whom to sport,
except for the god Nārāyaṇa, who seeks to take your hand in marriage.
"Go home, abandoning your asceticism, to this supreme abode of enjoyment.
Do not disturb the consort of Hara; O Kamalā, remain pure.
Having granted this boon, Soma, who is Hara, vanished right there.

Having heard those words, "A boon from Hara," Padmā— the beautiful woman— her face blossoming with joy at hearing what was appropriate for her heart's desire, bowed to Soma and entered the abode of her own father.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Bestowing of the Boon by Hara," in the glorious *Anubhāgavata*, the future *Kalki Purāṇa*.
The Fifth Chapter.
Śuka said:
After a long period of time had passed, Bṛhadratha beheld Padmā.
Astonished and fearing some evil, he said to his queen Kaumudī, whose youth was fully matured:
"O fortunate lady, which king endowed with noble lineage and character shall I choose here for the marriage of Padmā?"
The goddess spoke these auspicious words to her husband:
"Viṣṇu shall be her husband; of this there is no doubt.
Having heard her speech, the king asked her, "When?"
"Viṣṇu, who dwells within the heart of all, will take her hand.
I have no such rise of fortune by which I might choose Hari as my son-in-law for the sake of my daughter Vedavatī, as did the sage."
"Just as Viṣṇu seized Padmā during the churning of the great ocean by the gods and asuras, he shall likewise seize this Padmā at her svayaṃvara.
Having thus addressed the assembled hosts of kings, the monarch summoned them forward.
Having deliberated upon those endowed with virtue, character, age, beauty, learning, and wealth,
he had a residence for kings constructed in the highly auspicious island of Siṃhala for the sake of Padmā’s svayaṃvara. ||7-8||
There all the kings arrived, having resolved upon the marriage; surrounded by their own armies, adorned with gold and jewels,
those mighty ones mounted chariots, elephants, and excellent horses.
Shaded by white umbrellas and fanned with white chowries, they shone with the brilliance of weapons and missiles, appearing like the gods led by Indra.
Rucirāśva, Sukarman, Madirākṣa, and Dṛḍhāśuga were there as well. ||10-11||
Kṛṣṇasāra, Pārada, Jīmūta, Krūramardana,
Kāśa, Kuśāmbu, Vasumān, Kaṅka, Kathana,
Sañjaya, Gurumitra, Pramāthin, Vijṛmbha, Sṛñjaya, and Akṣama. (12)
These and many other mighty ones arrived;
honored and delighted by the celebrated tāṇḍava dance, wearing wonderful garlands and garments, they entered the arena and took their respective places. ||13-14||

Beholding those women who were overflowing with the pleasure of various enjoyments, delighting in sensual desires, and bestowing rapture— the King of Siṃhala [beheld] his own daughter, a woman of excellent complexion,
fair as Gaurī, moon-faced, youthful, and adorned with a necklace of pearls.
Adorned on all her limbs with jewels, pearls, and corals, she was auspicious;
was she the illusion that produces delusion, or perhaps Rati, the beloved of Kāma, for I have seen no other woman on earth endowed with such perfection of beauty and grace? (16–17)
Whether in heaven, on earth, or even in the netherworld, though I am omnipresent,
I shall later see her— surrounded by her female companions and throngs of maidservants—
being driven out from the inner apartments by guards with staffs in their hands.
She slowly reached that city, which was crowded with throngs of prisoners before her, enchanting the people with the tinkling of her anklets and small bells,
and [proclaiming] the many noble lineages, characters, and virtues of the kings who had welcomed her.
Moving with the gait of a swan, holding a jewel necklace in her hand, she listened while looking with a graceful arch of her beautiful eyes; adorned with dangling earrings,
she was graced by the circular expanse of her cheeks and her dancing locks of hair.
Her face illuminated by the luster of her teeth shining with a slight smile,
wearing a crimson silk garment upon her altar-like waist, and possessing a voice like the song of the cuckoo,
she seemed desirous of purchasing the three worlds with the merchandise of her beauty and grace.

Beholding her approaching, those kings—whose minds were deluded by desire—fell to the ground, forgetting their garments and weapons; they collapsed along with their chariots, horses, elephants, and mounts.
By the mere sight of her, which agitated the god of love, even women of lovely form became [overwhelmed].
Bowed by the weight of their broad hips and breasts, possessing slender waists, and appearing as if they were born from the memory of her form;
with faces full of grace, lips devoted to smiles, and eyes like red lotuses—the kings, beholding themselves in the form of women, followed after her with pure devotion. (25–26)

Standing upon the banyan tree, my soul overwhelmed and agitated by the sight of the festival for the marriage of Padmā, I remained there to hear the words of that sorrowful woman, while those men—due to their male nature—were unaware of her presence.
"O Kalki, abandon this impure lamentation; you have heard the wondrous history of the worlds, O Lord. (27)
When the auspicious festival of her marriage had departed, she placed Śiva, the refuge, within her heart;

then, seeing those kings— abandoned by their elephants, horses, and chariots, having entered into friendship with her, and now following her, endowed with feminine nature— as they stood near Padmā, [she was moved].
Dejected, having cast off her ornaments, that lovely woman scratched the ground with her toes;
wishing to make her own lord the Master, she remembered Hari, the truth of whose words as the Lord [had been proclaimed].
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Kings Becoming Women," in the Padmā-svayaṃvara section of the glorious *Anubhāgavata*, the future *Kalki Purāṇa*.
The Sixth Chapter. Śuka said:
Then Padmā, her face filled with wonder, surrounded by her own people, [spoke].
Meditating upon Hari as her husband, she spoke to Vimalā who was standing there:
"O Vimalā, what has the Creator done by writing this on my forehead— that even from the sight of me, men in the worlds are made to take on the state of women?"
For me too, unfortunate and sinful as I am, service to Śiva has come to fruitionlessness, like a seed sown in barren soil.
Hari, the lord of Lakṣmī, the sovereign and master of all the worlds—
"Even for my sake, what will the Lord of the World do?
If the word of Śambhu is false, and if Viṣṇu does not remember me,
then I, devoted to Hari, shall cast off my body into the fire."
Where am I, a miserable human woman, and where dwells the divine Janārdana?
I have been seized by Fate and utterly deceived by Śiva;
abandoned by Viṣṇu as well, who else but me lives here?
Having heard these words of lamentation, which were the refuge of her grief, from Padmā of beautiful gestures, [Kalki] has come into your presence.
Having heard the words of Śuka, Kalki was greatly amazed.
He said to him again, "Go once more to awaken my beloved Padmā;
having become the bearer of my message and having caused her to hear the praise of my form and virtues, O parrot, you shall return again, my friend. (9-10)
"She is dear to me, and I am her husband, ordained by fate; through you, who stand as a mediator, there shall be a union between us.
You are all-knowing, you are a knower of the sacred ordinances, and you are a knower of time; [speak] with the nectar of your words."
"Console her by recounting stories that bring me comfort.
Having heard these words of Kalki, Śuka was greatly delighted;
bowing to him with a joyful mind, he set out for Siṃhala.
Having bathed on the far shore of the ocean and drunk the nectar-like water, the bird,
subsisting on the fruit of the citron tree, went to the king’s residence.
Having gone there to the inner apartments of the women and staying in a tree sacred to Nāgeśvara, he remained there.
Beholding Padmā, the parrot spoke to her in human speech:
"Is it well with you, O lady of excellent hips, endowed with beauty and youth?
I consider you, with your tremulous eyes, to be like another Lakṣmī herself. (15-16)
I perceive you, with a lotus-face, the fragrance of a lotus, and lotus-eyes, holding a lotus in your lotus-hand, as the supreme Śrī;
are you not the very embodiment of the wealth of beauty and charm of all the worlds created by the Dhātṛ? (17)
"O lady of excellent limbs, you have been created as the one who causes delusion to living beings.
Having heard these immeasurably wonderful words spoken by Kīra,
the goddess Padmā, adorned with a garland of lotuses, laughed and said to him:
"Who are you? From where have you come? How is it that you have come to me in the form of a parrot? Are you a god or a dānava who has arrived here out of compassion? Śuka said:
"I am omniscient, moving at will, and a knower of the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures;
I am fully honored in the assemblies of gods, gandharvas, and kings. I roam through the sky according to my own desire, and have come here for the sake of beholding you. (21)
Seeing you— tormented in heart, having renounced all enjoyments, high-minded,
and deprived of the company of friends, of playful conversation, and of bodily ornaments— I, with a distressed mind, ask you to speak so that I may hear your words.
Sweet and soft, producing a cooling relief for the heat of the cuckoo’s song—
what can be said of the penance of those into whose ear-cavities the rows of syllables tumbling from the tips of your teeth, lips, and tongue have sunk? (23–24)
Where is the tenderness of the *śirīṣa* flower, or where is the splendor of the moon?
What will he produce by means of those futile austerities, gifts, and recitations?
For those who behold his face—adorned with dangling earrings, marked by freckles and moles, and radiant with its flickering eyes—there shall be no further rebirth. (26–27)
"O beautiful lady, daughter of Bṛhadratha, tell me the reason for this,
since I perceive your body to be as if wasted by penance, though free from illness— like a golden image soiled with dust. (28)
Padmā said:
"What is the use of beauty, lineage, wealth, or noble birth?
All these become fruitless for one whose destiny is unfavorable. (29)
"Listen, parrot, to this narrative, or perhaps it is already known to you:
'In my childhood, youth, and adolescence, I performed service to Hara.
Being pleased by that performance of worship, Maheśvara..."
"Choose a boon, O Padmā," said Śaṅkara to me as I stood before him with my face cast down in shame in the presence of his beloved. He then declared: "The Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa shall be your husband."
"Whether a god, a dānava, or another being such as a gandharva, by the mere glance of your mind with desire, a woman shall come into being; of this there is no doubt.
Having thus granted the boon, Soma spoke words of praise for Viṣṇu.
Thus I shall speak to you; listen with a concentrated mind.
O kings, these were my friends who were previously brought here by my father, seeking merit, when he saw that I was beautiful and endowed with youth. (34-35)
"Welcome to you, who have come here with the firm resolve to marry;
you are young, virtuous, and esteemed for your beauty and wealth. Having beheld me, of radiant splendor, as I stand here at my *svayaṃvara*..."
With their hands resting upon jeweled garlands, they fell down, utterly deluded by desire.
Then, rising up in agitation and perceiving their own womanhood, they were bent forward by the weight of their breasts and their heavy hips. ||37-38||
O Śuka, out of shame and fear of their enemies, and reflecting in their minds upon this female state which brings such extreme suffering even to friends, they have followed me alone;
these companions, devoted to Hara, are endowed with every virtue and worthy of service.
"Those esteemed ones perform austerity, meditation, and worship together with me.

Having heard that speech, which was pleasant to the ear and illuminated his own mind, the parrot, honoring Padmā with appropriate words, spoke again regarding the worship of the Lord of the Mountain (Śiva). 41.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Śrī Kalki Purāṇa, the Anubhāgavata, in the future section, within the dialogue between Śuka and Padmā.
Chapter Seven. Śuka said:
"O auspicious one, I wish to hear the worship of Viṣṇu as spoken by Śiva.
You are blessed and have performed meritorious deeds, for you have attained the status of being a disciple of Śiva. By the power of my good fortune, I have come here into your presence."
I joyfully hear of the most wonderful means for warding off the state of being a bird-eater (kīra),
as well as the yoga of devotion to the Blessed One and the rules for recitation and meditation— which are dear to the Vedas and skilled in bestowing a mass of supreme bliss.
Padmā said:
The worship of Śrī Viṣṇu, which has been described by Śiva as meritorious— whether it be heard, recited, or performed with faith—
immediately removes the sins of men, even those who have killed their gurus, cows, or brahmins.
Listen with a concentrated mind, O parrot, to that which has been spoken.
Having performed the prescribed rites, pure from bathing in the forenoon, and having washed both hands and feet and touched water, one should sit upon one's seat. (5–6)
Facing the east with a restrained mind, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) along with its ancillaries (*aṅga*).
Then, one should duly carry out the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and the installation of the *arghya* water.
Thereafter, through the ritual placement beginning with Keśava-kṛtya and the others, one should become absorbed in that [deity].

Having meditated upon himself as being identical with that [deity] residing in his heart, the preceptor should place [the deity] upon his own seat. Having worshipped [the deity] with the root mantra according to the prescribed services—beginning with water for the feet, the arghya offering, and water for sipping, and including bathing, garments, and ornaments—[he should proceed]. || 8-9 ||

One should meditate upon the Lord, who resides in the center of the heart-lotus, from the feet up to the tips of the hair, with a serene countenance, bestowing the fruits of the desires of his devotees. Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya svāhā.
Meditated upon by perfected beings through yoga,
the abode of Lakṣmī, where the bees of devotees are adorned by tulasī,
and which is variegated with the petals of its tall, red nails and fingers—
I take refuge in the lotus-feet of Hari, which possess the essence of the Gaṅgā.
I meditate upon the stalk of Hari’s lotus-feet, joined with beautiful anklets that sprinkle water as they strike the royal swans formed by the clusters of interlaced jewels;
and I remember his yellow garment, which flutters like a waving banner, and his three-fold golden bracelets.
His shanks were like the necks of Garuḍa, adorned with large sapphire gems;
they were radiant with the luster of beautiful, deep-red jewels and graced by the hanging beauty of his slightly reddened soles.

I remember the two knees of Hari, which cause a festival for the eyes of the world, whose variegated garments are like flashes of lightning amidst the embrace of the arms of the Lord of Sacrifice, and which have spread his own fame through the Sāman chants emerging from the mouths of the dancing celestial beings. I remember those two knees of Hari. 14.
[She who is] Viṣṇu’s hip, the ground for Brahmā, Yama, and Kāma;
whose middle is clothed in the fine silk of the multitude of living beings gathered within the cosmic egg;
and who wears variegated garments of yellow hue, representing the primordial nature (prakṛti) with its manifold qualities.
One should meditate upon her, dressed in garments and seated upon the back of a bird;
she has a slender waist marked by three folds, and her navel is a whorl from which the lotus of Brahmā’s birth expands.
I meditate upon Him who dwells within the cosmic egg, whose white entrails are like a river flowing from the juices of the multitude of channels, and whose fine body-hairs form its ripples;
His chest is illuminated by the saffron from the breasts of Lakṣmī, the daughter of the Ocean, and by the radiance of the Kaustubha gem.
I remember the auspicious mark of Śrīvatsa on the Blessed One’s chest, adorned with a garland of yellow sandalwood flowers.

(17) I remember with my mind those two beautiful right arms of the Blessed One—the abodes of fine attire, the locus of the splendor of bracelets, armlets, and other ornaments, capable of destroying the Daityas who are evil-doers, and strengthened by the power of the mace and the navel-jewel. (18)
The two left arms of the enemy of Mura hold the lotus and the conch; they are dark-hued, richly adorned with jewels like the trunks of lordly elephants,
and their clusters of red-fingernails touch the middle of his knees.
I remember his two beautiful hands, which are dear to her whose abode is the lotus;
I remember his throat, as stainless as a lotus stalk, encircled by the three lines and the forest garland upon his lotus-face.
Or rather, I long remember the auspicious stalk of the Blessed One, which bears as its fruit the true realization of the mantra-master who has attained liberation—
his lotus-face, made beautiful by the blossoming of his teeth and smile. (20)

I remember Hari’s face, which is delightful to the world and stainless; it is enriched by the nectar of speech from his excellent, soft, red lower lip, and is variegated by the moving petals of his eyes born of a noble mind. 21.
To him who knows the fragrance of the abode of the Sun’s son (Hanumān), who possesses a beautiful nose,
whose leaf-like eyebrows are skilled in the acts of maintenance, dissolution, and creation,
who is the festival of desire, and who illuminates the heart of Kamalā—
I contemplate those ears, which are skilled in the play of the lion’s face, shimmering with crocodile-shaped earrings upon their cheeks,
and which serve as expansive dwellings for the various directions and the sky.
I remember the two [earrings] whose tips are curved from kissing the mass of Her playful locks,

resting upon the edge of Hari’s jeweled crown; I remember His forehead with its wonderful tilaka, which, through the application of lovely-smelling gorocana by His beloved, has become a friend to the eyes of women.

One should meditate upon the Lord’s hair, which captivates both mind and eye, adorned with a crown as radiant as the jewel of the abode of Brahmā, and bound with various fragrant flowers out of affection for His own people.
24. Śrī Vāsudeva’s curly locks are tied with many kinds of sweet-smelling blossoms out of regard for His kin.

I meditate upon Him, who is as beautiful as a water-bearing cloud, who dwells within the lotus of my heart, who is the long-lasting pacifier of the heart’s desires, and who possesses beautiful eyebrows and a nose that is the sole measure of the bow of Indra’s chariot; He who shines with the brilliance of the moon and the sun. 25.25–26ab.
I take refuge in You, who transcend the world, whose eyes are as long as lotus petals, and who are clothed in lightning—You who are unprecedented.
My body is filled with sins and torments, made wretched and base by my service to Vedavatī;
overcome by greed and pierced by grief and delusion, protect me with Your compassionate glance, O Vāsudeva!

Those who know the ritual procedure, having praised, bowed to, and worshipped with the flowers of sixteen verses that beautiful manifestation of Viṣṇu being meditated upon with devotion and other virtues— being pure, they are liberated and attain the bliss of Brahman.
This meritorious [work] was spoken by Padma and expounded by Śiva.
Those fortunate ones who recite this— which is auspicious, conducive to fame, longevity, and heaven, and the supreme means of securing well-being— are liberated from all sin;
it bestows the fruits of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa both in this world and the next.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of Devotion to Hari," in the glorious Kalki Purāṇa, an Anubhāgavata of the future. ||7||
And this first part is completed.
The Second Part.
The First Chapter.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of Padmā, the parrot, who was steadfast and esteemed by the virtuous, [spoke].
Then Kalkidūta spoke to Padmā, who was standing in the midst of her friends:
"Tell me, Padmā, the complete worship of Hari of wondrous deeds,
by following which according to the prescribed rite I wander through the three worlds."
Padmā said:
Having thus meditated upon that Lord of the World from his feet to the tips of his hair, the preceptor, a knower of mantras whose self is perfected, recites the root mantra.
After the recitation, the wise practitioner should perform prostration with the staff-like body,
having offered what was dedicated to Viṣṇu to Viṣvaksena and the others;
then, having dismissed them, he should bathe them within his own heart along with his mind.
Dancing, singing the name of Hari, and beholding Him present everywhere,
one should then place Śeṣa upon one's head and partake of the food offering (naivedya).
Thus, O parrot, has this service of the Lord of Kamalā been described.
It fulfills the desires of those with longing and bestows the nectar of immortality upon those without desire;
it brings joy to the ears and is dear to the hearts of gods, gandharvas, and men.
Śuka said:
O virtuous lady, by your grace, I have heard from you that which is proclaimed as the characteristic of devotion to the Lord, which grants liberation on earth even to a sinner like me, Kīra.
However, [I have not seen] you, who are like a golden image adorned with jewels.
I see you as if you were Śrī herself in embodied form, difficult to find;
I see no other woman equal to you in beauty, character, and virtue.
No other virtuous husband worthy of you is to be seen even in this entire world.
But beyond the ocean, there was seen directly a certain superhuman being, most wonderful in form and endowed with virtues—
an embodied being whose every limb was beautiful, whom I do not consider to have been created by the Creator alone. (11)
For that glorious Vāsudeva, there is no interval [of difference] from the perspective of meditative yoga.
That form of Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor which was meditated upon by you has been directly realized; in that regard, what difference could there possibly be? (12–13)
Padmā said:
"Tell me that; O parrot, where were you born? You know both the higher and the lower, so describe here in detail the karma performed by him."
"Come from the tree; I shall perform worship for you according to the prescribed rites. Eat this citron fruit and drink the water well.
Your pair of beaks is brilliant and red like rubies. (15)
I shall make your neck, fashioned from a cluster of gems, dear to the mind;
with a sunstone set in gold, I shall make a covering for it, and your wing-base with beautiful pearls. (16–17)
With my body adorned with saffron and its fragrance, I shall assume such a form that brings joy to the eyes; it is made resonant by the tinkling of a multitude of jewels upon my tail. 18.
I shall make you speak with the tinkling of anklets upon your feet.
Teach me here how to abandon all mental anguish through the flood of your nectar-like words;
tell me, what shall I do with your friends who are gathered together? 19–20.
Having heard these words of Padmā, the wise parrot approached her presence and, with a tranquil mind, began to speak.
The parrot said:
Entreated by Brahmā, the Lord of Śrī, the Greatly Compassionate One, desiring to protect the Dharma, appeared in the house of Viṣṇuyaśas in Śambhala,
surrounded by his four brothers born of the same lineage and clan. (22)
Having performed his initiation and studied the Vedas in the presence of Rāma,
and having received from Śiva the science of archery, music, horses, swords, arrows, armor, and boons, he returned once more to Śambhala. ||23-24||
"Having approached King Viśākhayūpa, the wise one [the Buddha], by means of his specific instructions, proclaimed the dharmas and refuted unrighteousness.
Having heard this account, Padmā’s face was bright with joy.
Eager to bring back Kalki, Padmā sent Śuka forth;
having adorned him with gold and jewels, she spoke to him with palms joined in reverence.
Padmā said:
"You already know what has been reported; what else shall I say?
My soul is terrified by the fear of my female state, yet if that Lord does not come, you must nevertheless convey my prostration [to him] on account of the fault of my past actions."
"That very boon which was granted by Śiva has indeed become a curse for me," O parrot. Having heard this, he addressed Padmā and bowed down to her again and again. ||29-30||
Flying up, the parrot went to Śambhala, which was ruled by Kalki.
Hearing that he had arrived, Kalki, the conqueror of enemy cities,
took him upon his lap and beheld him adorned with gold and jewels.
Then Kalki, possessed of supreme splendor, spoke joyfully to him who bestows the highest bliss;
having honored the stainless Śuka in the highest manner and touched him with his hand, he gratified him by offering water for drinking.
Placing his own face against his [the other's] face, he asked various questions:
"From which country have you come after traveling about? What unprecedented thing did you see? Where did you stay, and from where was this jeweled gold ornament obtained?"
"My desire is for union with you day and night in every respect;
even a single moment without beholding you would become like an eon for me.
Having heard these words of Kalki, Śuka prostrated himself deeply.
He related the stories of Padmā as they had been told before; he described their entire conversation, including her wearing his own ornaments,
all preceded by her prostration to him.
Having heard these words, Kalki, accompanied by Śuka and with his mind fixed on that goal, joyfully and swiftly departed on the horse Śivadatta toward the pure island of Siṃhala,
which lies across the ocean and is filled with water.
Abounding in various celestial mansions, radiant with jewels and gold,
crowded at the tops of its palaces and dwellings with banners and arches, and adorned with rows of shops, assembly halls, markets, palm groves, cities, and gate-towers. ||40-41||
There he beheld before him the city of Kārumatī, which was filled with bees attracted by the fragrance of the lotus-scented women who were like lotuses;
its interior lakes were shimmering with clusters of swaying lotuses moved by flocks of swans.
He beheld a lake whose waters were agitated by swarms of bees hovering over blossoming lotuses;
it resounded with the cries of wild cocks, water-fowls, and cranes, and was fanned by waves rippling upon its clear surface. ||43-44||
The forest [was filled] with kadamba, kudāla, śāla, tāla, āmra, and kesarī;
with kapittha, aśvattha, kharjūra, bījapūraka, and rañjaka; and with punnāga, panasa, nāgaraṅga, arjuna, and śiṃśapa trees. ||45||
He beheld a beautiful forest adorned with betel-nut trees, coconuts, and various other trees,
covered with fruits, flowers, and leaves. Seeing this,
Kalki’s body thrilled with joy, and filled with compassion for Śuka, he entered the forest at the edge of the city.
There, with great respect, he spoke these pleasing words: "One must bathe here in this lake.
Having heard that, the parrot, filled with humility, said to his master, "I am going to Padmāśrama," and having now departed from here on his mission, he related that message.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Arrival of Kalki," in the second part of the *Śrī Kalki Purāṇa*, an Anubhāgavata of the future.
Chapter Two.
Sūta said:
Near the lake, along the path for fetching water,
stood a crystal staircase with a pedestal inlaid with coral,
resounding with the humming of bees distracted by the fragrance of lotuses. ||1||
When the sight of the sun was obscured by the rows of petals from the young *kadamba* trees,
Kalki, having been dismounted from his noble steed, sat upon a variegated seat and joyfully dispatched Śuka to the hermitage of Padma.
Having gone there, Śuka, standing amidst the lords of the nāgas, beheld her seated upon the palace roof,
reclining on lotus leaves and surrounded by her female companions;
her lotus-like face was withering from the heat of the sighs she breathed.
She was tossing a lotus offered by her friend, which was anointed with sandalwood paste;
she had come after bathing in the waters of the Revā, her face covered in pollen;
she held water in her hand and, having attained a state of aesthetic rapture, she was reproaching her beloved for being like the wind.
Śuka, filled with compassion, gratified her with words of praise: "Come, come! May it be well with you; welcome, may there be prosperity for me, O auspicious one!
While you were away, I was deeply distressed; may you find peace through this elixir."
"The elixir of rejuvenation is difficult for me to obtain, yet it is easily accessible to you in this hermitage of Śiva.
O lady of excellent complexion, where am I, devoid of fortune?
O Goddess, we have returned here after having installed it on the very bank of this lake."
Thus, with their hearts’ desires delighted by their mutual conversation, she gave her face to his face and her eye to his eye in a perfect likeness—
she who was stainless, garlanded, restless, lotus-like, and the very sprout of desire.
Vilāsinī, Cārumatī, and Kumudā—these are considered the eight heroines.
When they were prepared for a water-sport, Padmā said to her friends: "Let these women come to the shore of the lake with me. ||11-12||

Having spoken thus, she quickly mounted a palanquin and, surrounded by her friends who were dressed in beautiful attire, went out from her inner apartments in haste to see Bhaimī, just as the Lord of the Yadus had gone to see her.

The men who were standing ahead on the road fled toward the various quarters out of fear of her womanhood; and those who were situated at the crossroads or in the marketplaces, having placed their meritorious deeds upon their own limbs, were likewise [frightened].
The women carrying that palanquin, though exceedingly intoxicated and very powerful, were restrained.

At Śuka’s words, Padmā approached that place, surrounded by those [other women]. 15 They quickly entered the lake water, which resounded with the cries of cranes and swans and was perfumed by the pollen arising from full-blown lotuses; radiant as the moon, those beautiful women moved about for the sake of the blossoming lilies. 16

Blinded by the intoxication of the fragrance from their mouths, bees abandoned the lotuses to cling to their lotus-like faces; even when warded off, they did not leave them, perceiving the scent to be superior.
With laughter and jests, charming displays, musical instruments, dances, and aquatic sports—
As those women, distressed by the water-fight, pulled at her with their hands,

Padmā, tormented by love, reflected upon the words of Śuka in her mind; then, rising from the water and adorned with costly ornaments, she went together with her friends to the designated grove of Kadamba trees.
He gazed upon that Lord, who was reclining on his face upon a jeweled pedestal before him, possessing a splendor exceeding the sun;
adorned with a multitude of great jewels, he looked toward the Auspicious One together with Śukī—
himself dark as a tamāla tree, the Lord of Kamalā, wearing yellow garments, and having beautiful lotus-eyes.
With arms reaching to his knees and a broad, full chest, adorned by the splendor of the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha gem—
beholding that wondrous form, Padmā was struck with paralysis, forgetting her intended rites;
yet, as he proceeded to awaken the sleeping one, she, her soul filled with apprehension, restrained him.

"Perhaps this one of exceeding strength and exceeding beauty will, upon seeing me, manifest his womanhood before my very eyes. Then what would become of me in this world through a boon from Bhava that is equivalent to a curse?
Having awakened the Self of the moving and unmoving, the Lord of the worlds, he has discerned that heart of mine."
He beheld Padmā, whose beauty was as pleasing as that of Ramā in the presence of Śrī Madhusūdana.
Having gazed upon her— who was like a deluding Māyā— Kalki, agitated by desire,
spoke to that mistress who had approached with her companions, her face lowered by the casting of side-long glances.
"Welcome here! By good fortune, may this meeting with you lead to my well-being.

O beloved, your moon-like face is indeed for dispelling the fever of Kāma and for the happiness of this Creator, who has been bitten by the serpent of desire. O tremulous-eyed one, the nectar-essence of your beauty [is for him]. [26]
May this rite, performed with merit, extend peace—so difficult to obtain—for one who has taken refuge in life.
May these two arms of yours, so pleasing to the mind, fulfill the desire residing in your heart;
like a rider with beautiful, long arms and the hook of his lovely nails rending the temples of an elephant.
These two breasts of yours, rising like peaks and covered by your garment like the two goads of Kāma,
having shattered my own pride upon my chest— may these two well-rounded orbs grant me what is dear.
This triple-fold of the beloved’s waist is a staircase marked by the line of body hair, as if delineated by a thread.
May this beloved dwelling of Kāma, its center fixed upon the altar of her waist, be divided for my pleasure.

O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, may your orb-like hips, resembling a sandy bank, be for the sake of the bliss of union; O slender-limbed one, may they possess the beauty of clinging fine silken garments and serve as the sole arena for the exuberant exertion of intoxicated passion. (30–31)
May your lotus-foot— variegated with petals that are your toes, adorned with excellent anklets jingling like the cries of swans—
abide in my heart, which is as beautiful as a dense cluster of lotuses, for the pacification of me who have been bitten by the serpent of desire.
Having heard this nectar-like speech of Kalki, the destroyer of the Kali age, enough!

Seeing his state as a virtuous man, Padmā was filled with joy; surrounded by her friends, her mind weary, she bowed her neck and spoke respectfully to her steadfast husband—who was himself honored for his fortitude—with her hands joined in reverence. (33)
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Direct Dialogue with Padmākalki," in the second part of the glorious *Anubhāgavata*, the *Bhaviṣya-Kalki-Purāṇa*.
Chapter Three.
Sūta said:
Thinking him to be Hari, the goddess Padmā, her speech faltering with love and feeling bashful, praised that ocean of compassion:
"Be gracious, O Lord of the worlds, O you whose path is dharma, O Consort of Ramā!"
"You are known, O pure-souled one; O Lord, protect me who am under your control!
Blessed am I, and one who has performed merit through penance, charity, recitation, and vows;
having gratified you, who are so difficult to propitiate, I have attained your lotus feet."
"Give me your command; having touched your beautiful lotus-feet, I shall go to the palace to announce your welcome to the king.
Thus spoke Padmā, the abode of beauty, as she went to her father, the monarch.
Through messengers, he announced the arrival of Kalki, an incarnation of Viṣṇu,
on behalf of Padmā’s friends with the desire for her marriage;
upon hearing of Hari’s coming, Bṛhadratha became filled with joy.
Accompanied by his family priest, Brahmins, auspicious vessels, friends,
musical instruments, dancers, singers, and those with hands ready for the performance of worship,
the Lord went forth with his own people to bring back Kalki.
Having adorned Kārumatī with banners and golden archways,
Viṣṇuyaśas then went to the vicinity of the reservoir to meet his son,
the sole refuge of the world, who was seated upon a jeweled altar.
Just as beautiful flashes of lightning, rainbows, and the like shine upon thick clouds, even so do his ornaments shine; indeed,
his body is adorned with yellow garments and a most terrible luster.
The king beheld before him Śrīśa, a treasury of beauty, character, and virtue— a dwelling for the splendor of form and a destroyer of the rising power of passion.
With tears and his hair standing on end from joy, he honored that holy man.
"O Lord, this arrival of yours before me is beyond the scope of my knowledge, just as [the arrival] of the son of Māndhātṛ in the forest was [beyond the knowledge] of the Lord of the Yadus.
Having spoken thus, he honored him and brought him to his own hermitage.

Having established her in a residence crowded with mansions and palaces, he gave his daughter Padmā— lotus-eyed and like a lotus-pond— to Padmanetra; and by the command of the Lotus-born, he duly gave Padminī to Padmanābha.
Having recovered his beloved wife in Siṃhala and being honored by the virtuous, Kalki,
who was discerning of excellence, dwelt there after beholding that most excellent island.
The kings, having attained womanhood, became friends of Padmā.
They hastened together to behold Kalki, Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World.
Upon seeing him and touching his lotus feet, those women also regained their manhood through his command and by bathing in the Revā.
Let him behold Padmākalkī, who is both fair and dark with their colors inverted within, yet clearly manifest on the outside under the guise of blue and yellow garments.
Having seen the most wonderful power of Kalkī, the kings—

Bowing with supreme devotion, those seeking refuge offered praise: "Victory! Victory! Having perceived that the three worlds—the instruments for which were submerged in water through the transformation of all conceptual distinctions fashioned by Your own *māyā*—and having heard the prayer, You assumed the body of a great fish (*mahāmīna*) that appeared without a womb (*avija-nāvi-janāvirbhūta*). You have descended to protect the bridge of dharma established by Yourself. (20–21)

Furthermore, here, having assumed the incarnation of a boar through your resolute determination to slay Hiraṇyākṣa—whose prowess had conquered the three worlds and was honored even by Indra, the destroyer of the hosts of the sons of Diti—and to lift up the earth, protect us!

22 Furthermore, here, with a mind intent on providing assistance to the hosts of gods and demons who were distressed while bringing Mount Mandara for the churning of the ocean, you appeared in the form of a tortoise to perform the lifting of the mountain and the drinking of the nectar; O Supreme Lord, be gracious to these wretched kings! 23

Furthermore, here for the welfare of the best of gods who were tormented and terrified by Hiraṇyakaśipu—the conqueror of the three worlds and possessor of great strength and prowess—you, desiring the slaughter of the son of Diti, and reflecting that he was incapable of being slain by gods, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, humans, Nāgas, or by weapons, missiles, day or night, heaven, earth, or the depths of Pātāla due to the boon of Brahmā, assumed the form of Narasiṃha and rendered him lifeless, having split his thighs with the tips of your claws and bitten through his lips with your fangs. 24.

Furthermore, here in this world, at the sacrifice of Bali, you—the younger brother of Śakra, the conqueror of the three worlds—assumed the form of a dwarf brahmin to delude the Daitya; under the pretext of requesting three paces of land, your body became universal, and your desire for the earth increased upon touching the water offered by him. Thus, you accepted the office of Bali’s doorkeeper on the surface of the earth, which was a fitting fruit of your generosity. 25.

Furthermore, here, for the sake of destroying kings such as the Haihayas—who possessed immeasurable strength and prowess and transgressed the path of moral boundaries under various pretexts—the son of Jamadagni, born of the lineage of Bhṛgu, acting as the incarnation of Paraśurāma, brought the earth devoid of Kṣatriyas twenty-one times, impelled by the intensity of his wrath aroused by the theft of his father’s sacrificial cow. 26.

Furthermore, in this world, having resolved upon the destruction of Rāvaṇa—the night-stalker, the son of Viśravas, the ornament of Pulastya’s lineage, and the scorcher of the three worlds—you, the incarnation of Rāma, born as the son of Daśaratha of the solar dynasty, received weapons from Viśvāmitra; then, with your wrath increased by the abduction of Sītā, you bound the ocean with monkeys and slew the ten-necked one along with his hosts. 27.

Furthermore, here you are the incarnation of Rāma as Balabhadra, the moon for the ocean of the Yadu clan, whose pair of lotus-feet are served by the entire host of gods, who destroys various Dānavas and Daityas, and who dispels the suffering of the sins of the three worlds; you are the son of Vasudeva.

(28) Furthermore, here you are the incarnation of Buddha, who, through the performance of the various systems of philosophy prescribed by the Vedic dharma established by Brahmā, and by means of the rule for renouncing the karma of saṃsāra, accomplishes the mastery of manifesting as Brahman and the subduing of Prakṛti. (29)

Now, you have descended as Kalki for the destruction of the Kali age and for the protection of the bridge of Vedic dharma against the Buddhists, heretics, barbarians, and others; you have rescued us from the hell of womanhood—how can we describe your compassion here?
(30) Where is your descent, whose splendor was unknown even to Brahmā and the other gods, and where are our desires, which afflict the minds of those distressed by the mirage of women?
"The sight of your lotus-feet is exceedingly difficult to attain; O ocean of mercy, look upon us with joyful eyes and grant us consolation.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Hymn of the Kings," in the second part of the *Śrī Kalki Purāṇa*, the *Anubhāgavata* concerning the future.
The Fourth Chapter.
Sūta said:
Having heard the words of the devoted kings, Puruṣottama—
He proclaimed the dharma for the castes of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras;
he fully announced the entire teaching of the Vedas concerning the duties prescribed for those engaged in worldly action and those who have withdrawn from it.
Having heard these words of Kalki, the kings, pure in heart, prostrated themselves and spoke again regarding their own previous state:
"Whether it be womanhood or manhood, by whom was it created, or for whom?"

O All-pervading Lord, describe the actions—whether old age, youth, childhood, and so forth, or pleasure, pain, and the like—which are undetermined, unknown, and for which one might ask: "From what? Whence? In what? What is this? ||4-5||
Then, having heard that, Kalki remembered the sage Ananta;
and that excellent sage Ananta, whose feet are the sacred fords and who observes great vows,
arrived in haste, perceiving that liberation would come from the sight of Kalki.
Having arrived, he spoke again, saying, "What shall I do, or where shall I go? Hearing these words, Kalki laughed and said to the sage:
"Everything has been done; you have seen it all and understood it. Now go to that place from which there is no returning."
Having heard that [the realm] was unseen and unmade, the sage was delighted in his heart.
Then, seeing him prepared to depart, the hosts of kings, their minds filled with wonder, spoke to Kalki, whose eyes were like lotus petals: ||8-9||
The kings said: "What was said by this one, or what was said by you, or everything that was said to them— we wish to hear all that conversation between the two."
Having heard those words of the kings, Madhusūdana said to them: "Ask this peaceful sage, you who are intent on the exchange of stories.
Having again heard these words of Kalki, those best of kings [acted accordingly].
"Those who have bowed down and desire to cross to the further shore of their questions call him infinite.
The kings said:
"O Sage, what is the account here concerning Kalki, whose armor is righteousness?"
"O Lord, by whom was this difficult-to-understand reality produced? Describe it to us.
The sage said:
"In ancient times, in the city of Purikā, my father was a master of the Vedas."
O Lord, there was one named Vidruma, a knower of dharma, renowned and devoted to the welfare of others. Soma was my mother, who was entirely dedicated to the duty toward her husband;
when they both reached old age, I became a eunuch in appearance.
Born with a censurable form that brought grief to my parents and reproach from the world,
my father, overwhelmed by pain, sorrow, and fear upon seeing me as a eunuch,
abandoned his home, went to a forest sacred to Śiva, and praised Śaṅkara.
Having worshipped the Lord according to the prescribed rite with incense, lamps, and ointments,
Vidruma said:
"To Śiva, the peaceful one, the sole lord of all worlds, the abode of all beings, whose neck is adorned by Vāsuki..."
"I bow to him who has the waves of the Gaṅgā bound in his matted locks, who is capable of bestowing a mass of intense bliss.
(18) Having been praised with these and many other hymns, Śiva, the giver of auspiciousness, mounted upon his bull, spoke to my father with a gracious soul: "Choose a boon! (19)
"My father Vidruma, tormented by distress, told me that Śiva,
laughing and delighted by Pārvatī, had granted me manhood. Having obtained this boon of manhood for me, my father returned home once again.

Beholding me as a man, he was filled with joy along with his beloved wife. Then, when I had reached the age of twelve, my aged parents, having arranged my marriage through their kinsmen, attained great delight.
Having obtained as my wife the daughter of Yajñarāta— prideful and endowed with beauty— I became a householder with a deeply contented soul, yet remained under the sway of my wife.
Then, after some time, O kings, my parents passed away.
Surrounded by friends and Brahmins, I performed the rites for the next world for those two according to the prescribed rules; having fed many twice-born men,
I, tormented by the separation from my parents, became devoted to the service of Viṣṇu.
The Lord Hari, pleased by my acts of recitation, worship, and other rites, said to me in a dream: "This is an illusion created by the delusion of affection;
[it arises] for one whose mind is agitated by the sense of 'mine' in the thought, 'This is my father,' and 'This is my mother. (26)
"Causing grief, suffering, fear, agitation, old age, and death"—
having heard these words of Viṣṇu, and perceiving me prepared to offer a rebuttal, he vanished; from that moment, I became free from sleep.
Right there on the southern side, having fashioned an excellent hermitage, I shall perform service to Hari together with my wife, followers, and ministers;
remaining in the abode of Hari, I long for the manifestation of his illusory power.
Singing, dancing, chanting His name, and meditating upon Him who destroys all calamities;
when twelve years had thus passed, on the twelfth day (dvādaśī), the day for breaking my fast,
I went with my kinsmen, desiring to bathe in the ocean.
Immersed therein in the ocean, which is turbulent with surging waves,
and unable to rise up, aquatic creatures peck at me as my mind is distracted by the process of sinking and surfacing. (33)
With my limbs shattered by the tossing of the waves, unconscious and driven by the wind, I fell upon the southern shore of the ocean;
seeing me fallen there, Vṛddhaśarman, the best of the twice-born, [took pity]. ||34-35||

Having performed the twilight devotions, the compassionate and righteous Vṛddhaśarman, accompanied by his wife, children, and wealth, led me back to his own city; there, having treated me as one afflicted by illness, he protected me like a son. (36)
But I, dejected in spirit and ignorant of the directions and the country,
O kings, lived there thinking those two to be my parents;
he, however, recognized me as one who had practiced the Vedic duties in many ways.
Full of humility, he gave his own daughter in marriage;
having obtained her there—she who was like gold in form, endowed with beauty, character, and virtue, and named Cārumatī—I, the proud one, was filled with wonder. (38–39)
