With my soul completely satisfied by her, endowed with various enjoyments and happiness, and having fathered five sons, I was filled with joy:
Jaya, Vijaya, Kamala, and likewise Vimala. (40)
Budha and the others—these five sons of mine are well-known.
Through my kinsmen, relatives, sons, and various kinds of wealth, I am renowned and honored in the world, just as Indra is among the gods in heaven. 41–42.
Seeing that [Budha] was prepared for the marriage of his eldest son, the excellent brahmin Dharmasāra, who knew the Vedas, was pleased; desiring to give his own daughter,
he performed the auspicious rites as well.
With instrumental music, songs, dances, and groups of women adorned with gold,
I too, out of great devotion, entered the shore of the ocean to perform the libations for the ancestors and the celestial sages on the occasion of my son’s prosperity. ||44-45||

O kings, my body trembling from the waves, I rose quickly from the water; seeing my friends on the shore intent upon their bath and twilight prayers, I became immediately distracted in mind, for they were all observant of the breaking of the fast on the twelfth day.
Those inhabitants of Puruṣottama, who were intent on the service of Viṣṇu, placed me at their head;
seeing me—a treasury of beauty and youth—with minds filled with wonder, the people spoke to me. ||47-48||
O Ananta, you are a devotee of Viṣṇu; what have you seen here, whether in the water or on land?
We perceive that your mind is distracted; how is this so for you? Cast aside your astonishment and tell us, then perform your breaking of the fast.

I said to them, "O people, I have neither seen nor heard anything at all. (50) "With my mind intent on desire, wretched in intellect, and devoted to the display of that illusion, I was deluded by that illusory power of Hari, with my senses utterly agitated. (51)
"Under the sway of affection and delusion, I find no peace anywhere;
this is a forgetting of my own true nature—who knows it, however, once it has been realized?
(52) Thus, his mind was devoted to wife, wealth, home, and the marriage of his son.
"I am Ananta, yet with a dejected mind I know not even my own sleep.
Seeing me standing helpless like a fool, why does my proud wife now cry out and speak to me beside me all of a sudden? (53-54)
Having seen her here and remembered her there, my mind became distressed;
then a certain swan, firm, one who knows all truths, full, and a knower of the supreme dharma, came to awaken me with well-spoken words. (55–56)

Having worshipped before me that essence of beings— who is sun-like in form, tranquil, self-controlled, pure, and the destroyer of the world’s sorrow— my limbs (my disciples), desiring auspicious meditation, questioned me.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Vision of Ananta-Māyā," in the second part of the glorious *Kalki Purāṇa*, the *Anubhāgavata*, in its future narrative.
The Fifth Chapter.
Sūta said:
When the Swan had then sat down, having received the appropriate alms-offering, [the sage spoke].
Then, desiring the health of Ananta’s body, they spoke.
Having understood their intention, the swan said to me as I stood before him:
"Your wife is Cārumatī, and your sons are the five wise ones, headed by Budha."

Having abandoned your home, which was filled with wealth and jewels, crowded and teeming with palatial mansions, why have you come here at this unseasonable time— and not on the day of your son's wedding?
You, who were honored by the virtuous people of the city, now wander along the seashore.
Having invited me, you have come here with a mind agitated by grief.
And yet, O Lord, though you are seventy years of age, you appear to me there as if you were thirty; for this reason, my bewilderment is great.
This wife of yours was never seen there as your companion;
nor am I there—where, from where, or how could I have been seen by anyone?
Whether he is that very person or not, you are not he, nor am I he; he is simply a monk.
This union of ours here has become like a magician's trick.
You are a householder who knows your own duty, while I am a mendicant whose self is directed toward the Supreme.
Our conversation here is like that of a child and a madman.
"Therefore, O twice-born one, I consider this illusion of the Lord— which deludes the three worlds— to be unattainable through knowledge and attainable only through devotion.
Having thus spoken, the mendicant, filled with wonder, said something else.
O highly fortunate Mārkaṇḍeya, I shall tell you of the future.
That illusion which you beheld within the waters of the Person's belly during the dissolution— the illusion that produces delusion— is like a courtesan [leading one] astray from the path.
For Tamas, characterized by infinite torment, remains pervading this entire world through its state of activity, striving to impel it;
yet when the three worlds have dissolved at the time of reabsorption, it returns to the state of being merely the subtle element of Brahma.
In that state which is without limiting adjuncts and without light, the Supreme Being became desirous of creating.
Even within Brahman, having become twofold as Puruṣa and Prakṛti by his own radiance, he brought forth the Mahat through the conjunction of Time.
From that [Pradhāna] arose Ahaṃkāra, whose nature consists of time, inherent nature, and karma;
it is threefold, composed of Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Brahmā, and is the cause of transmigratory existence.
From that, the five subtle elements (tanmātras) were born, endowed with the qualities (guṇas).
From that, by abiding in the nature of Brahman, the great elements also arose;
and from them were born the gods, asuras, humans, and whatever other species of living beings there are,
whose very essence consists of the acts of creation and destruction within the vast vessel of the cosmic egg.
Through illusion after illusion, the individual soul, busily occupied with the refuge of worldly existence, never knows the course of the Self, which is the Supreme Soul.
Oh, how powerful is Māyā, under whose control even Brahmā and the other gods abide!
Like oxen bound by ropes through their noses, or like birds [bound by snares],

those lords of sages who wish to cross over that illusion composed of the gunas— a river with latent impressions for its crocodiles— they alone are the knowers of the ultimate goal on this earth. (19–20)
Śaunaka said: Having heard the words of their preceptor, what did Mārkaṇḍeya, Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, and the others say next, being intent on listening?
"O Sūta, having heard the words of Ananta, which are like nectar, what did the kings say? Oh, describe here what will happen!
Having heard those words, the Sūta, having honored him in return, [spoke].
He spoke in its entirety that which completely destroys grief and delusion.
Sūta said:
There, Ananta, having been questioned by the hosts of kings, spoke with due respect.
"Through austerity, there is the destruction of delusion and the restraint of the senses.
Ananta said:
"Therefore, having reached the forest and performed austerity according to the prescribed rules,"
Never has there been a restraint of my senses or of my mind.
While I am meditating on Brahman in the forest, my wife, sons, wealth,
and other objects of sense constantly remind my mind of them from within.
By the mere remembrance of them, suffering, grief, fear,
and the like pierce my vital breaths, destroying my concentration and meditation. Therefore, with a resolute mind, I am intent upon the destruction of the senses.
By that means, the restraint of the mind will come to pass; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, seeing me with my mind intent on restraining the senses, as well as the presiding deities of those senses, they approached me directly.
Then those embodied ones said to me, "O Infinite One!"—they being the ten:
the quarters, the wind, the sun, Varuṇa, the Aśvins, Agni, Indra, Upendra, Mitra, and Kāma.
"We are the gods presiding over the senses, established within your body. (30)
"You ought not to rend us here with the tips of your claws;
for it is not for your own welfare, O Ananta, to engage in the act of subduing our minds.
By cutting and tearing us, you shall die with your own vital organs shattered."
Ah! Even for the blind, the deaf, and those living with impaired senses, I observe that their minds remain distracted by sense-objects even in the forest.
For a householder, too, the body follows the mind as its home.
Understand this: Intellect is his wife, and we are her followers.
The mind of that living soul is dependent on karma; through the illusion (māyā) of Brahman, it causes the greedy soul to wander in saṃsāra, bringing about both bondage and liberation.
Therefore, for the sake of restraining the mind, practice devotion to Viṣṇu;
it eternally bestows blissful liberation and burns away all karmas.
Devotion to Hari is a mass of bliss that grants both duality and non-duality.
"O high-minded one, at the end of the destruction of the sheath of the individual soul through devotion to Hari, you shall attain supreme Nirvāṇa by beholding Kalki.
Thus was I enlightened by him; having worshipped Keśava with devotion, [I departed].
Desirous of beholding Kalki, the destroyer of the race of Kali, he has come to see Kṛṣṇa;
he has seen the form of the Formless One, touched the sprout-like feet of the Footless One, and heard the speech of the Supreme Self, who is beyond all expression. (39–40)
Thus, the sage Ananta, filled with joy, paid homage to his own lord Kalki, the lotus-eyed protector of the world, and departed.
By the words of the sage, the kings attained the path of liberation.
Having worshipped Kalki and having paid homage to Padmā, those of sage-like vows [listened].
Śuka said:
"This narrative of Ananta destroys the darkness of ignorance."

By reciting or hearing this *Māyāniyantrī*, one is liberated from bondage. Having composed this narrative called *Bhakti*— which is free from internal contradictions and rooted in righteousness— the noble-souled [Vyāsa], whose mind was once intent on the pleasures of the ocean of saṃsāra, now honors the service of Śrī Viṣṇu.

May the Vaiṣṇava—delighted by the sharp sword of the radiance of knowledge, taking refuge in the fortress of true devotion—conquer the group of six internal enemies residing within himself for the sake of all the worlds.
(44) Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Dispelling of Infinite Māyā," in the second part of the *Śrī Kalki Purāṇa*, the *Anubhāgavata*, in its future tense (*bhaviṣya*). (5)
The Sixth Chapter.
Sūta said:
After the host of kings had departed, Kalki, together with Padmā, [left] from Siṃhala.
He set his mind upon going to the village of Śambhala with his own army.
Then, having understood Kalki’s intention, Vāsava quickly summoned Viśvakarman and spoke these words: ||2||
Indra said:
"O Viśvakarman, O Śambhala, construct for me a residence crowded with houses, gardens, and watchtowers, filled with palaces and mansions, and adorned with heaps of gold. (3)
"Right there, exercise your skill as an artisan with those [materials] fashioned from jewels, crystal, beryl, and various gems.
Having heard Hari’s words, Viśvakarman recalled his own well-being.
In Śambhala, the Creator fashioned for the Lord of Kamalā houses headed by Svastika and others,
featuring mouths shaped like swans, lions, and garuḍas,
and made beautiful with upper windows that dispel the heat.
Śambhala became as beautifully adorned with various forests, groves, lakes, and ponds as Amarāvatī is for Indra;
and Kalkin, surrounded by his hosts of armies, [departed] from the island of Siṃhala.
Leaving Kārumatī on the shore of the ocean, he established his residence there.
Bṛhadratha, however, filled with affectionate anxiety, [offered] to Viṣṇu— the Lord of Padmā— along with Kaumudī and accompanied by Padmā.

With eyes brimming with tears of devotion and affection, he joyfully gave ten thousand elephants, a hundred thousand choice horses, two thousand chariots, and two hundred maidservants, as well as garments and jewels.
Because of looking at their faces, he was unable to say anything.
Having sent away that great Viṣṇu couple, he returned to his own city of Kārūmatī, where he was honored by Kalki and Padmā.
But Kalki, having plunged into the waters of the ocean with his hosts of troops and desiring to reach the far shore, became paralyzed upon seeing Jambuka.
Then, beholding that suspension of the waters, Kalki, along with his army and vehicles—
The abode of Śrī proceeded over the mass of waters.
Having reached the far shore, he said to Śuka: "Go to my residence at Śambhala, where there is much that was fashioned by Viśvakarman at the command of the King of the Gods."
"A pure and most beautiful dwelling, crowded [with people], for the sake of my pleasure.

There too, one should offer blessings as is appropriate for one's parents and kinsmen; O dear one, you ought to tell me everything regarding the marriage and other matters that take place there. (16–17)
"Afterwards I shall go, having been chosen by these; you, however, go first to Śambhala.
Having heard Kalki’s words, the wise parrot then departed through the sky—the omniscient one—to Śambhala, which is worshipped by the gods.

Agitated, he entered Śambhala, which was seven yojanas in extent, crowded with people of the four castes, radiant like the rays of the sun, adorned with hundreds of palaces, delightful, and providing comfort in all seasons. (20–21)
Having seen house after house, even from palace to palace, sky after sky,
forest after forest, and tree after tree as he traveled there,
that parrot joyfully approached the residence of Viṣṇuyaśas.
Having gone there and conversed with him using charming speech and pleasant words,
he announced the arrival of Kalki along with Padmā from Siṃhala. Then Viṣṇuyaśas, hurrying, summoned his noble subjects.
Filled with joy, he spoke to King Viśākhayūpa.
That king had the city, villages, and other areas adorned with golden jars filled with water and sprinkled with sandalwood paste. ||25-26||
Rich with the fragrance of black aloe-wood, and adorned with lamps, parched grain, sprouts, unbroken rice, delicate flowers, plantains, and betel nuts,
the village of Śambhala shone, enchanting to the wise. (27)
Then Kalki, who was distinct from the hosts of Bhīmasena’s army,
whose body was a temple bringing joy to the eyes of amorous women, and who was an ocean of compassion,
entered; accompanied by Padmā, he prostrated himself at the feet of his parents.
With her desire fulfilled, the virtuous Diti beheld her son Sumati and her daughter-in-law Mudita, just as Śacī beholds Śakra in Amarāvatī; meanwhile,
the city of the village of Śambhala was resplendent with banners and flags.
With beautiful hips like those of women in the inner apartments, with breasts as large as palace towers, with peacock feathers for nipples, and enchanting with necklaces made of flocks of swans;
clothed in garments of smoke from the incense of aromatic powders, she possessed a voice like the song of the cuckoo. ||30||
Like a virtuous woman with beautiful eyes who shines upon attaining a husband, the city— whose gateway was like a smiling face— glowed having obtained Kalki as its lord;
he, taking refuge in the Unborn, sported there with Padmā for many series of years.
In Śambhala, Kalki, who appeared in a state of agitation and was the destroyer of the Kali age, [was born].
Kavi’s wife, Kāmakalā, gave birth to two supreme sons, Bṛhatkīrti and Bṛhadbāhu, who possessed great strength and prowess. ||32-33||

The wise [Prājña] had Sannati as his wife, and by her two sons were born who were skilled in sacrifice, honored by all the world, and masters of their senses. Sumantaka, however, begot Śāsana upon Mālinī.
And these two, who possess great speed, are benefactors of the virtuous.
Then Kalki begot upon Padmā two sons, Jaya and Vijaya, who were world-renowned and possessed of great strength. ||35-36||
Surrounded by these ministers and endowed with every prosperity,
Kalki, the Lord, beheld his father intent upon performing the horse sacrifice and spoke to him like the Supreme Lord to Brahmā.

"Having conquered the guardians of the quarters and having gathered wealth, I shall indeed perform the horse sacrifice; therefore, O sirs, I am going forth for the conquest of the directions. Having thus spoken, Kalki, the conqueror of enemy cities, bowed to him with affection.
Surrounded by his military hosts, he set out for the city of Kīkaṭa—
a vast abode of Buddhists, excluded from the Vedic dharma, devoid of worship of ancestors and gods, and a destroyer of the world beyond. ||40-41||
Abounding in the doctrine that the body is the self, devoid of [regard for] family and caste,
regarding wealth, women, and various foods as [the goal], seeing no distinction between self and others,
and surrounded by many people intent on drinking and eating— ||42-43||
Upon hearing of Kalki’s arrival, the Jina, filled with wrath, went outside the city accompanied by his own followers and two *akṣauhiṇī* divisions.
The earth was covered with elephants, chariots, and horses, and with excellent warriors adorned with golden ornaments.
She shone with hundreds upon hundreds of charioteers, who held weapons and missiles, and whose heat was warded off by rows of silken banners. 45.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Journey to the City of Kīkaṭa," in the section on the Subjugation of Buddha, within the second part of the glorious *Kalki Purāṇa*, an Anubhāgavata of the future.
Chapter Seven.
Sūta said: Then Viṣṇu, the all-conquering Kalki, the destroyer of the wicked,
drove back that army like a lion against a female elephant.

To that woman of the army, wounded in the battle of passion, her garments smeared with blood, her thighs and waist exposed, fleeing with beautiful hair disheveled and crying out, that leader Kalki said:
"O Buddhists, do not flee! Turn back onto the field of battle!"
"Fight! Show me your prowess once again!
Hearing those words of Kalki, the Jina, though of inferior strength, became enraged;
mounting his bull and wielding sword and shield, he went forth to counter-attack.
Equipped with various weapons and skilled in diverse arms,
the steadfast one fought with Kalkin, causing amazement among the gods;
having pierced the horse with a trident, he bewildered Kalkin with an arrow.
Having swiftly embraced the earth, he was unable to lift her due to his excessive weight;
then the Jina, perceiving him to be Viśvambhara, his eyes agitated with wrath,
cut away the armor and the weapon of Kalki like a servant.
Viśākhayūpa likewise struck the victorious Kalki with his mace;
having rendered him unconscious, he effortlessly mounted the chariot. Then Kalki regained consciousness and once again inspired his servants with zeal.
Leaping from that king's chariot, the noble steed approached the Jina;
having abandoned the pain of the spear in battle, the great being repeatedly struck with the forceful stamping of its wandering hooves. ||9-10||
Then, amidst the ranks of the Buddhist army, he struck his enemies in anger by the hundreds and thousands with blows from his staff and tosses of his mane;
some, blown up by the wind of his breath, fell upon other continents.
Crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots, they fell at the front of the battle.
Garga slew one hundred and sixty [thousand]; Garga [slew] ten million and a hundred thousand;
but Viśāla, acting with haste in the fray, slew twenty-five thousand.
In battle, Kavi, accompanied by his two sons, slew twenty thousand; likewise, the wise Sumantraka slew one million five hundred thousand.
Laughing, Kalki said to Jina, "Stay before me, O evil-minded one! (14)
"Know me to be Destiny everywhere, the bestower of the fruits of both good and evil.
With your limbs pierced by my net of arrows, you shall go to your destruction free from attachment;
before that happens, behold now the lovely faces of your kinsmen."
Having heard this spoken by Kalki, the powerful Jina laughed and said:
"In your scripture, this killing is sanctioned as an invisible fate;
we Buddhists are proponents of direct perception, while you are merely engaged in futile exertion. (17)
Whether you are a manifestation of the gods, we still stand before you;
if you would pierce us with floods of arrows, then what use have you for the Buddhists here? You have spoken what should not be blamed; let it remain with you alone—be steadfast.
Thus, out of anger, he covered Kalki with terrible nets of arrows.
But he [Kalki] brought that rain of arrows to an end, like the sun dispelling the frost.
[He neutralized] the Brahma, Vayavya, Agneya, Parjanya, and other weapons.
By the mere sight of Kalki, they became fruitless in an instant—just like seed sown in barren soil, or a gift given to one who lacks Vedic learning;
for alas, by him devotion was shown even toward Viṣṇu out of hatred for the virtuous. ||21-22||
But Kalki, having leaped upon him as he was mounted on the bull, seized him by the hair;
then they both fell to the ground in fury like two roosters.
Having fallen, he grasped Kalki’s hair with his hand and seized that hand with his own.
Then those two great heroes rose up, eager like Cāṇūra and Keśava; grasping each other by the hands and pulling at the hair, they fought like two mighty bears, Jinakalkī and Nirāyudha, being unarmed.
Then Kalkī, the great yogi, struck his hip with a kick and felled him like a palm tree brought down by an elephant in rut.
When Jina had fallen, his powerful brother Śuddhodana—
On foot and mace in hand, he went swiftly to slay Kalki.
But the poet, the slayer of enemy heroes, surrounded him on all sides with showers of arrows and roared like a lion that has cornered an elephant.
Beholding his lord with mace in hand, that wise poet, skilled in dharma,
mounted on a chariot and bearing a mace himself, stood before Śuddhodana.
Then Śuddhodana, possessed of terrible prowess, fought with him.
Like two elephants with their tusks,
those two great heroes, both experts in mace-fighting, fought on, striking blow for blow, intoxicated and roaring with terrible cries. (31-32)
But Kavi, shouting, quickly snatched Śuddhodana’s mace from his hand with his own heavy mace and struck him in the chest with it.
Struck by the blow of the mace, the hero Śuddhodana fell to the ground.
Having fallen down, he rose up suddenly and struck him again with his mace.
Though struck by that blow, the sage remained paralyzed;
he did not fall, but stood there like a pillar, his senses overwhelmed.
Upon seeing that great treasure covered by ten thousand chariots, Śuddhodana swiftly set out to bring Māyādevī;
at the mere sight of whom gods, asuras, humans, and others [are captivated].
The refuges of the world became like insubstantial images.
Then, placing that [image] at their head, the Buddhists led by Śauddhodana and others arrived to fight again, surrounded by hundreds of millions of Mlecchas. ||37-38||
She whose chariots are raised with lion banners, who is surrounded by throngs of jackals and crows,
who is the mother of all missiles and weapons, who is attended by the six internal enemies,
who possesses manifold forms, who is powerful, and who is characterized by the manifestation of the three qualities. ||39||
Beholding an illusion before him, Kalki’s army charged forward.
Seeing his own brothers, kinsmen, and friends aged by the illusory wife, the Lord Kalki stood before them.
Beholding that woman of excellent hips and beautiful form, the Lord Hari entered her body as if she were his beloved;
and those excellent Buddhists, not seeing their mother, [asked] how many times...
Distressed and deprived of their own strength and prowess, they wept in groups;
with minds overcome by wonder, they then asked, "Where has she gone?
Thereupon Kalki, having raised up his own people with a glance, [spoke].
Taking up a sharpened sword, he set his mind on slaying the Mlecchas;
equipped with armor, mounted upon a horse, and holding a sword with a hilt firmly in his hand,
he was constantly illuminated by his bow, quiver, and multitude of arrows.
Adorned with a hand-guard, armor, a leather arm-guard, and finger-protectors; resembling stars scattered across a cloud; marked by golden spots like teeth;
and resplendent with rows of jewels set upon the crest of its crown.
He is the abode of the essence of the mass of bliss for the eyes of amorous women, casting harsh side-glances that scatter the wings of his adversaries;
he whose lotus feet are the dwelling place for the joy of his own devotees. 49.
Beholding Kalki, those Buddhists, revilers of the Dharma, were terrified;
while the hosts of gods in the sky rejoiced at the sacrificial fires fed by the oblations of their rites.
Subala, filled with joy at the gathering [of allies] and thirsting solely for the destruction of his enemies, [advanced].
May he who is the graceful sport of the best of battles, the field for honoring the virtuous,
the remover of the misfortunes of his own kin, and the sustainer of all living beings—
the incarnation of Kāmapūra— bestow well-being upon you. (52)
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Battle with the Buddhists," in the second part of the glorious *Kalki Purāṇa*, an appendix to the *Anubhāgavata* concerning the future.
The Third Part: The First Chapter.
Sūta said: Then Kalki led the hosts of Mlecchas, who had been cut down by his sword, and others who had been struck by his arrows, to the abode of Yama.
Viśākhayūpa, as well as Kaviprājña, Sumantraka,
Gārgya, Bhārgya, Viśāla, and others, led the Mlecchas to the abode of Yama;
so too did Kapotaroman, Kākākṣa, Kākakṛṣṇa, and others.
The Buddhists, followers of Śauddhodana, went forth and fought with the soldiers of Kalki.
Their battle was terrible, causing fear to all embodied beings,
bringing joy to the Lord of Spirits (Śiva), and turning the ground into a mire reddened with blood.
With the streams of blood flowing from the falling multitudes of elephants, horses, and chariots,
that river had hair for its moss, horses for its crocodiles,
and was difficult to ford; it had bows for its waves, was hard to cross, and carried away the embankments of elephants.
With heads for its tortoises, chariots for its rafts, hands for its fish, and blood for its waters,
a river flowed forth there in many directions, gladdening the high-minded; it resounded with the noise of kettledrums and brought joy to jackals and birds.
Elephants by elephants, horses by men, camels by donkeys, and chariots by chariots fell down,
their limbs pierced by arrows, their arms, feet, and necks severed;
their faces smeared with ashes, they were covered in blood-stained garments.
With their hair disheveled, they fled in all directions like wandering ascetics;
some ran away in agitation, while others begged for water again and again;
crushed by the swift arrows of Kalki’s army, the Mlecchas found no peace.
Their women,
having abandoned the refuge of the happiness derived from husbands and children, arrived to fight, mounted on chariots, elephants, birds, and horses, or riding upon donkeys, camels, and bulls.
They were beautiful, youthful, and exceedingly powerful, devoted to their husbands;
adorned with various ornaments and finery, they were armored and possessed brilliant luster, with their lotus-like hands grasping swords, spears, bows, arrows, and bracelets. ||12-13||
Even wanton women, those excessively lustful, and even unchaste women became devoted wives; distressed by the death of their husbands, they went forth to fight Kalki’s armies.
By the command of the traditional scriptures, sovereignty over clay, ashes, wood, and paintings was established.
Could even those young women endure the actual slaughter of their husbands?
Having first rendered their own husbands—pierced by arrows and with their senses overwhelmed—unconscious, they then took up arms and fought against the armies of Kalki. ||15-16||
Beholding those women, all those warriors, their minds filled with wonder and smiles, approached Kalki and spoke to him with respect.
Having heard the talk of the women who were eager for battle, the high-minded one—
Kalki set forth, accompanied by his followers and his armies on chariots.
Beholding them— bearing all manner of weapons and missiles, mounted upon various vehicles, and arrayed in battle formations— the Lord of Padma spoke to them.
Kalki said:
"O women, listen to our words, which are beneficial and supreme: what is the use of war for men against women? Such conduct is not found here. (20)
Who would strike at those faces, which are like moon-disks with rows of shimmering locks of hair, bestowing joy upon the eyes,
and possessing the luster of fresh red lotuses with wandering bees for pupils? (21)
Who would strike her there, where her eyes have long outer corners?
Who would strike her there, where her breasts— born of Śambhu— are adorned with serpents in the form of pearl necklaces and crush the pride of Kandarpa?
Who here would dare to strike that moon-like face, which is devoid of blemish and whose moonlight is swallowed by the *cakora* birds of her shimmering, playful tresses?
[24] It possesses a waist utterly emaciated, overwhelmed by the heavy burden of her breasts.
What man would strike that which is bound with a web of fine lotus fibers?
(25) Who would strike with arrows that faultless, dense, and beautiful hip, which is covered by a pair of eyes that delight the eye? (26)
Having heard these words of Kalki, they laughed and said with respect:
"O Lord, you are slaying our husbands; therefore we have perished.
For those who go forth to kill, weapons are indeed brought to their very hands. (27)
Swords, spears, bows, arrows, tridents, javelins, and staffs—
these they say appeared before him in embodied form, adorned with gold.
The weapons spoke:
"O women, having reached him by whom we were formerly harmed through our own power,
know him with certainty to be the Self, the end of all, and the embodiment of everything.
O women, we move about as his subjects by his permission."
He by whom we are known through the distinctions of name, form, and so forth;
he upon whose support the five elements—form, smell, taste, touch, sound, and the rest—move; he is this Kalki, whose nature is the Supreme Self.
The supreme primordial nature (prakṛti), whose names are Time, Essential Nature, and Formative Forces, and by whose will it emits the cosmic egg, the Great Ego, and the rest;
through whose Māyā there proceeds the course of the world, known as creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
He who was at the beginning is the very same at the end; he is this Lord.
"He is my husband, I am his wife, and these are our sons, relatives, and kin"—all such various attachments are like a dream or a magical illusion. (33-34)
This is the view of those bound by affection and delusion, who see only the coming and going of worldly affairs;
it is not for those who consume the dregs [of existence], who harbor passion and hatred, and who act with malice.
Where is time? Where is death? Where is Yama? And where are the gods?
That very Lord Kalki has been multiplied through his illusory power (māyā).
We are not weapons, nor are we women to be struck;
this distinction between those who wield weapons and their targets is the ignorance of the Supreme Self.
"Even we are not worthy to slay Kalkidāsa; this is a wondrous tale!
We shall slay him just as [the gods] slew Hari, the Lord of Daityas, for Prahlāda.
Having heard these words of the weapons, the women were filled with wonder in their minds.
Freed from attachment and delusion, they went for refuge to that Kalki.
Beholding them prostrate with steadfastness in knowledge, the Lord of Padmā spoke with a smile the yoga of devotion which destroys all impurity.
Mādhava explained to them the yoga of action established in the self, the yoga of knowledge based on the various paths of speech, and that characterized by freedom from action (naiṣkarmya).
Through the knowledge spoken by Kalki, those women conquered their senses.
Through devotion, they attained that supreme state which is difficult even for yogins to reach.

Having granted liberation to those dear to the Mlecchas and Buddhists, and having waged a terrible battle of fearsome deeds, Kalki—having slain the Buddhists and the hosts of Mlecchas and having filled their realm of light—shone resplendent. ||42-43||
Those people who with devotion listen to and proclaim this account of the Buddha’s passing and the destruction of the Mlecchas—
during the month of Mādhava, which always removes sorrow, brings auspiciousness, and bestows devotion—
for them alone there is no further birth or death, and it grants the fulfillment of all goals.
[It is] the destroyer of illusion and delusion, the daily cutter of the heat of worldly existence.
||44|| Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Destruction of the Mlecchas," in the third part of the glorious *Kalki Purāṇa*, the *Anubhāgavata* of the future.
Chapter Two.
Then, having conquered the Buddhist Mleccha hordes along with their armies and having seized wealth and jewels from Kīkaṭa,
Kalki— the supremely resplendent protector of the dharmas— returned once more.
Having arrived at Cakratīrtha, he performed his ablutions according to the prescribed rites.
Surrounded by many brothers who resembled the guardians of the world and by his kinsmen,
he beheld the sages who had arrived there with dejected minds.
To those who had spoken thus in many ways— "O Lord of the World, protect us who have come here from the depths"— Hari, the Supreme,
spoke to the Vālakhilyas and others, who were of no small stature and wore bark garments and matted hair.
Bowing with humility, Kalki spoke to those wretched ones who were trembling with fear:
"Why have you come here, and by whom have you been terrified? Alas!
I shall slay him, even if he should be Purandara himself."
Having thus heard the words of Kalki, their minds were uplifted by him, and they spoke to the lotus-eyed one concerning the stories of Nikumbha’s daughter.
The sages said:
Listen, O son of Viṣṇuyaśas: the daughter of Kumbhakarṇa’s daughter, renowned as Kuthodarī, rose up halfway to the sky;
she was the queen of Kālakañja and the mother of Vikañja.
Having placed her head upon the Himalaya and her feet upon Mount Niṣadha,
she lies there suckling Vikañja, her breasts flowing with milk.
Overwhelmed by the wind of her sighs, we have arrived here.
"O Rākṣasa, these sages have been brought by destiny itself and have reached the abode of your feet; they must be protected by you in both prosperity and adversity.
Having heard these words of theirs, Kalki, the conqueror of enemy cities, [acted accordingly].
Surrounded by his army, he went to the Himalaya mountain. Having reached the foothills, he spent one night there;
desiring to depart in the morning, he beheld with his troops the river of milk.

Seeing her—white as a conch or the moon, frothy, vast, and moving swiftly—all were struck motionless and filled with wonder, even though she was surrounded by hosts of armies, elephants, horses, chariots, and warriors. 13. Senāgaṇagajāśvādirathayodhaiḥ samāvṛtaḥ.
But the Lord Kalki, although he already knew the matter, questioned the lords of sages there: "What river is this, and how did it come to flow with milk?
Having heard Kalki’s words, the sages spoke with reverence:
Listen, O Kalki, to the origin of the *payasvatī* [plant] on the Himavat mountain:
it has arrived here from the flow of the breast-milk of Kuthodarī. Within seven *ghaṭikās*, another [plant] will also come forth with great speed.
"O Mahāmati, it will become a lake of inferior essence.
Having heard these words of the sages, [he said] along with his soldiers:
"Aha! From the breast of this rākṣasī, how is it that this single river has come forth?"
"Out of affection, she suckles her son Vikañja from one breast;
I do not know how many times the measure of this night-stalker's body might be! Thus they spoke, filled with wonder regarding her strength.
Kalki, the Supreme Self, having equipped himself for battle, set out suddenly with his armies along the path shown by the sage to where that night-stalker resided on a mountain peak,
resembling a dark cloud while suckling her son at her breast. ||20-21||
By the intense wind of her breath, the forest elephants were driven far away;
in the dwelling of her ear-cavities, she slept amidst a pride of lions, surrounded by sons and grandsons who roamed through mountain caves. (22)
Clinging to the roots of his hair, the deer lay there for a long time;
they were not at all agitated by intense fear of the hunter, as if they were lice.
Beholding her upon the summit of the mountain, most wonderful like a mountain itself, [the deer remained there]. (23–24)
Kalki, whose eyes were like lotus petals, spoke to all those soldiers who were agitated by fear, deprived of their wits, and having abandoned their efforts and equipment:
"Let my men remain here, having established a fire-fortress within this mountain fortress."
"Let the elephants, horses, chariots, and warriors come along with me.
Accompanied by a small force, I shall go slowly toward her to strike her with volleys of arrows, swords, spears, and battle-axes. (26–27)
Having spoken thus and stationed them behind him, the powerful one struck her with arrows;
she, rising up suddenly in rage, let out a most wonderful roar.
By that great sound, the people became terrified.
All the soldiers fell to the surface of the earth, unconscious;
and that terrifying, gaping-mouthed Kuthodarī, drawing them in with the wind of her breath, devoured both the chariots and the elephants.
The hosts of armies entered his belly along with Kalki, just as ants enter [an anthill] driven by the wind from the mouths of bears.
Seeing that, the gods and gandharvas raised a cry of "Alas! Alas! (hāhākāra).
The sages stationed there lamented, while other great seers cried out; some Brahmins who were exponents of the Veda fell down, overcome with grief;
the disciplined warriors wept, whereas those night-stalkers rejoiced.
Beholding the destruction of the worlds, the lotus-eyed Kalki, the slayer of the enemies of the gods, remembered his true self by means of his own self;
he [prepared] a fire of arrows with pieces of cloth and leather for the sake of his task, using the wood of his vehicle.
Having ignited [the fire] within his belly, he grasped a sword;
with that great sword, having pierced open his own side, he was surrounded by his powerful kinsmen and brothers, who held weapons and missiles in their hands. ||35-36||
The Lord of All, Kalki, the destroyer of sin, emerged like the thousand-eyed Indra with his thunderbolt from the belly of Vṛtra;
from the opening of the womb, elephants, chariots, and horses came forth.
Some emerged from the cavities of her nose and ears.
Once they had emerged from her, those blood-soaked soldiers pierced her as she was swiftly casting down her feet and hands.
With her body shattered, her belly and neck broken, she died,
making the quarters of space and the heavens resound and pulverizing the mountains. Seeing his mother thus, Karañja also became terrified.
Devoid of weapons, Vikañja rushed into the midst of the army in a rage;
his chest was crowded with rows of elephants, his body was adorned with lines of horses, he wore a turban fashioned from great serpents, and his fingers were marked with lions.
Afflicted by his mother’s distress, that Kalki crushed that army of Kalki with the desire to slay him;
he took up a weapon against the five-year-old Rākṣasa with his bow, employing that Brahma-weapon given by Rāma.
With that weapon, he severed his head and cast it to the ground;
smeared with blood and variegated with minerals, it was as wondrous as a mountain peak.
Having slain the Rākṣasī along with her son at the word of the sages, the Lord [departed].
On the bank of the Gaṅgā at Haridvāra, he established his residence;
well-honored by the gods with showers of flowers and by the hymns of sages,
Kalki spent that night there surrounded by his attendants.

In the morning, on the bank of the Gaṅgā at Haridvāra, in the Piṇḍāraka forest near the river’s edge, he beheld many groups of sages who were agitated by the sight of Viṣṇu himself under the pretext of bathing there. 47.

Having praised with repeated hymns according to the prescribed rites that glorious Kalki, who was dwelling there surrounded by his own attendants and gazing upon the daughter of Jahnu, the hosts of sages went to see him. 48.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Vision of the Sage," following the slaying of Kuthodarī, in the third part of the *Śrī Kalki Purāṇa*, the *Anubhāgavata* of the future.
Chapter Three.
Sūta said:
Seeing that the sages had arrived with a warm welcome, Kalki, the knower of the supreme dharma,
honored them according to the prescribed rites and spoke to them as they sat comfortably.
Kalki said:
Who are you, appearing like the sun, who have arrived here through my good fortune— you who are eager to visit sacred fords and are benefactors of the three worlds?
We are the meritorious, the fortunate, and the renowned ones in this world.
Since they were looked upon by you with a compassionate glance,
therefore they are Vāmadeva, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Gālava, Bhṛgu,
Parāśara, Nārada, Aśvatthāman, Rāma, Kṛpa, and Trita. ||3-4||
Durvāsas, Devala, Kaṇva, Vedapramiti, Aṅgiras—
these and many other sages of celebrated vows [were there].
Having first established Marudeva and Āpī, who were born of the lunar and solar lineages, respectively...
Those two kings of great prowess, having long been devoted to ascetic penance,
spoke with joyful minds to Kalki, the destroyer of evil,
who was situated on the shore of the great ocean, just as the hosts of gods address Viṣṇu.
The sages said:
Victory to you, O Lord of the entire world, who knows the minds of all;
O Supreme Self, presiding over creation, maintenance, and dissolution, be gracious to us! 8.
"O abode of time, karma, and the gunas; O Lord of Lakshmi, whose own activities are ever-expanding; O you whose lotus feet are praised by Brahma and the other gods—be gracious to us!
Having heard these words of theirs, Kalki, the Lord of the World, spoke.
"Who are these two great beings and ascetics standing before you?
How have they come here, praising the Gaṅgā with joyful minds?
What was the hymn of praise for the daughter of Jahnu, and what were the names of the two of you? (10–11)
Of those two, the virtuous Maru, being delighted and with palms joined in reverence, first spoke modestly, proclaiming his own lineage.
Maru said:
"You know everything, even though you are the Supreme Self, dwelling within the heart as the inner witness.
By your command, I shall relate all this; listen, O Lord!
From your navel arose Brahmā, and Marīci was his son."
From him was born Manu, whose son was Ikṣvāku, whose valor was truth;
he was known as Yuvanāśva, and his son was Māndhātṛ.
His son was Purukutsa, and his son was the high-minded Anaraṇya.
From him was born Trasaddasyu; from him, Haryaśva; from him, Tṛyaruṇa;
his son was the wise Triśaṅku, and his son was the powerful Hariścandra. Harita was his son, from whom came Bharuka, and his son was Vṛka.
His son was Sagara; from him came Asamañja, and from him Aṃśumat.
From him came Dilīpa, and his son is known as Bhagīratha, by whom the daughter of Jahnu was brought down to earth and became famous as the Bhāgīrathī.
Having praised, honored, and worshipped her, she sat at your feet.
From you was born Bhagīratha; from him came Nābha; from him arose the powerful Sindhudvīpa; and from him was born Āyutāyus.
Rtuparṇa was his son; Sudāsa was his son;
the wise Saudāsa was his son; Aśmaka is considered his son;
from Mūlaka came Daśaratha, and from him Eḍaviḍa.
From him came King Viśvasaha, then Khaṭvāṅga, and Dīrghabāhuka;
from him came Raghu, then Aja, and from him the virtuous son Daśaratha; from him was born Rāma, the Lord of the World, Hari himself manifested in person.
Having heard of the incarnation of Rāma, Kalki was exceedingly delighted and said to Maru: "Tell me in detail the life-story of Śrī Rāma;
who on this earth is capable of recounting the deeds of the Lord of Sītā? (23)
Even with a thousand mouths, one might never reach the end of it;
nevertheless, by your command, my intellect shall describe the meritorious life of Rāma, which grants liberation from sin and suffering.
Solicited by the gods beginning with Brahmā, the Unborn (Aja), the destroyer of demons, was born in the lineage of the Sun through four portions;
he who, as a child, forcibly destroyed the sacrifice of the son of Kuśika and annihilated the Rākṣasas.

Victorious is the beloved of Jānakī, the mighty one with his neck gracefully curved! [26] The younger brother of Anusahā followed the sage; he who had mastered all sciences of weaponry, the lord of the forest at Gayāvati, entered the resplendent assembly hall of King Janaka.
Having assumed a form of extraordinary splendor that deludes people, like a tree of desire for those who oppose their will,
and possessing a fierce radiance capable of shattering his own birthplace,
he— whose brilliance was equal to the dispelling of darkness— approached the son of Daśaratha along with his younger brother.
Following the sage’s instruction, Janaka joyfully beheld the supreme primordial deity who resembled the moon; regarding him as the highly esteemed husband for his daughter,
fit for the bride-price appropriate to himself, he returned home while inwardly reproaching [his own pride].
Honored by the king and worshipped with glances from the daughter of Janaka,
he firmly grasped a bow as formidable and hard as a lotus in his hand;
then, breaking that powerful and sturdy bow, he cried out loudly, "Victory to you, O scion of Raghu!"
Having caused his fame to pervade the three worlds, Rāma shone forth.
Then King Janaka, with joy, gave four beautiful maidens in marriage to the four excellent sons of Daśaratha.
Then, on the road, the descendant of Bhṛgu (Śukra) placed his own army— his sons being well-adorned— in front of himself,
yielding the foremost place of honor to the Lord of the Raghus.
Thereafter, Daśaratha returned to his own city, having obtained the husband of Sītā.

Then Kaikeyī quickly restrained the king— who, accompanied by his ministers and attendants performing their duties, was intent on placing him upon his own variegated throne so that he might possess stainless splendor. (31)
Then, at the command of his guru, the wise one set out for the forest accompanied by the daughter of King Janaka, followed by the son of Sumitrā,
leaving his own attendants behind and dwelling with devotion in the house of Guha.
Having quickly cast off his royal insignia and donned matted hair and bark garments, the Lord of the Raghus,
accompanied by his beloved wife and younger brother, was honored according to the wishes of the sages in the Pañcavaṭikā hermitage in the forest; there he met with the distressed Bharata.
Having warded off his father’s death and having resolved upon his own course, the Lord of the Raghus, afflicted by grief, dwelt for those years in the forest of asceticism;
[he who had previously rescued] the sister of the Ten-faced one, who was tormented by the piercing of the arrows of the God of Love.
Having observed the virtuous Sundarī of excellent form, who was smiling and desiring his protection,
the Lord of Janaka’s Daughter then transformed her into a hideous shape from Lakṣmaṇa’s formidable sword.
Having finished [the task] on the path, he gradually destroyed the fourteen thousand demons with his sharp arrows; he struck Khara along with his followers—
those who were under the sway of the Ten-faced one— as well as the deer that was beautiful with its shimmering golden hue.
In the forest, he who acts for both the beloved and the unloved forcibly slew the rākṣasa.
Then the ten-faced one, seeing Rāma proceeding with haste toward him in anger along with Lakṣmaṇa, abducted the daughter of Janaka from the hermitage.
Then the Lord of the Raghus, not seeing his beloved seated within the leaf-hut, fainted and lamented greatly for her, crying "Sītā!"—
searching through the forest, his own hermitage, the foot of trees, the water, and the ponds.
Having searched along the path, he saw the fallen bird with the son of Sumitrā;
then, from Jaṭāyu’s words, the Lord discerned that Jānakī had been carried off by the Ten-faced one, and performed the fire-rites for his deceased father.
Anxious at the thought of separation from his beloved, with his younger brother preceding him, Rāghava—the foremost of archers—beheld the army of monkeys led by Sugrīva.
He saw the son of the Wind-god, the beloved younger brother of Vālin, who had come from Mount Ṛṣabha; he was mature, well-disposed, and had been sent as a messenger.
Then, the opinion expressed by the son of the Wind and Sugrīva was accepted.

Having discerned that the lord of the monkeys, Vālin— who was seated upon his own royal throne— was a destroyer of the sovereign of the grasses (Śambūka), Rāma killed his dear friend and made Sugrīva his own companion. 39.
Then, searching for this daughter of Janaka to the north, the son of the Wind-god, crossing the ocean by means of the words spoken by Jaṭāyu’s brother,
entered the city of Daśānana and brought joy to the daughter of Janaka.
He returned once more to the Lord of the Raghus at the hermitage in the Aśoka grove.
Then, by the power of Hanumān, Laṅkā city was set ablaze and consumed by a mass of blazing, flaming fire, bringing about the destruction of immeasurable rākṣasas.
Having discerned the ocean's intent, the Lord, the leader of the Raghus, surrounded by the monkey commanders, grew enraged and bound the sea while drying it up with mountains.

The skillful Lord of the Raghus, whose course is ever auspicious, shattered the city and its port— though it was fortified with various types of ramparts— with wrath against the Lord of the Night-stalkers.
Thereafter, accompanied by his younger brother, he took up his powerful and fierce bow in battle.

Having struck down the foremost rākṣasas with exceedingly sharp arrows and formidable swords— amidst a tumult of elephants, chariots, horses, and swans— the king, together with his followers, shone like the tip of the tongue of powerful Time (Kāla). 42.
Then, with their arms raised like mountains and trees, those exceedingly powerful enemies, through their most terrible blows,
slaughtered the followers of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa— who were themselves capable of crushing the gods— out of their rage for Janaka’s daughter.
Nala, Aṅgada, the lord of monkeys, the son of the Wind-god, the king of bears, and others—
then the exceedingly powerful Lakṣmaṇa slew the enemy of the lord of the gods in battle,
while he was followed by hosts of blood-drinking [demons] making sounds like the rumbling of clouds. ||43||
Then, with furious blows from his sharpened sword, he struck down the night-stalkers who had assembled there— Prahasta, Vikaṭa, Nikumbha, Makarākṣa, and the others—
in that battle, along with the lords of elephants, chariots, horses, and infantry. Thus did the Ten-faced One [Rāvaṇa] act in the fray.
Surrounded by millions of invincible hosts armed with weapons,
that unconquerable one suddenly encountered the blameless scion of Raghu, who possessed infinite divine armaments and was the lord of the monkey king and his army commanders. 45.

The leader of the Raghus struck down with sharpened arrows that arrogant ten-faced enemy— who had grown powerful through the grace of Brahmā, who possessed great strength and prowess, and who stood like an immovable mountain in battle.
Then, as Kumbhakarna, the powerful commander of the night-stalkers' army, [advanced],
the sky shone, completely covered by their exceedingly sharp arrows,
resembling a mass of clouds accompanied by thundering, intoxicated lightning-flashes.

The surface of the earth was covered by the terrifying and incessant sounds of the great thunderbolts that were the bowstrings of both the Lord of the Raghus and the Lord of the Rākṣasas. Then, through the wrath of the Earth-born goddess and the power of Rāma’s various arrows, [the world was shaken].

Rāvaṇa, the terrifier of the lord of the gods, fell to the earth. Then Hari, filled with great curiosity, having restored Jānakī—who had been protected by the Fire—to the bull among the Raghus, departed for his own city, rejoicing. 48.
Then Rāghava, who had been intent on the story of Purandara, immediately rendered the lord of the rākṣasas, Vibhīṣaṇa, free from fear;
he was surrounded by the hosts of the Lord of Monkeys and accompanied by the daughter of the Earth and his younger brothers.
In the spotlessly radiant Puṣpaka chariot driven by Śiva’s friend (Nandīśvara),
the Lord of the Raghus— worshipped by hosts of lords of sages— departed for Ayodhyā,
reflecting upon the sage’s emblem and remembering his profound friendship with Guha. 50.
Then, surrounded by his own attendants and consoling the distressed Bharata according to the words of his group of mothers,
the lordly king was consecrated upon his father’s own throne by Vasiṣṭha, the preeminent among sages.
He shone like the Lord of the Gods, the protector of all people.
Men possessed many mines of wealth; the best of the twice-born were devoted to austerity and firm in their resolve to perform their own duty; they lived in the company of their kin, free from fear.
The clouds rained down abundantly and the earth was ever joyful;
while that exceedingly powerful king, the Lord of the Raghus, reigned, the world remained in a state of prosperity.
Having passed ten thousand years, he delighted his subjects with his own cherished virtues.
Delighting his own beloved with the stirrings of his own passion, the Lord of the Raghus,
though accompanied by hosts of great sages, performed sacrifices for the primordial gods with wealth and abundant sacrificial fees, through three horse-sacrifices that were like incomparable clouds.
Then, contemplating some cause within his mind, that best of the Raghus, the king, became pitiless and abandoned Janaka’s daughter in the forest;
thereafter, remembering his own resolve, the son of Pracetas brought her back.

Then, at her own hermitage, the daughter of the Earth gave birth to two sons, Kuśa and Lava, who were of noble intellect, possessed of great strength and prowess, and who sang the praises of the glory of the Lord of the Raghus— she, the beloved wife of the Lord of the Raghus, who was herself filled with sorrow.
That best of sages then entrusted her, who was accompanied by her daughter, blameless and ever worshipped by the foremost of gods, into the presence of Rāma.
Then the Lord of the Raghus [beheld] her, weeping before him along with her daughter.
He spoke again: "Enter the fire for the purification of yourself.
Having heard these words of the Lord of the Raghus, she bowed at his lotus feet and, together with her mother, entered the ground which was radiant with clusters of jewels.
Beholding the departure of Janaka’s daughter and remembering it, the Lord of the Raghus,
accompanied by his younger brother and through the yoga of his preceptor Vasiṣṭha, went to his own abode,
touching those people standing before him who were pure like cattle.
Surrounded by excellent chariots, the Lord joyfully proceeded along the banks of the Sarayū.

Those who listen with devotion to the nectar-like deeds of the scion of Raghu— which dry up the ocean of worldly existence for those who read them, bestowing fragrance and the gift of liberation— [shall attain the highest goal].

For the pacification of diseases in this world, for the attainment of wealth, progeny, heaven, and other prosperities, and for the increase of one’s lineage, the Lord Śrīśa, the Supreme Sovereign, is the source of power.
(58) Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Life of Śrī Rāmacandra," in the description of the Solar Dynasty within the third part of the *Śrī Kalki Purāṇa*, the *Anubhāgavata* of the future. (3)
The Fourth Chapter. From Rāma was born Kuśa; from him came Atithi; from him Nabha, ruler of the Niṣadhas; from him was born Puṇḍarīka; and from him Kṣemadhanvā arose. (1)
From Devānīka was born Hīna; from Hīna came Pāripātra; from him Balāhaka; from him Arka; and from him Rajanābha was born.
From Khāṇa was born Vidhṛta, and from him came the one known as Hiraṇyanābha.
From Puṣpa came Dhruva; from him, Syandana, who was the color of fire;
from him was born my father Śīghra, whose prowess was incomparable.
From him [were born] Maru, myself (Māndhātṛ), Keśin here, Budha, and also Sumitra.
"Know that having reached Kalāpagrāma, I have been established in true austerity; having learned of your incarnation from Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī,
and having awaited the time for a hundred thousand years of the Kali age, I have arrived in your presence."
The teaching of the Dharma destroys the heap of sins accumulated over ten million births;
it brings fame and renown to the Supreme Self and fulfills all desires.
Kalki said:
“Your lineage is known; you are born of the solar dynasty.
Who else besides you could be so illustrious, possessing the marks of a Great Man?
Having heard these sweet-syllabled words of Kalki, Devāpi—
Endowed with humility, he began to speak these words.
Devāpi said:
"At the end of the dissolution, the four-faced one arose from your navel-lotus."
From that Ātreya came Candra; from him, Budha; from him, Purūravas was born; from him, Yayāti; and from Nahuṣa [came Yayāti]. Yayāti, however, begot Yadu and Turvasu upon Devayānī. ||9-10||
Likewise, O Lord of the virtuous, Śarmiṣṭhā gave birth to Druhyu, Anu, and Pūru, just as the Source of Beings creates all beings out of a desire to bring them forth.
From Pūru was born Janamejaya, and from him came Pracinvān.
Pravīra was his son, and he was indeed mindful; from him came Abhayada.
From Urukṣaya came Tṛyaruṇi, and from him Puṣkarāruṇi.
From Bṛhatkṣetra came Hastī, after whom Hastināpura was named.
Ajamīḍha, Dvimīḍha, and Puramīḍha were his sons.
From Ajamīḍha was born Ṛkṣa; from him [came] Saṃvaraṇa, and from him Kuru. From Kuru were born Parikṣit, Sudhanus, Jahnu, and Niṣadha.
Suhotra was the son of Sudhanus; from Cyavana was born Kṛti.
From him came Bṛhadratha, and from him Kuśāgra, from whom Ṛṣabha was born.
Then came Satyajit, whose son was Puṣpavān, and from him Nahuṣa.
From Bṛhadratha’s wife was born Jarāsaṃdha, the scorcher of foes;
from him came Sahadeva, and from him Somāpi, who was also known as Śrutaśravas.
From Suratha was born Vidūratha, and from him Sārvabhauma arose.
From Jayasena came Rathānīka, and from him was born the wrathful Yutāyus.
From him came Devātithi; from him, Dṛkṣa; from him, Dilīpa;
from him, Pratīpaka; and his son was I, the lord Devāpi. (18–19)
Having given the kingdom to Śāntanu, he devoted his mind for a long time to asceticism;
now, having reached Kalāpa village and attained the lotus feet of these sages, he has come here desiring to see you.
20. Maruṇānena munibhir ebhiḥ prāpya padāmbujam.
"From your mouth, terrible as Death, I shall go to the abode of the self-possessed.
Having heard these words of the two of them, the lotus-eyed Kalki laughed and, having comforted Marudeva, spoke to her.
Kalki said:
"Both of you are known as kings who understand the supreme dharma; by carrying out my command, you shall sustain your own kingdom. (23)
"O Devāpi, having slain the most unrighteous Mlecchas who harm living beings, I shall now consecrate you in my own city of Ayodhyā;
you shall rule in your kingdom at the city of Hastināpura."
"O royal sage, having slain the Pukkasa demons in battle, I shall consecrate you.
By staying in Mathurā, I will remove your fear of the Śayyākarṇas, the Uṣṭramukhas, the Ekajaṅghas, and the Vinodarās. (25-26)
Having slain [the enemies] and established the Kṛta Yuga, I shall protect the subjects,
having cast off my ascetic garb and vows and mounted my excellent chariot.
You two, skilled in weapons and missiles, shall be equipped with hosts of troops and attendants.
Having become great chariot-warriors in this world, you two shall wander with me.
King Viśākhayūpa will bestow upon you in marriage his daughter Sundarī, who is endowed with modesty and possesses beautiful, long-cornered eyes.
"O virtuous protector of the earth, for the welfare of the world, do as I say:
O Devāpi, marry Śāntā, the daughter of Rucirāśva.
Having heard these words of consolation from Kalki along with the sages, those two—

With hearts filled with wonder, they both recognized Hari as the Lord. While he was thus speaking, granting fearlessness, two chariots resembling the sun, constructed from various clusters of jewels and moving at will, appeared before them from the sky.
Surrounded by blazing divine weapons and missiles, they arrived;
the kings, the hosts of sages, and the members of the assembly saw them in the midst of the gathering—crafted by Viśvakarman—and, filled with joy, exclaimed, "What is this? ||32-33||
Kalki said:
"These people know that you two kings, born from the sons of Āditya, Soma, Indra, and Yama, have manifested for the sake of protecting the world. (34)
"O Kāla and Ākāra, you two who have arisen here through my association, mount this chariot given by Śakra at my command.
While the eternal Padmanātha, the Lord of the Universe, was speaking thus—

The gods rained down flowers, and the sages offered praises before him. A breeze blew gently, auspicious like the touch of the daughter of the mountain (Pārvatī), carrying the pollen from the sacred ashes that moistened his head with the waters of the Gaṅgā.
There arrived one whose body was radiant with joy, resembling molten gold;

a dwelling-place of Dharma, wearing beautiful matted hair and bark garments, holding a staff in his hand; transcendent of the world, his own body like the wind, who had destroyed the assembly of unrighteousness.
A mass of splendor, like Sanaka, a mendicant with eyes as large as lotus petals.
||38|| Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Genealogy of the Lunar Lineage," in the third part of the *Śrī Kalki Purāṇa*, the *Anubhāgavata* of the future.
Chapter Five.
Śuka said:
Then Kalki, having beheld him along with the lords of the assemblies,
rose up and honored him with water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping, and other rites.
Having seated that aged mendicant, who was honored by all hermitages, he asked: "Who are you that have come here by my good fortune?
For generally, men in this world [come] with the desire to reach the further shore of the worlds."
They move about as friends to all, full and free from stain.
Maskarī said: "O Lord, I am the supreme Kṛta Age, carrying out your command."
I have come here for the purpose of beholding the glory of your manifestation.

You, who are Time itself, are without attributes; yet through your own *māyā*, you have assumed the state of being possessed of attributes by means of parts such as moments (*kṣaṇa*), hours (*daṇḍa*), and minutes (*lava*). ||4-5||
By your gaze, these—days and nights, fortnights, months, seasons, years, yugas, and so forth—as well as the fourteen Manus, proceed in their courses.
Svāyambhuva was the first; after him came the Manu Svārociṣa.
The third was Uttama; after him, the fourth is remembered as Tāmasa.
The fifth is celebrated as Raivata, and the sixth as Cākṣuṣa.
Vaivasvata is indeed the seventh, and Sāvarṇi is the eighth.
The ninth is Dakṣasāvarṇi; after that is Brahmasāvarṇika;
the tenth is Dharmasāvarṇi, who is called the eleventh;
and Rudrasāvarṇika is indeed remembered as the twelfth Manu there.
The thirteenth Manu is Veda-sāvarṇi, renowned throughout the world;
the fourteenth is Indra-sāvarṇi— these are your manifestations,
which go forth, come back, and shine forth through the distinctions of name, form, and so on.
Twelve thousand years of the gods constitute a *caturyuga*;
it is considered that [the four ages] are calculated as four, three, two, and one thousand [divine years].
Likewise, there are four hundred, three hundred, two hundred, and one hundred [years for each respectively].
By the sequence of the *sandhyās*, their *sandhyāṃśas* are likewise of that same nature.
There, a Manu enjoys the earth for seventy-one *yugas*.
Such is the duration for all the Manus as well.
That which is day for Prajāpati is proclaimed as night for him;
his day and night constitute a fortnight, and from those come the months and years.
Time, fashioned by these various conditions, brings about the birth and death of Brahmā.
At the end of a hundred years, Brahmā indeed attains dissolution into you; then, at the conclusion of that dissolution, the Lord arises from the center of your navel and creates [the world].
There, at the end of the Kṛta Yuga, I [shall manifest] Time as the protector of the true Dharma.
"Where the subjects have accomplished all that was to be done, they know me by that name.
Having heard those words, Kalki, surrounded by his own people,
attained incomparable joy upon hearing that nectar-like speech.
Perceiving the hypocrisy of the age, the Lord, desiring to fight and eager for the slaughter in the city of Kali, spoke these words for the benefit of the people:
"The elephants, chariots, horses, and men who are warriors..."
Count and bring those whose limbs are adorned with various golden ornaments, who carry a multitude of diverse excellent missiles and weapons, and who are skilled in battle. ||20||
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Arrival of the Kṛta Yuga," in the third part of the glorious *Kalki Purāṇa*, an *Anubhāgavata* of the future.
Chapter Six.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of Kalki, those two mighty-armed ones, Marudeva and Āpi, performed their marriage ceremony in his presence, mounted their chariot, and arrived,
surrounded by armies bearing various weapons and considering themselves heroes.
With their fingers and arms protected by leather guards and finger-cuffs, clad in armor, and with their hands bound [in readiness],
they wore helmets of black iron; as preeminent archers,
they caused the earth to tremble with the weight of their sixfold akṣauhiṇī armies.
King Viśākhayūpa, however, was surrounded by hundreds of thousands of elephants,
hundreds of thousands of horses, seven thousand chariots,
and two hundred thousand foot soldiers, all armored and bearing bows.
Surrounded on all sides by fifty thousand chariots of the Magas, each with horses as red as blood and topped with turbans fluttering in the wind,
and encircled by ten hundred thousand rutting elephants, he shone resplendent. ||5-6||
Kalki, the conqueror of enemy cities, was surrounded by ten akṣauhiṇīs as well as by the gods, just as Indra, the sovereign in heaven,
is surrounded by his brothers, sons, friends, and joyful soldiers.
The Lord and Master of the worlds set out, desiring the conquest of all quarters.
At that time, Dharma, having become a twice-born brahmin, arrived accompanied by his attendants, though he had been cast out by the powerful Kali.
Then [he gave] truth, serenity, fearlessness, happiness, joy, and himself;
then yoga, purpose, freedom from pride, mindfulness, security, and a refuge.
Both Nara and Nārāyaṇa were portions of Hari, devoted to austerity and vows.
But Dharma, having taken these sons and daughters with him, arrived in haste:

Faith, Friendliness, Compassion, Tranquility, Contentment, Prosperity, Action, Excellence, Intelligence, Wisdom, Forbearance, and Modesty—the embodiments of Dharma, who protect righteousness. ||11-12||
They arrived there with him, together with their own groups of kinsmen, to behold Kalki and to report their own business.
Kalki, having approached the brāhmaṇa, honored him according to the prescribed rites.
Overcome with humility, he said: "Who are you, and from where have you come?
Accompanied by women and sons like a planet whose merit has been exhausted, from which king's realm do you hail? Please tell me all of that."
"Your sons and wives are wretched, their own strength and prowess diminished,
like virtuous Vaiṣṇavas who have been insulted by heretics.
Hearing these words of Kalki, Dharma remembered his own true nature.
Extremely distressed and helpless, he spoke to the Lord of Kamalā;
having praised, bowed to, and worshipped Hari—who was joyful and supremely compassionate—with his sons, wives, and kinsmen with palms joined in reverence. ||17-18||
Dharma said: Listen, O Kalki, to my narrative; I am Dharma, born from the chest of you who are the embodiment of Brahman, the granter of desires to all embodied beings. (19)
The leader of the gods, the fulfiller of desires, the all-pervading lord of offerings to the gods and ancestors—
I move about day after day performing righteous deeds solely by your command.
Yet, I have been cast out by powerful Time and by Kali as well.
O Support of All, now all those inhabitants of Āvāsa— the Śakas, Kāmbojas, and Śabaras— have come to the soles of Your feet,
just as afflicted holy men, tormented by the fire of the world’s time, seek refuge.
Thus gratified by these unprecedented words according to the Dharma, the illustrious Kalki, the destroyer of all impurity, spoke slowly, causing great joy:
"Behold, O Dharma, the Kṛta Age and Maru, born of the lineage of the Sun!"
Know me as one born with a body assumed at the request of the Dhātṛs; being thus,
remain at ease, considering that the destruction of the Buddhists— and of others who are non-Vaiṣṇavas and who cause you distress— is my task.
"I am going forth with my armies, desiring to slay; you, however, roam the earth free from fear.
What fear do you have? Where is there delusion for you? O Lord, wander about accompanied by sacrifices, gifts, austerities, and vows, now that Truth has been established in me. (25-26)
"I am departing; you go with your sons and kinsmen for the sake of conquering the quarters and subduing the enemies, O beloved of the world.
Having heard these words of Kalki, Dharma was exceedingly delighted.
Having resolved to go, remembering his own lordship,
he left his own people and those women behind at Siddhāśrama;
equipped with the honors of the virtuous, he was a great chariot-warrior of the Vedas and Brahman.
With the bow of his excellent resolve,
the seven musical notes as his horses, the Brahmins as his charioteer, and the sacred fire as his refuge,
the leader of Dharma set forth, endowed with the power of various ritual distinctions. (30–31)
Surrounded by those worthy of sacrifice, charity, and austerity, as well as by restraints and observances,
Kalki went forth to conquer all the Khaśas, Kambojas, Śabaras, and Barbaras, wherever the desired abode of Kali might be.
It was endowed with the power of the abodes of spirits and crowded with excellent dogs;
it was filled with the foul stench of putrid beef and swarmed with crows, owls, and jackals;
it was a refuge for women addicted to gambling, quarrels, disputes, and vices.
Hearing that Kalki, the lord of women, had made an effort against his formidable home— which causes terror to the world— Kali, surrounded by sons and grandsons,
departed from the city in wrath upon a chariot drawn by peacock-eyed horses.
Beholding Kali, Bharma, surrounded by sages and impelled by the words of Kalki, suddenly fought with him; likewise,
Dambha fought in the battle, and Prasāda challenged Lobha.
Through the agreement, Krodha obtained fearlessness, while Bhaya attained happiness;
having found joy, he fought with various weapons.
Likewise, Vyādhi [arose] through Ādhi, and [the latter] through powerful security.
Likewise, through humility, exhaustion summoned mindfulness;
thus occurred that great, terrible, and most dreadful battle,
which the gods, led by Brahmā, came to behold from the sky with their divine splendors.
Maru fought with the Khaśas and the Kāmbojas of terrible prowess;
Devāpi fought in battle with the Cauṇas, the Barbaras, and their tribes;
and King Viśākhayūpa fought with the Pulindas and the Śvapacas.
Kalki fought with various weapons and highly radiant divine missiles against Kokavikoka and his armies equipped with excellent arms;
those two, Kokavikoka and his companion, were arrogant due to the boons granted by Brahmā.
The two brothers, the best of Dānavas, intoxicated with pride and skilled in battle, were of identical form, possessed of great strength, and increased the fear of the gods;
they were foot-soldiers with maces in hand, their limbs as hard as adamant, and victorious over all directions.
Because they were both surrounded by Śumbhas and were victors over death, they fought together in one place.
Kalki, accompanied by his multitude of troops, fought with those two; a tumultuous battle took place between Kalki’s auspicious forces and their opponents.
All the quarters were filled with neighing, trumpeting, the clashing of teeth,
the sound of sword-strikes, the war-cries of heroes, the force of arms, and the slapping of palms;
all the worlds found no peace.
And the gods, terrified with fear, fled through the sky along scattered paths;
[they were pursued] by nooses, staffs, swords, spears, lances, and tridents,
by blows from maces, and by the terrible discharge of arrows.
In the battle, heroes fell by the hundreds and by the millions in the conflict, their arms, feet, and torsos severed.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Battle of Kalki’s Army," in the third part of the *Śrī Kalki Purāṇa*, the *Anubhāgavata* concerning the future.
The Seventh Chapter.
Sūta said:
While the battle was thus proceeding, Dharma became exceedingly enraged.
Accompanied by Kṛta, he fought a terrible battle with Kali.
Kali, overwhelmed by the floods of arrows from Dharma and Kṛta,
fled toward the city, abandoning his donkey mount.
With his horses and chariot shattered, his mass of limbs dripping with blood,
smelling of raw flesh, and possessing a terrifying countenance, Dambha went to the house of his mistress,
where he was struck by a multitude of arrows drawn and discharged without any thought of enjoyment.
Agitated, a mere cinder of his own lineage and devoid of essence, he entered the house.
Struck down by the grace [of the Lord] and having his head split open by the mace, Lobha abandoned his severed dog-chariot and fled, vomiting blood.
Conquered by fearlessness, Krodha, whose eyes were stained with impurity,
abandoned his severed scent-elephant mount and fled to the slaughterhouse.
From the blow of the palm of [Abhaya’s] hand, he fell lifeless upon the ground.
Niraya, tormented by Mudā and Muṣṭi, went to Yama.
All [afflictions] such as mental anguish and physical disease, having abandoned their vehicles, fled in agitation from various regions, tormented by the arrows he had discharged. ||7-8||
Accompanied by Kṛta, Dharma went to the city of Kali’s slaughter and, together with Kali, consumed it with showers of arrows and fire.
Kali, his entire body scorched, was left with his wife dead and his offspring dead.
Wailing and dejected, he went alone and unobserved to another region.
Maru, however, slew the Śakas and Kāmbojas by the power of his divine weapons;
Devāpi likewise struck down the Śabaras, the Colas, the Barbaras, and their tribes as well. ||10-11||
The valiant King Viśākhayūpa tormented the Pulindas and even the Pukkasas with the discharge of divine missiles and weapons;
he of stainless wisdom struck them down in great numbers with the falling of his sword.
By showers of various missiles and weapons, those warriors perished in many ways.
Kalki, the lord of battles, armed with a mace and skilled in strategic deployment, fought against Kokavikoka, instilling fear in the worlds.
Hari fought with those two sons of Vṛkāsura, the grandsons of Śakuni, just as Kalki had fought with Madhu and Kaiṭabha;
by the blow of their mace, the body of that lord fell, crushed to pieces.
Seeing it fall from his hand to the ground, the people exclaimed, "Aha!
Then, filled with wrath once more, the mighty-armed Lord Viṣṇu, desiring to conquer the world, severed the head of that Vikoka with a broad-headed arrow (bhalla).
The dead Vikoka rose up upon seeing Koka;
at that sight, the gods and Kalki, the slayer of enemy heroes, were struck with wonder. Then, Kalki severed the head of Koka, who was armed with a mace and seeking retaliation.
The dead Koka rose up from the glance of Vikoka.
Once again those two met and, possessing great strength and assuming forms at will, those heroes fought like two other embodiments of Time and Death. ||19-20||
Wielding sword and shield, the two struck Kalki again and again;
in his wrath, Kalki likewise struck off their heads with an arrow. Seeing them fallen once more, Hari became lost in thought.
Then, perceiving his state of attachment, the horse struck him with its hooves.
Greatly afflicted by the horse, those two, who were like Death himself and difficult to overcome,
their eyes copper-red with indignation, struck Kalki with their maces.
Between those two, that horse bit fiercely in his rage;
with their bones and arms shattered and their armlets and bows torn away, they both seized the tail of the winged steed like two boys grasping the tail of a cow.

With their tails held up, those two fainted; at that very moment they rose again, and thereafter he struck them firmly on the chest with his feet as if with a thunderbolt. Having abandoned their tails, those two fainted; at that very moment they rose again.
Beholding Kalki before them, they spoke with clear articulation.
Then Brahmā, approaching him with his palms joined in reverence, slowly said to Kalki: "He does not deserve death by means of weapons or missiles."
Since the death of both was brought about by a single blow of the hand at the same time,
yet neither died from merely seeing the other, knowing this, O self, bring about the simultaneous destruction of these two.

Having heard these words of Brahmā, Kalki— having laid aside his weapons, missiles, and mounts— angrily shattered the heads of those two Dānavas as they were striking him at will with fists like thunderbolts.
With their brains shattered, those two fell there like two bulls with broken horns—
causing fear among the gods in heaven and bringing affliction upon the earth.
Seeing that great marvel, the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases [were struck with wonder].
The sages, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas danced, sang, and offered hymns of praise;
and the gods, their hearts filled with joy, rained down showers of flowers. In the heavens the kettledrums resounded, and the quarters of the sky became serene.
Delighting in their slaughter, the wise Kavi, with his divine arrows, directly slew ten thousand great chariot-warriors along with their horses at the front of the battle.
||32|| He, the prudent one, [slew] hundreds of thousands of warriors at the head of the fray.
Sumantra caused the destruction of twenty-five chariot-warriors among the Nityas;
likewise, other great car-warriors such as Gārgya, Bharga, and Viśāla, being enraged in battle, slew the Niṣādas, Mlecchas, and Barbaras. ||33-34||
Having thus conquered them all along with the hosts of kings, Kalki,
together with the Śayyākarṇas and the Varāstras, set out to conquer the city of Bhallāṭa amidst various musical instruments and throngs of people. ||35||
With his limbs adorned with various garments and ornaments,
being fanned by fly-whisks borne by various mounts,
the exceedingly fierce Kalki went forth to fight. (36)
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Slaying of Kokavikoka and Others," in the third part of the *Śrī Kalki Purāṇa*, the *Anubhāgavata* in the future age.
Chapter Eight.
Sūta said:
Surrounded by hosts of armies, the lord Kalki Nārāyaṇa,
wielding a sword and mounted on a horse, proceeded toward the city of Bhallāṭa.
That yogin, the lord of Bhallāṭa, recognized him as Viṣṇu, the master of the universe.
Accompanied by his own hosts of troops and desiring to fight, he went toward Hari.
