That illustrious one, his hair standing on end with joy, tall-limbed, meditating upon Kṛṣṇa, bearing the moon as his banner, possessed of great splendor, the strength of ten thousand elephants, and highly intelligent—[he went]. ||2-3||
His wife, the great queen Suśāntā, who was devoted to the vows of Viṣṇu, spoke to her husband as he was preparing to fight with Kalki:
"O Lord, O Beloved, [speak of] the Lord of the World, the Master who dwells within all. (4)
"How will you strike Kalki, who is Nārāyaṇa himself?
Śaśidhvaja said:
"In the Suśānta age, the supreme dharma was ordained by Prajāpati."
In battle, a blow is received everywhere, whether by the teacher or the disciple, just as in the case of Hari.
For one who lives, there is the enjoyment of kings; dead, one rejoices in heaven.
Victory or death in battle brings happiness to Kṣatriyas.
Suśānta said:
"Divinity or kingship may indeed belong to those who are intoxicated by sense objects and lustful, but never to those who serve the feet of Hari. (8)
"You are a servant and he is a lord; you are free from desire and he is a giver.
How can a meeting for battle between you two come about through delusion?
Śaśidhvaja said:
If there were duality between the Lord and the servant when He has transcended all duality, then that service would be merely a play arising from the entry of the body; such is my [view].
Through the entry of the body, the qualities belonging to the body, such as desire and the like, belong to the Lord.
If the limbs of Māyā are born, why are the objects not likewise?
When the Lord of Brahman possesses a body through Brahman, the servant who perceives non-difference likewise undergoes birth, dissolution, and emergence. (11–12)
The relationship of master and servant regarding Viṣṇu is proclaimed as his *māyā*;
this activity, characterized by both duality and non-duality, produces the three goals of life for the virtuous.
Therefore, my beloved, I am going with my own army to fight against Kalkin.
"O beloved, worship today that Lord, the husband of Kamalā.
Suśāntā said:
"I have attained my life's purpose through you, whose soul is united with the service of Viṣṇu."
"O Lord, the goal of the Vaiṣṇavas is renowned both in this world and the next.
As she spoke these charming words while bowing down, Śaśidhvaja,
his eyes filled with tears, remembered Hari and considered himself a true Vaiṣṇava.
Embracing her with great joy, surrounded by many heroes, and speaking while remembering her name and form, he advanced to fight with the Vaiṣṇavas.
Having entered Kalki’s army, he put the vast host to flight.
Surrounded by hosts of brave warriors with ears like beds, armored and with weapons raised,
the illustrious and mighty Sūryaketu, son of Śaśidhvaja, a devotee of Viṣṇu and the best among archers, fought with King Maru. ||18-19||
His younger brother was Bṛhatketu, handsome and possessing a voice like the cuckoo;
skilled in mace-fighting, he fought with Devāpi. King Viśākha-yupa, however, fought with King Śaśidhvaja.
Surrounded by elephants, he fought with various weapons.
The powerful Rudhirāśva, a bow-wielder of light hand,
fought in that dust against the archer Bharga, the son of Śantanu.
A battle took place with spears, lances, blows from maces, arrows, javelins, double-edged swords, iron clubs, bhallas, scimitars, bhuśuṇḍīs, and kunta-spears;
it was filled with banners, standards, emblems, iron pikes, umbrellas, and chowries.
A great darkness arose from the rising masses of dust.
In the sky, which was filled with clouds, which gods did not take up residence?
[They were accompanied] by Gandharvas, singers of exquisite compositions who are sources of nectar. ||24-25||
All the worlds gathered to witness that wondrous battle; yet,
despite the blaring of conchs and kettledrums, the slapping of arms, and the neighing of horses,
as well as the shouts of the warriors, the people became as if mute.
Chariot-warriors with chariot-warriors, and foot-soldiers with foot-soldiers;
horses with horses, and elephants with elephants—the battle between the gods and the dānavas became as dense as it was, increasing the population of Yama’s kingdom. ||27-28||
Along with the generals of the army of Śaśidhvaja and the commanders of Kalki's forces,
the soldiers fell to the ground with their arms, feet, and necks severed;
running, crying out, and contorting themselves, they were drenched in blood.
Covered one upon another and crushed by elephants, horses, and chariots,
heroes fell by the thousands of millions in that battle,
while the hosts of spirits rejoiced as they drank the flowing water of blood.
With the heads of slain elephants for their rafts,
with arms for their fish and ornaments, and with swords for their golden sands—
thus did these most terrible rivers flow forth instantly in the battle.
The powerful Sūryaketu, accompanied by Maru, fought on;
that invincible one, who was like Death itself, struck Maru with arrows.
But there, Maru pierced him deeply with ten shafts.
Struck by Marutbāṇa, the indignant hero Sūryaketu,
in his wrath, slew the horses and crushed that chariot with a kick of his foot.
Then, having pulverized it, he struck him [Marutbāṇa] on the chest with that same [kick].
By that blow of the mace, Maru fell into a swoon;
the charioteer, knowing his duty, carried him away on the chariot and not otherwise.
And the powerful Bṛhatketu covered Devāpi with arrows.
Drawing his bow with speed, he surrounded [the enemy] with a rain of arrows using his own weapons, like the sun obscured by mist; then,
with stone-sharpened shafts feathered with heron plumes, he struck Bṛhatketu firmly.
Then, seeing his spear shattered,
Bṛhatketu took up a bow and struck Devāpi along with his troops with three swift arrows— gold-tufted, vulture-feathered, iron-tipped, and sharp-edged— as they fell upon him. (39–40)
Devāpi also cut that divine bow with sharp arrows;
his bow severed, Bṛhatketu, sword in hand,
sought to slay Devāpi’s charioteer along with his horses in that great battle.
That Devāpi, casting aside his bow, struck that enemy with his palm;
bringing him between his arms, he mercilessly crushed him— him who was sixteen years of age, fallen, unconscious, and afflicted by his foe.
Seeing his younger brother Devāpi, Sūryadhvaja struck him on the head with his fist as if with a thunderbolt; he fell to the ground unconscious,
and his enemy, out of rage, struck the host of his army.

Śaśidhvaja beheld Kalki, the abode of the entire world, standing before him with the brilliance of the rising sun—dark-complexioned, clad in saffron robes, lotus-eyed, with mighty arms, and adorned with a beautiful crown;
his body’s splendor, composed of a multitude of various jewels, dispelled the darkness from the eyes and hearts of all people in the world. (45)
He beheld the Lord, who was surrounded by Viśākha, Yūpa, and others, and honored for the dharma he had performed.
(46) Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Battle between the Armies of Śaśidhvaja and Kalki," in the third part of the *Anubhāgavata*, the future *Kalki Purāṇa*.
Chapter Nine.
Sūta said:
Having beheld the form of Kalki— the object of meditation within his heart— standing full, holding a sword, and mounted upon a beautiful horse, Śaśidhvaja spoke.

With his hair standing on end, Śaśidhvaja spoke to that Supreme Soul, who held a bow and arrows, whose limbs were adorned with beautiful ornaments, and who was intent upon destroying the suffering of sin for the sake of the worlds.
"Come, come, O lotus-eyed one! Strike me in the heart with a blow.

Or else, O Self, out of fear of my arrows, enter my heart which is blinded by darkness; for in me, who am devoid of qualities, there is the state of being a knower of qualities, and in me, who am non-dual, there is the striking of weapons."
"Let the worlds behold my army in battle, which serves as an aid for the effort to conquer [the enemy] on behalf of the Supreme Soul who is free from desire; provided that,
while you possess such power, another's intellect remains firm enough to strike."
"I shall go to the world of battle to create a division between Śiva and Viṣṇu.
Having heard these words of the king, the Lord, free from anger though appearing as if enraged,
struck his enemies in the fray with arrows as they held their weapons, bringing them under control.
Śaśidhvaja, disregarding that blow, struck him with excellent weapons and a shower of arrows, as one strikes a mountain with torrents of rain.
Kalki, his inner being pierced by that shower of arrows, became exceedingly enraged.
A battle took place between them with multitudes of divine weapons and missiles:
the Brahmāstra against the Brahmāstras, the Vāyavya against the Pārāvatas, the Āgneya against the Pārjanya, and the Pannaga against the Gāruḍa.
Thus they struck one another with various kinds of weapons;
the worlds, along with their guardians, were terrified and thought the end of the age had come.
Indeed, the gods, fleeing through the sky, were struck with fear by the fire of the arrows.
Then Vāsudeva and Śaśidhvaja,
both exerting themselves with great effort, being deprived of their weapons, fought each other in hand-to-hand combat with kicks, slaps, and blows from their fists.
The two heroes, skilled in wrestling, rejoiced at one another;
with a roar like that of a boar being uprooted, Hari struck him with his palm.
That king, though stunned by the blow, rose up from his rage in that very instant.
With his two fists, which were like thunderbolts, he struck Kalki with great force;
from that blow, Kalki fell to the ground unconscious.
Seeing the Lord of the World thus rendered unconscious, Dharma and Kṛta [were overcome].
When they arrived, the king seized them both by the armpits to bring Kalki back;
having achieved his purpose, he took Kalki by the chest and returned home,
having seen that the two sons of the other kings were invincible in battle.
Having defeated Kalki, the lord of the gods, in battle,
and having established Dharma and the Kṛta age within his own two armpits, the Destroyer,
his heart throbbing with joy, was covered in horripilation.
Having gone home, he saw her, perfectly tranquil, in the house of Hari. Seeing her beautiful face amidst the Vaiṣṇava women who were singing stories of Hari’s virtues, the king then spoke to her.

Through the words of discipline for the gods and others, by his birth in Śambhala, or by the attainment of knowledge, Kalki himself has truly come here to bring about the marriage rite and the destruction of the barbarians and heretics.
||19|| He has indeed arrived here in person within my heart.
Under the pretext of fainting, you have served me for the sake of a glance; O beloved, look upon and honor the merit I have performed, and provide for it within your two peaceful armpits. 20.

Thus, at the king’s words, filled with delight, the women— shameless in their dancing and devoted to chanting the virtues of Hari— bowed to the Lord who was joined by Hari and performed a dance together with their companions. Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Bringing of the Dharma-Kalkis," in the third part of the *Śrī Kalki Purāṇa*, the *Anubhāgavata* concerning the future.
The Tenth Chapter. Suśānti said:
Victory to you, O Hari! Your lotus feet, adorned with many ornaments, are served by the lords of the immortals.
Place me at your forefront, O virtuous one; abandon your own delusion, O high-minded one!
Your body is fashioned from the excellence of the world’s forms and dwells in the minds of the good; perform an act that captivates the mind of the Lord of Love and is intoxicated with passion.
May your fame, which destroys the sorrow of the world and bestows joy through the nectar of its gentle discourse,
and may your moon-like face, sprinkled with the ambrosia of your smile, bring abundant auspiciousness to the world.
(3) Even if this husband of mine, who is invincible to all, should perform an act displeasing to you...
Therefore, subdue that enemy of yours; do not show compassion if you are such a Lord.
Your body, composed of the five elements and joined with the ego (ahaṃkāra), was fashioned by Prakṛti as his wife;
yet through your mere glance, the world—conceived by Brahmā—is effortlessly brought about, maintained, and dissolved.

O All-pervading Lord, through Your own three-fold *māyā* which rests upon the elements of earth, water, air, ether, and fire, and which resides within the body and the senses, please show mercy to those who seek Your service.
Those who chant Your holy name, "Guṇālaya," which purifies and removes the impurities of the Kali age— [may they be blessed].
Alas! People tormented by suffering repeatedly wander through cyclic existence, failing to destroy the fear of worldly becoming.

May your birth—increasing the honor of the virtuous, the destroyer of the lineage of Jinas, the protector of gods, the bestower of the Kṛta Age, the fulfiller of Dharma, and the ender of the Kali age—grant me auspiciousness.
My house, my husband, my sons, and my grandsons—[all these] along with elephants, chariots, banners, chowries, and wealth.
Without the honor of your two lotus feet, do the finest jewels and thrones truly bring any splendor?
O you of graceful movements, if your world-embodiment, your face with its beautiful smile, and your faultless, lovely radiance do not please me, then alas, let death come upon me here and now! 9–10.
"O rider of the horse, remover of fear, *karahara*, refuge, most fierce one, wielder of the excellent arrow, subduer of those with the ten powers,
victory to you who have destroyed the burden of others, consumer of the veil of existence, equal to a hundred moons, O you whose face is filled with the essence of nectar!
(11) Thus, he was thoroughly gratified by the song of that Suśāntā.
Kalki rose from his bed of battle like a hero established in combat.
Seeing Suśāntā before him, Dharma on his left, and Śaśidhvaja behind him, he spoke with a face cast down in shame.
"Who are you, O lotus-petal-eyed one, who has set out for the sake of serving me?
O lovely one, the heroic Śaśidhvaja stands behind me.
O Dharma! O Kṛtayuga! How have we come to this place?"

Tell me, having abandoned the field of battle, how is it that the wives of this enemy joyfully serve me, their foe, within his inner apartments? And why does Śaśidhvaja, who prides himself on his heroism, not slay me while I am unconscious? (15-16)
Śuśānta said:
Whether in the netherworld, in heaven, or on earth, among men, nāgas, gods, or asuras—who among them does not perform service to Nārāyaṇa in his Kalki incarnation? (17)
Since even the state of enmity ceases upon merely seeing those who are servants, friends of the world, and allies— how much more so his actual enemy?
My husband was engaged in battle with you in a state of hostility.
If he is fit, why bring him to your own home?
You are my master and I am your own slave;
O mighty-armed one, you have come for the sake of bringing us together in favor.

Dharma said: "O destroyer of the Kali age, by your devotion and by your chanting of the names and forms of these two, I have attained my purpose; I have attained my purpose; I have attained my purpose. (21)
The Kṛtayuga said:
"Now, by the sight of you, my servant, I am the Kṛtayuga; indeed, through the splendor of this servant of yours, who is worshiped by the world, you are the Lord. (22)
Śaśidhvaja said:

O Lord, punish me, who am worthy of punishment, for I have raised my weapons out of a warrior's duty—that passion of desire and the like by which enmity even toward You has arisen within my own self. (23)
Having heard these words of theirs, Kalki, with a smiling face,
said to the king again and again, "I have been defeated by you.
Then King Śaśidhvaja, having summoned his sons from the battle, [spoke].
Having understood the mind of Suśāntā, he gave Ramā to Sakalki. Then Marudevā also arrived, as did King Viśākhayūpa and Rudhirāśva, who had been brought together by Śaśidhvaja from the battle.
King Śayyākarṇa also arrived at the city of Bhallāṭa;
that city was crushed by countless hosts of troops, crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots, as well as foot-soldiers, parasols, and banners. ||27||
The Kalkins also, together with their armies and vehicles, arrived in haste out of joy to witness the magnificent wedding festivities of Ramā;
they were accompanied by the resounding blasts of conchs, kettledrums, clay drums, and various musical instruments.
With dances, songs, and various auspicious rites performed by the women of the city,
the marriage of Kalki with Ramā was exceedingly joyful.
Honored with various kinds of foods, the kings entered the assembly hall.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those of lower castes, adorned with various ornaments and garments, sat down to behold Kalki;
in that assembly, the lotus-eyed Kalki shone resplendently. ||31-32||
Standing in the midst of the host of stars like the full moon, the sovereign of the assembly of kings shone, utterly bewildering all the worlds.
Beholding Kalki, the Lord of Ramā, who had arrived at the assembly with eyes as broad as lotus petals, the king—
Having recognized his son-in-law through his devoted service, he sat down there in their midst.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Marriage of Kalki and Ramā," in the third part of the *Śrī Kalki Purāṇa*, the Anubhāgavata of the future.
The eleventh chapter.
Sūta said:
There, in the midst of the assembly, they spoke of that devotee of Viṣṇu, Śaśidhvaja.
[They saw him] whose body was entirely devoted to devotion as described by the sages,
and who was perfectly tranquil even through the performance of dharma according to the prescribed rules.
The kings said:
"You two have attained the status of fathers-in-law to this Nārāyaṇa Kalki;
we— these kings, these worlds, the sages, and the brahmins—
are struck with wonder at beholding the canopy of your devotion to Hari."
We ask you: where was this devotion to the Supreme Self obtained?
By whom was it taught, O King, or is it innate to you?
O King, we wish to hear about that which purifies the inhabitants of the three worlds.
[Please tell us] the Bhāgavata story from you, which destroys the fatigue of worldly existence.
Śaśidhvaja said:
O you of unfailing prowess, listen to that [story] concerning us two, a woman and a man.
The account of his birth, deeds, and so forth, which is characterized by devotion, is as follows:
"Formerly, at the end of a thousand yugas, I was a vulture, a consumer of putrid flesh; this female vulture was my beloved, and we had built our nest in a tree in the forest. (6–7)
They roamed at will everywhere through the thickets of forests and groves, providing sustenance for living beings with floods of putrid flesh from deceased creatures.
Once, a cruel hunter lured those two meat-eaters.
Seeing us, he placed a well-fed vulture there as well.
Seeing it, the man and woman, tormented by hunger and their minds lured by the sight of meat, fell there with full confidence.
Seeing us bound, the hunter then approached with joy and swiftly seized us by the neck, unharmed except for the blow from the tip of his beak.
Having captured us, he [placed us] upon a rock near the water at the Gaṇḍakī river.
The flesh-eating hunter crushed his brain;
yet at that very moment, by dying in the Ganges on the stone marked with the discus,
they instantly became four-armed and ascended in a celestial chariot composed of light.
Upon reaching the abode of Vaikuṇṭha, which is honored by all the worlds,
they remained there for a hundred yugas of Brahmā and then returned to his world.
Having indeed enjoyed themselves in the world of Brahmā for five hundred yugas, they departed.
Four hundred cycles passed in the world of the gods under the sway of time.
Then, on earth, there were kings for that same duration, while I remained in the world as one whose son was bound, remembering the grace of Hari and devoted to the practice of the Śālagrāma stone.
"I do not know what will come of serving Vāsudeva.
Thus, our minds overwhelmed with joy during the worship of Hari, we remain here dancing, singing along, and rolling about on the ground.
"The incarnation of Kalki, a portion of Nārāyaṇa, who shall bring about the destruction of the Kali age— whose prowess was known of old and heard from the mouth of Brahmā"—
having thus recited his own accounts in the assembly of kings, he [spoke]. (20)
With devotion, he respectfully gave ten thousand elephants and one hundred thousand horses;
and with great piety, he gave six thousand chariots and six hundred young female servants to the Lord of Ramā.
Having given away highly precious jewels, King Śaśidhvaja, together with his own people and kinsmen, considered himself to have achieved his life's purpose.
Having heard these stories concerning former births, he addressed the members of the assembly.

With their minds filled with wonder, the people of the world regarded that king as the perfect one; praising, meditating upon, and extolling Kalki, they again addressed that monarch, who was the very embodiment of both devotion and the object of devotion. 24–25.
The kings said:
"Out of a desire for devotion to the Blessed One, who among the devotees—knowing the ritual injunctions—performs what, eats what, where does he dwell, and what does he say? (26)
"O Indra among kings, describe these with due respect; you know everything because of Kṛṣṇa’s desire to purify the worlds through his power of recollecting past births.
Having heard their words, the king’s face blossomed with joy.
Having addressed them with words of praise, he spoke that which was uttered by Brahmā.
Śaśidhvaja said:
"Formerly, in the midst of the assembly of Brahmā, crowded with hosts of great sages..."
Sanaka said to Nārada:
"I have dwelt there through the grace of those whom you have mentioned here; having heard the stories from them, I shall relate them here. Listen, for they are destroyers of sin."
Sanaka said: O Sage Nārada, what is that devotion to Hari, honored by the world, which removes the cycle of worldly existence? Describe that first, for we are attentive. (31)

Nārada said: Having restrained the senses, with the mind as the sixth, by means of supreme intelligence, one who is expert in the governance of the world should even cast his body down before his guru. (32)
When the Guru is pleased, the Lord Hari himself becomes gracious.
By his command, the preceptor, being well-composed, should meditate with undistracted intellect upon the letter *ma* within the *praṇava*, the fire, and the beloved woman. (33)

Having worshipped the lotus feet of Vāsudeva with water for the feet, the respectful offering, water for sipping, and so forth, as well as with baths, garments, and ornaments, one should, with a concentrated mind,
meditate upon that beautiful and charming form situated within the lotus of the heart.
Having meditated thus, the wise man, knowing the state of single-minded devotion, should offer himself to Hari along with his speech, mind, intellect, and the group of senses;
for the gods are his limbs, and their names are indeed known to him.
Those very [attributes] do not exist apart from Viṣṇu, Kalki, and Ananta.

Kṛṣṇa is the one to be served; I am his servant. Others, such as Prabhava and the rest, speak of them as having the nature of ignorance (avidyopādhayaḥ) due to their lack of knowledge, though they are actually the very forms of His own self. 37–38.
Even for the devotee, duality regarding Hari—such as that between the served and the server—does not exist at that time;
other than Him, nothing whatsoever exists anywhere.
The devotee remembers that Viṣṇu and sings His names.
He indeed performs those very actions, arising from that flood of blissful joy;

he dances as if wildly, cries out, laughs, moves about with his mind fixed on that, rolls about, and through self-forgetfulness does not perceive how great a distance there is [between himself and others]. 40–41.
Such unwavering devotion to the Blessed One instantly purifies the worlds, including the gods, asuras, and humans.

Or even though she is the bestower of boons upon those who know the Vedas and other scriptures, appearing in the forms of Śiva, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā, devotees—due to being permeated by the quality of *sattva*—are intent on the senses through *rajas*, and through *tamas* they possess terrible resolves; thus, people with dualistic vision worship her. ||43-44||
Beings fall into a state devoid of virtue through *rajas*, which causes craving for sense objects;
through *tamas*, they go to hell, O you whose nature is the non-duality of *saṃsāra*. [That which is] leftover, remaining, wholesome, pure, and desired—[is the food]. 45.

The food of devotees offered as *naivedya* to Viṣṇu is considered *sāttvika*. Food that produces gratification for the senses and increases semen and blood is *rājasa*; pure food that increases longevity and health is [also *sāttvika*]. ||46-47||
Beyond this, the food dear to those of tamasic nature should be known as pungent, sour, salty, burning, putrid,
and stale; the dwelling in the forest belongs to the sattvic, while dwelling in the village belongs to the rajasic.
Gambling, intoxicants, and the like are proclaimed to be the abode of *tamas*.
Hari gives nothing, and his servant does not beg; nevertheless, why is there such eternal, supreme love between the two? (49–50)
Having thus understood this narration of the qualities of the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, Sanaka,
being pure, praised the best of divine sages with words full of humility and devotion, and departed for the city of Indra.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Narration of the Recollection of Past Lives," in the third part of the *Śrī Kalki Purāṇa*, the *Anubhāgavata*, within the future section, in the dialogue between the host of kings and King Śaśidhvaja.
The Twelfth Chapter.
Śaśidhvaja said:
O kings, this which was to be told regarding the deeds of Aruka has been narrated to you.
"What more shall I say regarding the devotee and the Lord of devotees?
The kings said:
"O King, you are the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas, devoted to the welfare of all living beings."
How indeed can there be your absorption in acts such as violence on the field of battle?
For generally, the virtuous in this world act for the benefit of living beings through their lives, intellects, wealth, and words, toward all those whose souls are attached to sense-objects.
Śaśidhvaja said:

That primordial nature (prakṛti), which manifests duality and can assume any form at will, being composed of the three qualities (guṇas), gives birth to the entire triple world as well as the Vedas. 4.
Those Vedas, which govern the dharma of the three worlds and destroy unrighteousness,
promote devotion in the world for those who possess desire and seek sense objects;
[so too do] the sages such as Vātsyāyana and others, and the Manus who have reached the further shore of the Vedas.
"Directed by the words of the Veda, they carry the offering to the Lord;
we are their followers, devoted to the dharma of action and fond of battle.
Having reached a firm conclusion regarding the meaning of the Veda, we seek to strike down him who seeks to strike us down."
"The sin in killing one who should not be killed is equal to the merit in protecting one who deserves to be killed," so said the venerable Vyāsa, who is devoted to the true meaning of all the Vedas.
There is no atonement for that act; rather, unrighteousness prevails therein.
Therefore, having destroyed here your army which is difficult to conquer in battle,
we have returned after bringing Dharma, Kṛta, and Kalki;
this is my devotion as I see it— now declare what you desire.
I shall explain that in accordance with the words of the Vedas:
if Viṣṇu is everywhere, then whom does he kill, and who is killed? If it is said that Viṣṇu is the killer and Viṣṇu is the slain, then whose killing could there be in that case?
"In the killing [of enemies] during sacrifices of war and the like, there is no killing because of the injunction of the Vedas"—
thus sing the sages and the fourteen Manus;
in this way, through both wars and sacrifices, we worship Viṣṇu, the Lord.
Therefore, by resorting to the Māyā of the Lord and worshipping according to the prescribed rule through the relationship of master and servant, one becomes happy; not otherwise. 14.
The kings said:
O protector of the earth, how can detachment be spoken of for one who has died due to the curse of King Nimi, the preceptor of kings, while still in such a body that is the seat of enjoyment?
And [how can it be said of] Vasiṣṭha, who, having died, obtained a new body through the curse of his disciple?
It is indeed heard that for those who are liberated, there is birth and liberation from devotees.
Therefore, the Bhāgavatī [knowledge], which is difficult to understand for those who have not conquered their selves,
deludes them in saṃsāra through its manifoldness, like a magical illusion.
Having heard their words once more, King Śaśidhvaja,
the best among speakers, spoke with a mind inclined toward devotion.
Śaśidhvaja said:
At the end of many births, through the power of destiny and by association with sacred fords, holy fields, and the like, one may encounter a virtuous person; from that comes the vision of the Lord.
Then, having attained residence in the same world as Him, they worship Him with a devoted mind.
Having enjoyed incomparable pleasures, he becomes devoted to worldly existence;
though addicted to passion and intent on ritual action, he is always devoted to the worship of Hari, singing His names with an eager longing to remember His form. ||20-21||
The great festivals of the vows and parvas that commemorate the incarnations are rich with devotion to and worship of the Blessed Lord, and they are flooded with supreme bliss;
therefore, those who have experienced the arising of the fruit of liberation do not desire liberation [beyond this]. ||22||
Having been liberated, they obtain births that manifest the state of devotion to Hari;

they take the form of Hari, purify sacred fields and pilgrimage sites, are devoted to dharma, distinguish between the essential and the non-essential, serve as both the served and the server, and embody non-duality. ||23-24||
Just as was the descent of Kṛṣṇa, so too here is the play of Nimi’s blinking eyes for those who serve Him;
even for the liberated Vasiṣṭha, there was a regard for assuming a body.
O kings, this majesty of devotion and the devotee has been told to you;
it instantly removes the sins of men and increases devotion to Hari.
It is the reservoir of the bliss and happiness of the gods, residing within all the senses.

The sages of the three worlds, such as Vyāsa and others who are seekers of the truth, having churned for a very long time the ocean of the nectar-like pure commentaries on various Śāstras, Purāṇas, and Vedas— which destroys the defects of sensual desire and the like and wards off illusion and delusion— [attained this work]. ||27||
"Having thus obtained this stainless, fresh butter-like devotion toward Kṛṣṇa that is focused on no other, which destroys rebirth and is equal to Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself throughout the three worlds.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Devotion to Bhakti," in the third part of the *Śrī Kalki Purāṇa*, the *Anubhāgavata*, concerning the future.
The Thirteenth Chapter.
Sūta said:
Having thus related his own stories in the assembly, that king—
Śaśidhvaja, with a joyful mind and palms joined in reverence, spoke to Kalki.
Śaśidhvaja said:
"O Lord, you are indeed the sovereign of the three worlds; these kings are dependent upon you."
"Know me, O Hari, to be such a king who carries out your commands.
I am going at my will to perform austerities at Haridvāra, which is dear to the sages;
these sons and grandsons of mine, who take refuge in you, must be protected by you."
"O Lord of the Gods, you surely know how my death occurred long ago, as did that of Jāmbavat and Dvivida; [know all that] at that time.
Having spoken thus, he prepared to depart with his wife from that king.
The kings said to Kalki, who stood with his face cast down in shame,
"O Lord, what was said by him that you have lowered your face upon hearing?
Tell us that at once, or instruct us as to how we may be freed from our doubt."
Kalki said: O kings, ask this Śaśidhvaja, who is highly wise and firm in his resolve through devotion to me, for he shall sever your doubts.
Having heard these words of Kalki, those kings, who were intent on carrying out what was commanded,
spoke again to that king, whose mind was filled with doubt.
The kings said:
"What have you said, O King, O great-minded Śaśidhvaja? How will Kalki come to be? Having heard this, he immediately cast his face downward. Śaśidhvaja said:
Formerly, during the incarnation of Rāma, having observed the slaughter of Indrajit by Lakṣmaṇa and his own liberation from that dreadful state of being a rākṣasa,
Dvivida contracted a one-day fever through the killing of a Brahmin hero in a fire-sanctuary.
The deluding [demon] had entered Lakṣmaṇa’s body.
Seeing him so distressed, Dvivida, the best of physicians born of the horse lineage, announced that it was Lakṣmaṇa.
Having unweariedly written this love-letter for Rāmabhadra,
the mighty-armed one stood upright and showed it to Lakṣmaṇa.
Upon seeing that letter, the powerful Lakṣmaṇa was freed from his fever.
Then he said to Dvivida, "O monkey, choose a boon.
Hearing those words, Dvivida spoke joyfully to Lakṣmaṇa: "I pray for death at your hands, and thereby liberation from my state as a monkey."
Again Lakṣmaṇa said to him: "O monkey, in another birth you shall be liberated by me when I have taken the body of Balarāma.
On the northern shore of the ocean there is a monkey named Dvivida. (16)
"It destroys quotidian fever for whoever sees it written.
Having thus written these mantra-syllables on a palm leaf and placed them at the door,
the quotidian fever of even one who sees it shall perish.
Thus, having obtained that boon, the long-lived and robust monkey,
his body pierced by the weapons of Balarāma, attained liberation from all fear.
Likewise, the son of a Sūta, Lomaharṣaṇa, was slain in that sacred field.
In Naimiṣa, Balarāma, endowed with divine weapons, appeared by his own will.
And formerly, when Hari had assumed the form of Vāmana, King Jāmbavat also performed a circumambulation there of His upward-pointing foot.
Beholding him who was as swift as thought, the dwarf Vāmana, filled with wonder, said:
"O mighty lord of bears, choose from me whatever boon you desire.
At these words, Jāmbavān, an incarnation of Brahmā, his face beaming with joy, replied with delight:
He said, "O Cakradahana, my death shall come from your discus.
When this was said, Vāmana replied, "At the birth of Kṛṣṇa, your liberation will occur when your head is split by my discus."
In my incarnation as Kṛṣṇa, however, a false accusation arose regarding the jewel on account of King Satrājit, who was a devotee of the Sun;
furthermore, the killing of my brother Prasena was caused by that very jewel.

For the sake of that jewel, even the lion was slain by Jāmbavān. For Kṛṣṇa, who possessed immeasurable splendor, who was terrified by the fear of malicious rumors, and whose mind was intent on searching for the jewel, there occurred a battle with the bear in the cave.
Having recognized his own lord, he was suddenly liberated from the bondage of being seized by that discus; seeing Kṛṣṇa together with Lakṣmaṇa,
dark as a fresh blade of dūrvā grass, he gave him his daughter.
Then, having taken the maiden Jāmbavatī along with the jewel,
he arrived at the city of Dvārakā and summoned me to the assembly hall; having called me there, he presented to me the jewel worshipped by hosts of sages.
Out of shame, I gave that maiden of my own to him in marriage along with that jewel; Lāvaṇya took the jewel. Taking Satyabhāmā and having entrusted the jewel to me, that lord—
Having gone to Dvārakā, the Lord returned once more to Hastināpura.
After Kṛṣṇa had departed, Śatadhanvan killed me and seized the jewel;
therefore, I know here what was done by me in a previous birth.
Because of the false accusation against Kṛṣṇa, my liberation did not occur;
therefore, having offered Ramā in the form of Satyabhāmā to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul who will appear as Kalki, I shall go to the supreme destination.
"By the blow of the Sudarśana weapon, my death is desired;
knowing that death has occurred, I desire liberation in battle.
Thus spoke Kalki, the Lord of the worlds, regarding the slaughter of his father-in-law.
Upon hearing this, the Lord stood with his face cast down out of shame and fear of violating the Dharma.
Having heard this most wonderful, unprecedented, and supreme account, the kings were struck with amazement,
the people in the assembly were filled with joy, and the hosts of sages were drawn by the virtues of Kalki.
This narrative, spoken by King Śaśidhvaja, became a source of supreme joy, auspicious, glorious, most illustrious, and a bestower of liberation through its utterance with the highest reverence.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Death of Cakra as Told by Śaśidhvaja," in the third part of the *Śrī Kalki Purāṇa*, the *Anubhāgavata* within the *Bhaviṣya*.
Chapter Fourteen.
Sūta said:
Then the highly effulgent Kalki [approached] his father-in-law, that son of Śaśidhvaja.
Having consulted with the kings through various words, Hari departed. Having obtained the boon from Maheśvarī, Śaśidhvaja—
having praised her and cast off his illusory power (māyā)— went to the forest together with his beloved, his delusion now dispelled.
Kalki set out for the golden city with his hosts of troops;
it was protected by fortresses and guarded by serpents emitting poisonous fumes.
Having breached the fortress, Kalki, the conqueror of enemy cities, proceeded together with his followers.
Having severed the weapons of poison with his arrows, Acyuta beheld that city—
richly adorned with jewels, gold, and variegated ornaments, surrounded by hosts of Naga maidens,
abounding in Haricandana trees, and deserted by men.
Beholding this, Kalki laughed and said to the kings: "Aha! Why is it that this beautiful city of serpents causes fear to men?
It is crowded with hosts of male and female nagas; tell me, shall we go here? (6)
An incorporeal voice spoke from the sky to Lord Hari, the master of Ramā, who was preoccupied with his duties, and to the kings who were suited to him:
"O King, you ought not to advance against this [city] with your armies."
"Without you, others will perish even from one such as the Poison-Maiden.
Having heard this voice from the sky, Kalki, accompanied by Śuka and wielding a sword, set out alone on his horse with great haste.
Having gone there, the hero beheld her, who destroyed the fortitude of the steadfast;
with a smiling face, she spoke to him whose splendor was invisible due to his beauty.
Viṣakanyā said:
In this saṃsāra, how many kings— possessing exceedingly fierce valor and yet whose bodies were worn away by my eyes’ gaze— have been slain by me?
Deprived of the love of being gazed upon by wretched gods, asuras, and men, I—
now flooded by the nectar of the rasa from Your two lotus-eyes— bow down to You.
(11) Where am I, miserable and with eyes like poison, and where is union with the eyes that are nectar?
"Alas, by whom has this state been brought upon this unfortunate woman in this world?
Kalki said:
"Who are you, O girl of beautiful hips? Why have you come to this condition?"
"Tell me, by what deed did your eye become poisoned?
The Poison-Maiden replied:
"O high-minded one, I am the wife of the Gandharva Citragrīva."
Renowned as Sulocanā, she granted every desire to her husband.
Once, accompanied by my husband Pīṭha in a celestial chariot,
I took delight in the groves of Gandhamādana, absorbed in the arts of love.
There, seeing the Yakṣa-muni of deformed appearance and afflicted with illness, she spoke out of intoxication with her beauty and youth, casting a sidelong glance at him.
Having heard those words, which were full of reproach and unpleasant to him, the sage [reflected].
There, in her anger, she cursed me; because of that, I became one whose very sight is poison.
Cast into the city of serpents, Kāñcanī, among the host of nāginīs, I wander, deprived of my husband and deprived of fate, raining down venom.
I do not know by what austerity I have come within the range of your vision; having had the nectar of my eyes released from the curse, I shall now depart for the world of my husband.
Oh, let that curse be a blessing for those virtuous ones here!
"From the curse of my husband, through the liberation granted by the sage, I have beheld the sight of your lotus feet.
Having spoken thus, she departed for heaven in a celestial chariot radiant as the sun;
and Kalki then installed that highly intelligent king as the sovereign of that city.
Amārṣa was his son, and the wise Sahasra was his son;
from Sahasra was born a son, the king known as Asi,
from whose lineage were born kings with the name Bṛhannala.
Surrounded by various hosts of sages, Hari consecrated that Manu, a tiger among kings,
in Ayodhyā and departed for Mathurā;
there, he consecrated the highly radiant King Sūryaketu.
Then, having gone to Vāraṇāvata,
Ariṣṭhala, Vṛkasthala, Mākanda, and Gajāhvaya,
Hari made Devāpi the sovereign of those five regions and returned to Śambhala.
Affectionate toward his brothers, he bestowed upon Kavi, Prājña, and Sumantu the kingdoms of Śaumbha, Pauṇḍra, Pulinda, Surāṣṭra, and Magadha;
as well as Kīkaṭa, Madhyakarṇāṭa, Andhra, Oḍra, and Kaliṅga.
The Lord of the World gave Aṅga and Vaṅga to his own kinsmen.
The powerful Kalki, himself residing in Śambhala, gave the region of Kaṅkaka along with the Kalāpakas to Viśākhayūpa. ||27-28||
Kalki gave the regions known as Cola, Barbara, and Karvā, situated in the midst of the Dvārakā country, to his sons, with Kṛtavarman placed at their head;
he also bestowed wealth and jewels upon his father with supreme devotion.
Having comforted the subjects, Hari, as Kalki, dwelt as a householder with Padmā and Ramā in the village of Śambhala and rejoiced greatly;
Dharma stood upon its four feet, and the three worlds were filled with the Kṛta age.
The gods, bestowing the fruits as described, move everywhere upon the earth;

the ground is filled with all kinds of crops and covered with people who are joyful and well-nourished; it is free from deceit, theft, and falsehood, and devoid of mental anguish and physical disease. (32)
The Brahmins were knowers of the Vedas and endowed with great auspiciousness; the women were noble and devoted to their vows.
The Kṣatriyas were intent on worship and fire-offerings, observant of the vow of devotion to their husbands, and prepared for sacrifices.
The Vaiśyas, through lawful exchanges of goods, were dedicated to the worship of Śrī Viṣṇu.
"But the Śūdras, through service to the twice-born, shall engage in discourse on the stories of Hari and be devoted to worship.

(33) Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Practice of Dharma by Those Who Have Attained Liberation from the Poison-Maiden," in the third part of the *Śrī Kalki Purāṇa*, the *Anubhāgavata* of the future.
Fifteenth Chapter.
Śaunaka said:
The great king Śaśidhvaja, having offered praise, was made to go to the earth.
"O Sūta, best among those who know the truth, what indeed is this 'Māyā-stuti'?
For that discourse of yours which is a discourse on Viṣṇu must be spoken for the sake of purification.
Sūta said:
"Listen, all you sages, as Mārkaṇḍeya asks;
Śuka, whose soul is purified, has spoken this unsurpassed hymn to Māyā.
Listen to that, for I shall proclaim it exactly as it was studied and exactly as it was heard."
It bestows all desires upon men and destroys their sins and afflictions.
Śuka said:
Having abandoned the city of Bhallāṭa, Śaśidhvaja, a devotee of Viṣṇu, [departed].
For the sake of liberating himself from saṃsāra, he sang this hymn to Māyā.
Śaśidhvaja said:
"Oṃ! She whose essence is the syllable Hrīṃ, who is the quintessence of existence, and who is utterly pure..."

I salute Svāhā, the mother of Brahmā and the other gods, who is to be known through the Vedas, who is slender, whose domain consists of the elements and subtle essences, and who is worthy of worship by the gods, Gandharvas, and Siddhas. 5.
I praise that which transcends the world, which has become non-dual,
which is extolled by beings past and future through detailed and concise expositions,
which is sung by the wise, and which is tossed by the waves of time.
She who, by the playful cast of her sidelong glances, has cast away the difficult path of saṃsāra;
she who is full, attainable, obtainable through duality, and the refuge; she who shines in the beginning, at the end, and in the middle.
I bow to that support in the form of Brahman, which shines with its own luster through all beings as the three worlds, appearing in various forms as gods, animals, and humans. ||7||
In the absence of that [Light], this world does not shine; time, destiny, and karma are merely its limiting adjuncts. I bow to that Light which illuminates them all. 8.
Fragrance resides in the earth, taste in water, form in fire, and touch in air;
sound is in space— or whatever appears as manifold within consciousness.
I bow to that Sāvitrī of universal form who approaches [the Lord].
You are Sāvitrī, whose nature is Brahman; you are Bhavānī, the consort of the Lord of Beings; you are Śrī, the very embodiment of the Lord of Fortune.
Śacī, the preeminent wife even of Śakra, the lord of heaven, you shine as Māyā among the worlds;
you are a young girl in childhood and a young woman in youth.
In old age, you appear as the ancient one, equal to Time itself; worshipped through various forms of sacrifice and yoga, you shine forth, transcending knowledge and assuming any form at will.
You are the most excellent, the bestower of boons, the accomplishment of the world’s success, the virtuous, the blessed, the one honored by the world, the noble maiden;
you are Caṇḍī, Durgā, Kālikā, and she who is known as Kālikā.

O Goddess, you shine in various lands with diverse forms and attire. O Goddess, if one here meditates with devotion upon your lotus feet— which are worthy of worship by gods and others— within the lotus of one's own heart, [one attains liberation].

Whether heard from the hollow of the ears or from the mouth of a teacher, this meritorious hymn of Māyā spoken by Śukadeva produces the perfection of dharma and all spiritual accomplishments for those who hear it in this primordial world. 13.13
Having obtained instruction from Mārkaṇḍeya, Śaśidhvaja attained perfection;
having performed penance at Kokāmukha and meditated upon Hari in the depths of the forest, he was slain by the Sudarśana discus and went to Vaikuṇṭha for refuge. ||14-15||
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Hymn to Māyā," in the third part of the *Śrī Kalki Purāṇa*, the *Anubhāgavata* of the future.

The Veda, Dharma, the Kṛta age, the gods, and the worlds with all their moving and unmoving beings—

While Kalki, whose entire body was adorned with sectarian marks, reigned somewhere as king, there were no heretics— rich in illusion and delusion— who deceive the virtuous;
he resided in Śambhala together with Padmā and Ramā.
Viṣṇuyaśas said to his son, "Sacrifice to the gods who are the benefactors of the world.
Having heard that, Kalki, being exceedingly delighted, bowed down with humility and spoke to his father for the sake of accomplishing dharma, kama, and artha.
With Rājasūya, Vājapeya, and Aśvamedha sacrifices— great rituals—
and with various other sacrifices and systems of ritual action, he worshipped Hari, the Lord of Sacrifice,
together with Kṛpa, Rāma, Vasiṣṭha, and others, as well as Vyāsa, Dhaumya, and Akṛtavraṇa.
Together with Aśvatthāman, Madhucchandas, and the high-souled Mandapāla,
he bathed with devotion in the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā for the final purificatory rite (avabhṛtha),

There, Vahni was appointed to the cooking; Varuṇa was the server;
and Marut satisfied the twice-born with various desired foods and drinks, as well as with instrumental music, dances, songs, and the great festivals of the ancestral sacrifices.
The lotus-eyed Kalki bestowed wealth upon all—
women, children, the elderly, and others— as was appropriate for each.
Rambhā held the cymbals, while Nandin and Hūhū sang and danced.
Having bestowed gifts upon worthy Brahmins,
that lord dwelt on the bank of the Gaṅgā, in accordance with his father’s words,
in the assembly hall of Viṣṇuyaśas, listening to beloved stories of former kings.
Speaking, laughing, and gladdening the wise twice-born ones,
Nārada, who is honored by the gods, arrived there along with Tumburu;
he joyfully honored him together with his father according to the prescribed rites.
Having honored them both, Viṣṇuyaśas, filled with humility,
spoke with affection to the great sage Nārada, the devotee of Viṣṇu who held a lute in his hand.
Viṣṇuyaśas said:
"Oh, what fortune! Oh, what fortune for me, earned through hundreds of births, that I have had the vision of perfected beings like you for the sake of my liberation!
Today the sacred fires have been well-sacrificed, and the ancestors are supremely satisfied."
And the gods were thoroughly satisfied by their beholding and worshiping you.

Since Viṣṇu is the one to be worshiped in the act of worship, and since there has been a vision of me, what more could there be? Oh, what a meeting with the virtuous! For even by a mere touch, the entire mass of sins is destroyed.

The heart of the virtuous is dharma, their speech is the eternal gods, and their actions are for the exhaustion of karma; for the virtuous one is Hari himself. I believe that the body of a Vaiṣṇava in the three worlds is not composed of material elements.
Since Kṛṣṇa has appeared for the suppression of the wicked,
I therefore ask you, O Brāhmaṇa: in this ocean of the worldly existence of Māyā,
you are the helmsman who brings one to the further shore by means of the boat of devotion to Viṣṇu.
"O Lord of the World, tell me by what action I may obtain here that supreme state of Nirvana and find peace from the houses of torment.
Nārada said:
Oh, how powerful is this auspicious illusion, full of all wonders!
Viṣṇu never abandons his father and mother at any time.
He whose son is the Lord of the World, Kalki, the perfect Nārāyaṇa.
"Abandoning him, Viṣṇuyaśas desires liberation from me. Having thus reflected in private, the son of Brahmā spoke to Viṣṇuyaśas, the son of Brahmayasas,
who increases the wealth of Brahman.
Nārada said: Listen to that which grants liberation, which Māyā spoke when she saw the individual soul at the end of the body desiring to take up another body. 28.

Māyā said:

The Jīva said:

Māyā said: [33]
A man lives by means of illusion; though his consciousness is destroyed, he still exerts himself.

The Jīva said:
Born from my association, you possess various names and forms;
why do you revile me, O fool, like an unchaste woman her husband?
In my absence, your own existence ceases, just as darkness vanishes when the sun has risen.
O noble lady, you shine before me like a fresh cloud before the sun.
O Māyā, who consists of the world, you are the granary of the seeds of my play;
you do not appear at the beginning, the end, or in the middle, due to your manifold nature, like a magical illusion.
Having thus observed that the body is eternally devoid of objects, free from mental activity, non-material, and insentient, she abandoned it;
and having abandoned me, she uttered a curse— this is what is unpleasant to you in the world.
O you who are like a piece of wood or a wall, there shall be no stability for you in any way.
That is the illusory power (māyā) of your son Kalki, the Lord and Soul of the Universe;
having understood it, wander at will across the earth, contemplating Hari.
Free from hope, free from the sense of "mine," peaceful, and devoid of longing for all enjoyments;
knowing this world to be Viṣṇu and Viṣṇu to be the dweller within the world, having absorbed the self by means of the Self, be completely detached. 41

Having thus addressed Viṣṇuyaśas, the two lords of sages circumambulated Kalki and departed for the hermitage of Kapila. Having heard what was spoken by Nārada regarding his unsurpassed son Kalki, [they went].
Viṣṇuyaśas went to the forest of Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World.
Having gone to Badarikāraṇya and performed most severe austerities, he joined the individual soul (jīva) with the Supreme (Bṛhat), and being perfected, he abandoned his physical body. ||43-44||
Embracing her deceased husband, the virtuous Sumati, overwhelmed with affection, entered the fire; praised by the gods in heaven, she was clothed in beautiful garments.
Having heard from the mouth of the sage regarding the passing of his parents, the lord Kalki—
Out of affection, he performed the funeral rites for the two of them with eyes full of tears.
In Śambhala, which is desired by the gods, the righteous Kalki, honored by the world and the Vedas, ruled the kingdom together with Padmā and Ramā. ||46-47||

From the peak of Mahendra, Rāma, the creator of sacred fords, intent on wandering among holy sites, set out for Śambhala in order to behold Kalki. Upon seeing him, he rose up suddenly together with Padmā and Ramā.
Kalki, who was full of joy and knew the ritual procedures, performed the worship according to the rules.
Having fed him with various flavors and qualities,
he placed him upon a decorated couch enriched with priceless garments and attained great delight.
When his teacher had finished eating and was resting, Kalki, full of humility, gratified him by massaging his feet and spoke these sweet words:
"O Guru, through your grace, that which pertains to the three aims of life has been accomplished for me."
"Listen, O Rāma, to what was declared by the daughter of Śaśidhvaja.
Having heard these words of her husband, the lady, desiring the attainment of a son as wished for in her heart, asked:
"By what vows, recitations, observances, or restraints did she joyfully give birth here to the son of Jamadagni?"
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Liberation of Viṣṇuyaśas and the Vision of Rāma," in the third part of the glorious Kalki Purāṇa, the Anubhāgavata of the future.
Chapter Seventeen.

Having heard that Ramā was longing for a son, and perceiving it to be the desire of Kalki, the son of Jamadagni caused the Rukmiṇī-vrata to be performed. By that vow, the virtuous Ramā became fortunate and endowed with sons.
She became endowed with all enjoyments and possessed enduring youth.
Śaunaka said:
O Sūta, tell me the procedure for this vow and what its fruit is.
"By whom was this supreme, righteous Rukmiṇī-vrata performed in ancient times?
Sūta said:
"Listen, O Brahmin, to the story of Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan."
Having plunged into the waters of the lake, she beheld Soma, the bearer of the crescent moon.
Surrounded by her friends and accompanied by Devayānī,
she rose up in fear of Śambhu and quickly put on her garment.
There, having noticed the exchange of garments between Śukra’s daughter and herself, she spoke in anger: "O mendicant woman, cast off this garment!
Thus addressed, that daughter of the Dānavas was surrounded by her handmaidens.
Having tied her up with her own garment and cast her into the well, they went home.
While she was submerged and weeping in the well, the son of Nahuṣa, seeking water, touched her hand, lifted her out, and said: "Who are you, O lovely-faced one? (7–8)
Having put on her garment, that daughter of Śukra, looking at the king, spoke of everything done by Śarmiṣṭhā out of shame and fear.
Having understood her intention, Yayāti followed after her beautifully.
Having consoled her, he went home, intent on her marriage.
She went to her own abode and told Śukra what had been done by Śarmiṣṭhā.
Hearing that, Vṛṣaparvan spoke soothingly to the angry brahmin.
"O Lord, if you have anger toward me, punish me who deserve punishment;
or, if Śarmiṣṭhā has offended you, do whatever you desire in your mind.
Seeing the king prostrate at his father's feet, she spoke thus in wrath.
"Let this maiden Devayānī become my slave," [said Śukra]. Then the wise king, having brought her and appointed her to servitude, went to his own home, reflecting upon destiny as the supreme power.
Then Śukra, having brought Yayāti back in the reverse order, gave Devayānī to him according to the prescribed rites along with her.
Having given her, the brahmin also said to the king: "When this princess..."
"Upon your bed you shall be summoned this very day; old age will soon consume you.
Having heard these words of Śukra, the king, out of fear, placed that woman of excellent complexion in concealment, keeping Devayānī as her attendant.
That princess Śarmiṣṭhā, overwhelmed by misery, grief, and fear,
constantly served Devayānī, who was surrounded by hundreds of maidservants.
Once, having gone to the forest, she was weeping on the bank of the Jāhnavī.
She beheld that sage Viśvāmitra surrounded by women—
himself observing vows, perfumed with holy fragrances, and attended by beautiful women who were providing him with ritual observances through offerings of garlands, incense, lamps, and other gifts.
Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus on the altar, well-marked with signs,
and adorned at its four corners by four banana plantain-leaf canopies,
one should construct a house made of cloth, decorated with strips of gold.
An image of Śrī Vāsudeva, inlaid with various jewels, was fashioned;

and with the Pauruṣa Sūkta, with auspicious waters scented with various perfumes, with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), it was consecrated according to the mantras recited by the twice-born. ||22-23||

Having bathed [the deity], one should worship [them] upon the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha) at the center of the pericarp (karṇikā), with either five, ten, or sixteen types of ritual offerings (upacāra).
The water for the feet (pādya) removes the fatigue of the journey; it is cool and most enchanting.
O Supreme Lord, accept that which generates supreme bliss.
O Lord of Rukmiṇī, accept this arghya-offering, rich with the fragrance of dūrvā grass and sandalwood, prepared with great care by me, Your gracious master. 25–26.
O Śrīnivāsa, together with Śrī, please accept this fragrant and most enchanting water for rinsing the mouth (ācamanīya), originating from various sacred bathing places;
as well as this excellent [garland] strung on thread, rich with the fragrance of various flowers.
O Lord of the Gods, take this beautiful garland that adorns the chest;
O Hari, take this pure covering, which is fashioned by the joining of continuous threads, O you who are yourself without covering, along with your beloved. 28–29.
"O Lord Vāsudeva, accept this sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra) fashioned by Prajāpati, together with Rukmiṇī and Ramā;
it is adorned with various jewels and set with gold and pearls. (30)
O Lord of Gods, together with your beloved, please accept my ornaments. O Lord of Rukmiṇī, accept the curd, milk, jaggery, rice, cakes, sweets, and sugar-candies; O Master, make me your own.
O Giver of Boons, together with your beloved from Vidarbha, accept this incense, rich with the fragrance of camphor and agallochum,
which bestows supreme bliss and destroys the darkness of saṃsāra for devotees who are unable to leave their homes. 33.
O Lord, look upon this lamp; O World-Illuminator, show me favor! (34) O Śyāmasundara, lotus-eyed one, wearer of yellow garments, four-armed one!
Protect me who have taken refuge in you, O Lord of Gods, O Acyuta, together with Rukmiṇī! (35)
Having observed their vow and having bowed to the sage, the deeply distressed Śarmiṣṭhā,
speaking sweet words with palms joined in reverence, said to them: Śarmiṣṭhā said:
"O goddesses, you ought to protect me, an unfortunate princess abandoned by my lord, through this vow and this ritual act.
Having heard her words, they were moved with compassion to a certain degree.

Having offered the articles for worship, they performed [the rites] with devotion. Having observed the vow and obtained her husband, the Lord, Śarmiṣṭhā gave birth to sons; being well-contented, she remained in the bloom of youth.
And Sītā, having performed a vow in the midst of the Aśoka grove together with Saramā,
obtained her husband Rāma, the destroyer of the Rākṣasas. By the grace of Bṛhadaśva, Draupadī likewise performed this vow.
Devoted [to her husband], she became free from suffering and possessed of perpetual youth.
Likewise, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha,

That virtuous woman gave birth to two sons, Meghamāla and Balāhaka,
who were benefactors of the gods through sacrifices, gifts, austerities, and vows;

Regarding this as the most excellent vow, she becomes one who has realized the truth, honored, and fulfilled in her desires through the abundance of all prosperity;
