He goes to an unprecedented state, inaccessible even to those who possess the knowledge of Brahman.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Vow of Rukmiṇī," in the third part of the glorious *Kalki Purāṇa*, the *Anubhāgavata* of the future.
Chapter Eighteen.
Sūta said:
O brahmins, this vow, renowned throughout the three worlds, has been narrated to you.
Hereafter, O twice-born ones, listen to the deeds performed by Kalki.
One thousand years passed while he resided in Śambhala together with his brothers, sons, kinsmen, and relatives.
In Śambhala, the guilds shone forth with their assembly halls, marketplaces, and crossroads.
Richly adorned with various banners and flags, it was like Indra’s Amarāvatī;
there, in Śambhala, the sixty-eight sacred sites (tīrthas) came into being,
where liberation from death on earth is attained by taking refuge at the feet of Kalki, who is free from all impurity.
I consider the village of Śambhala, adorned with groves, gardens, and various clusters of flowers, to be the abode of liberation on earth.
Therein dwells Kalki, who increases the joy of the eyes of the city women.
The lord of the world took his pleasure at will with Padmā and Ramā,
indeed upon a chariot that moves according to one's desire and was bestowed by the Lord of the Gods,
amidst rivers, mountains, groves, and islands, with supreme joy.
Taking delight with Padmā, Ramā, and the others, the Lord of Ramā—addicted to women and lustful—did not perceive day or night as he entered [the palace].
He enjoyed the fragrance from Padmā’s mouth, the lotus-liquor, and her garments; he was the abode of exquisite dalliance.
Kalki entered a particular cave that shone with the brilliance of many sapphire gems.

Padmā, whose form was as beautiful as hundreds of lotuses, and Ramā, who possessed the playful grace of a digit of nectar—those two went after their husband had entered the mountain cavern crowded with thousands of women. ||9-10||
Beholding her husband seated in the cave, the lovely Padmā entered after him to sport;
then Ramā, accompanied by the host of women, followed behind him, O wonder, desiring to be foremost.
There, at the edge of a thicket of sapphire-blue lotuses, [she saw] the Lord with his beloveds who were like reflections of himself.
Then, seeing Kalki standing there like a mass of fresh clouds, she fainted as if struck by a stone.
Ramā, distressed and with eyes agitated as she gazed in every direction along with her young female companions, shone no more;
though Padmā was as radiant as a hundred lotuses, she appeared dejected at heart and pained.
Drawing a picture of that parrot with her own collyrium on the ground,
and fashioning its head with the saffron from her breasts and with musk, she embraced it and bowed down with deep emotion.
Then Ramā, intent on sweet speech, praising him and placing him in her heart, was afflicted by desire.
Having meditated and worshipped him with her own ornaments, she stood dejected and overcome with compassion.
Rising after a moment, the beautiful woman wept for her lord, who resembled the throat of a peacock;
not finding him again though he was embraced within her heart, she said, afflicted by desire: "O Hari, be gracious! (15-16)
Padmā too, casting off her own bodily ornaments, sported amidst the dust;
and even with musk, she made her neck dark blue, assuming the nature of Śiva to slay Kāma.
Hari, the friend of the distressed, having perceived through a fraction of the arts of those women whose eyes were now dimmed, [acted].
Kalki entered the midst of his beloveds for the fulfillment of their desires and for the festival of amorous sport.
Like female elephants approaching the leader of the herd with devotion, those charming women—
joyful in spirit, pure in conduct, and having their every wish fulfilled— approached their lord in the forest.
In Vaibhrājaka, Caitraratha, Supuṣpa, Sunandana, and at the edge of the caves of Mount Mandara,

Kalki, possessed of noble splendor, took delight with those beautiful women in a chariot that moved through the sky with radiant birds. Intoxicated by drinking the nectar from the lotus-faces of the women, he was eager for the day of embracing Ramā.
Smeared with the saffron from the breasts of beautiful women during the course of love-making, engaged in inverted sexual positions,
and with his mouth bitten so that only the fragrance of the tongue remained— Kalki, indeed, did not even perceive his own body.
Placing that Supreme Person between their breasts, the steadfast women, who were equal to Lakṣmī herself, [embraced him].

Laughing as they embraced one another, their bodies radiant, they took delight in Mukunda. Then, overcome by the fever of exhaustion, the women hurried to the lake while their beloved Kalki was sporting within the forest.
Having entered the lake, those beautiful women, by means of that Padmā who was the very embodiment of delusion, offered water [to him] just as female elephants offer water to a male elephant;
thus did Kalki, the Lord of the World, engage in the play of young women.

Surrounded by his beloved young wife Padmāyā, the Lord of the Gods, Vāsudeva, who delights in Śambhala, triumphs as he instructs the masses of people through the diversions of his own amorous play. 24.

Those virtuous ones who, being skilled in discerning the true nature of things, always listen to and speak of the life-story of Śrī Puruṣottama— the nectar for the ears of Kalki— and who meditate upon it with devotion;
even for them, this [story] does not bring happiness without a longing for service to the Enemy of Mura.
"Saṃsāra and liberation [arise] from the ocean of the nectar of supreme bliss.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Kalki," in the third part of the glorious *Anubhāgavata*, the future *Kalki Purāṇa*. Chapter Nineteen.
Sūta said: Then all the hosts of gods, together with Brahmā and surrounded by their respective attendants, approached in their chariots to behold Kalki.
The great ṛṣis, along with the gandharvas, kinnaras, and hosts of apsarases,
gathered joyfully in Śambhala, which is honored by the gods.
Having gone there, they [beheld] Kalki, the lotus-eyed one, in the midst of the assembly.
He grants fearlessness to those who have taken refuge in him, the treasury of splendor;
he resembles a dark blue cloud, possesses long and thick arms,
and is adorned with a crown the color of the sun, like steady lightning.
He was radiant with a celestial jewel and a brilliantly shining earring;
his face, adorned with a smile, was joyful and blossoming like a fresh *alpa* flower;
and he had cast away all adversaries with the casting of his compassionate side-glances.
His chest shines with the splendor of moonstone gems through the play of his bright laughter;
he brings joy to the night-lotuses with the shimmering garment of Indra’s weapon (the rainbow);
his form is radiant with the essence of bliss that is the mass of all-encompassing delight.
The gods, Gandharvas, and others who had gathered there beheld his wondrous form, illuminated by the radiance of various clusters of jewels,
an embodiment of supreme bliss, endowed with the highest devotion.
They praised Kalki, whose eyes were like lotus petals, with the utmost reverence.
The gods said:

"Victory to you, O Lord of Devas, Lord of the Universe, Lord of Beings! You are the state of being (Bhāva) that is as fierce as a spreading fire for scattering the thickets of all afflictions, O Lord of Lakṣmī."
O Infinite One, whose infinite power is won by the radiance of the jewels upon Your limbs;
O Lord whose chest is darkened by the shining Kaustubha gem that illuminates the entire three worlds;
O Lord with a body like a mass of dark clouds and a face like a multitude of moon-like lords of birds—O Viṣṇu, protect us, along with our wives, Śeṣa, and all others, for we have taken refuge in You!
"If you have favor toward us, O Lord, go to Vaikuṇṭha,
leaving behind the realm you govern, provided it does not conflict with truth and dharma.
Having heard these words of theirs, Kalki was exceedingly delighted.
Surrounded by worthy friends, he set his mind on departure.
Having summoned his four sons, who were endowed with great strength and prowess, righteous and beloved by the subjects, he suddenly entrusted the kingdom to them. ||13-14||
Then, having summoned his subjects and related his own story,
he spoke to them of his impending departure due to the request of the gods.
Upon hearing that, all those subjects wept, filled with wonder.
Bowing down, they spoke to that lord as sons speak to a father.
The subjects said:
"O Lord, knower of all dharmas, it does not behove you to abandon us here."
"Wherever you are, there we shall go, O you who are affectionate toward those who bow before you. Our dear homes, wealth, and sons follow after you as their very life-breath;
for, knowing you to be the Lord of Sacrifice, we seek freedom from sorrow both in this world and the next."
Having heard those words and having consoled him with well-spoken words, he,
with a heart moistened by emotion, departed for the forest together with his two wives—
to the Himalayas, which were crowded with hosts of sages and the waters of the Ganges.
Filled with hosts of gods, frequented by them, and dear to the mind—
having gone there, Viṣṇu, surrounded by the throngs of deities and possessing beautiful four arms,
stayed on the bank of the Jāhnavī and, by means of his own self, recollected his true nature. ||20-21||
The ancient Supreme Self, the witness consisting of perfect light,
shone with a splendor equal to a mass of radiance from thousands of suns;
he was glorified by the conch, discus, mace, lotus, Śārṅga bow, and other emblems.

The gods showered him with flowers from various ornaments and with the form of a collective decoration; they covered his neck, which was adorned with the Kaustubha gem, with showers of fragrant blossoms and the sounds of celestial drums. ||23-24||
All the worlds, including both the stationary and the moving, praised him and were filled with wonder upon seeing the formless Lord’s Vaiṣṇava station at the time of his departure.
Having beheld that great marvel of the high-souled Lord Kalki, they were struck with amazement.
Rama and Padma entered that fire and attained him.
By the command of Kalki, Dharma and the Kṛta Yuga remained on the surface of the earth;
free from rivals and exceedingly happy, they wandered through the world of mortals for a long time.
Devāpi and Maru, acting as Kalki’s messengers, protected the earth while governing the subjects; the two lords guarded the world.
King Viśākhayūpa [observed] such a departure of Kalki.
Having heard that his own son had gone to the forest after being made king over the realm,
other kings who were emaciated by the separation from Kalki would become detached from the royal throne, merely meditating upon him and chanting his name. (29–30)
Having thus related this account of the infinite Kalki, which purifies the world, Śuka departed for the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa;
as did Mārkaṇḍeya and the other sages whose very conduct was tranquility.
Having heard of the majesty of Kalki, they sang his glory while meditating upon him:
"By his instruction, the people on earth were neither unrighteous, nor short-lived, nor poor; there were no heretics and no rationalists."
Mental anxieties, physical ailments, and afflictions arising from gods, spirits, or oneself ceased to exist;
all classes of living beings became free from envy and were ever joyful.
Thus has been described this most auspicious incarnation of Kalki.
It is auspicious, conducive to fame, longevity, and heaven; it is the supreme means of securing well-being.
It destroys grief, anguish, and sin, and eradicates the confusion of the Kali age.
It bestows happiness and liberation in this world, granting the fruits of all desired objects. (35-36)
"The light of the lamps of the scriptures shines upon the earth for only so long as the sun known as the Purāṇa shines, fulfilling the desires of the world.
Having heard this, the self-controlled sage of Bhṛgu’s lineage, together with the hosts of sages, was filled with joy.
Having recognized Sūta, the son of Śrī Lomaharṣaṇa, as one who has realized immeasurable awakening,
and desiring to hear the pure words concerning the descent of Śrī Kalki which bestow devotion to Śrī Hari,
he, being honored, spoke again with virtuous words a hymn to the Gaṅgā. (38)
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Departure of Kalki," in the third part of the glorious *Anubhāgavata*, the *Kalki Purāṇa*.
Chapter Twenty.
Śaunaka said:
O Sūta, knower of all dharmas, regarding that which was previously told by you—
that the sages, having praised the Gaṅgā, arrived in the presence of Kalki—
please recite that hymn to the Gaṅgā which destroys all sins.
It bestows liberation and auspiciousness upon those who hear or recite it here with devotion.
Sūta said:
Listen, all you sages, to this unsurpassed hymn of praise to Gaṅgā.
It has been proclaimed by the seers as that which removes the sorrow and delusion of men.
The seers said:
This river of nectar is the means of crossing the ocean of worldly existence.
Praised by the lotus feet of Hari, she has come from the assembly of the world;
her waters are beloved by the gods on the peaks of Mount Sumeru, washing away impurities.
With a gracious countenance, she is auspicious and the dispeller of the fear of worldly existence. 4.
Then that white river, which removes the pride of the lordly elephants of the gods,
serves as a banner upon the mountain peak with the radiance of Maheśa’s crown;
she is praised by the gods, asuras, humans, and serpents, as well as by Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu.
Resplendent with the fruit of liberation and destroying all impurities, she shines forth;
she is the creeper whose seed for liberation originates from the water-pot of Brahmā,
praised by the multitude of Śruti and Smṛti, and encircled by the basin of the twice-born lineage.
Falling from the peak of Mount Sumeru, encompassing the three worlds,
abounding in the fruit of the sublime Dharma, and possessing the foliage of happiness,
the Mandākinī shines forth; it is garlanded by wandering birds, bestows liberation upon the lineage of Sagara, delights the foremost of sages, and is esteemed in heaven.

The daughter of Himavat, whose breasts are like the peaks of the Lord of the Snowy Mountains, who smiles with her foamy waters and is graced by the movement of white swans, shines eternally throughout the worlds through the destruction of evil, the sight of her pure waters, prostrations, and the chanting of her virtues. 7.
She who laughs with her frothy waters and moves amidst white swans.
Moving with a graceful gait, adorned with excellent garlands of lotuses, and appearing like the beloved of the ocean, she shines resplendent.
In some places her sound is a sweet clamor; in others, her groups of women are restless.
Praised in some places by hosts of sages, worshipped in others by Ananta;
blazing in some places with the rays of the sun, agitated by fierce currents in others;
frequented by people in some places—victorious is the virtuous mother of Bhīṣma! 9.
Only that virtuous person bows here to Bhagīrathī;
only that treasury of austerities chants the praises of Jāhnavī with devotion;
only that supreme among men rightly remembers Mandākinī.
That very victorious Lord now serves the river of the gods (Surataraṅgiṇī),
which is filled with your pure waters, scarred by birds, jackals, and fish,
tossed by moving waves, and beautiful with its marshy banks.
O Ganges, daughter of the three paths, when indeed shall I behold my beloved with such exceeding joy— even though I am already praised by gods, men, and serpents—
dwelling upon your banks, bathing in your pure waters, and beholding you? 11.111–112ab.

O Gaṅgā, when— having praised you, my sins gone, and being delighted and honored by those who are uniquely skilled in serving you— shall I wander upon this earth, purified by the remembrance of your name and by conversing with those who discourse on the story of your manifestation? (12)
Thus has this unsurpassed hymn to the Gaṅgā been proclaimed by the seers;
it leads to heaven, brings fame and long life, and by its recitation or even by hearing it,
it removes all the sins of men while increasing their strength and vitality.
"In the morning, at midday, and in the evening, the presence of the Gaṅgā shall be attained.
Thus I have heard this narrative of Bhārgava from Śukadeva;
when read or recited, it is meritorious, auspicious, and bestows fame.
The supreme and most wonderful incarnation of Mahāviṣṇu as Kalki destroys all inauspiciousness for those who read or hear it with devotion.
(16) Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Hymn to Gaṅgā," in the third part of the Śrī Kalki Purāṇa, the Anubhāgavata, concerning the future. (20)
The Twenty-first Chapter.
Herein also is the dialogue between Śuka and the wise Mārkaṇḍeya;
then follows the narration of the lineage of unrighteousness and the description of the Kali age.
The departure of the gods for the abode of Brahmā together with Gobhū;
by the word of Brahmā, the birth of Viṣṇu in the house of Viṣṇuyaśas;
and [his incarnation] in the city of Śambhala through his own portions as four brothers in the womb of Sumati.
The dialogue between the father and son, as well as the initiation (*upanayana*) of Hari;
his dwelling together with his son, the supreme study of the Vedas,
the mastery of all weapons and missiles, and thereafter the vision of Śiva.
In Śivapura, there was the praise of Kalki and the obtaining of boons;
in Śuka, the arrival of Śambhala and the proclamation of his excellence to his kinsmen;
and in Viśākhayūpa, the description of himself as the soul of all by King Yūpa.
Then, through the great fortune of the brahmins, there is the arrival of Śuka;
the dialogue between Kalkin and Śuka; the excellent narrative of Siṃhala; and Padmā, who received a boon from Śiva, at her king’s svayaṃvara.
The proclamation of her female nature upon seeing the assembly of kings;
her despondency regarding Kalki, yet her exertion for the sake of marriage;
the dispatching of a parrot as a messenger by her, and his subsequent sight of him.
The acquaintance with Śuka and Padmā, the worship of Lord Viṣṇu and so forth,
the meditation on the body from the feet up to the end of the hair,
the gift of ornaments to Śuka, and the reunion with Śuka are described. ||9-10||
The departure of Kalki for the sake of Padmā’s marriage, the meeting with the two of them,
the marriage following the occasion of their water-sports, the restoration of virility to the kings, and the appearance of Kalki before them. 11.
The arrival of Ananta and his dialogue with the king in the assembly;
[the account of] his own birth and deeds due to being a eunuch, and here the hymn to Śiva;
after his father’s death, the display of Māyā at the field of Viṣṇu. 12–13.
Herein is the narrative of Ananta, the majesty of his knowledge and dispassion;
the departure of the kings and of Kalki to Śambhala with Padmā;
the construction by Viśvakarman, and the dwelling together with Padmā.
The subduing of the Buddha by kinsmen, brothers, friends, sons, and armies was recounted here, as well as the means of combat employed by those women;
thereafter, the Vālakhilya sages presented their own report. ||15-16||
Herein is proclaimed the slaying of Kuthodari along with her son,
as well as the meeting of Kalki with the sages upon his arrival at Haridvara; furthermore, there is the narration of the Solar dynasty and the Lunar dynasty according to their ordinances.
The beautiful life of Śrī Rāma is [told] in the description of the Solar Dynasty (18).
Furthermore, the encounter of Devāpi with Maru for the sake of battle is celebrated here;
as well as the striking down of the Kokas and Vikokas in the Great Terrible Forest (19).
Therein is the journey to Bhallāṭa, along with [the accounts of] Śayyā, Karṇa, and others;
here is the battle with Śaśidhvaja and the glorification of the devotion of Suśāntā.
In the battle, there is the bringing forth of Kalki, as well as Dharma and Kṛta.
Therein is the hymn of Suśāntā, the marriage of Rama with Kalki,
the previous account in the assembly regarding the cause of his own vulture-skin, and the liberation of the lord Śaśidhvaja who had prayed with devotion. 21–22.
The liberation of the Poison-Maiden, the consecration of kings,
a hymn to Māyā in Śambhala, the performance of various sacrifices and other rites,
and the liberation of Viṣṇuyaśas from Nārada are all proclaimed here.
The engagement in dharma by Kṛta and the glorification of Rukmiṇī’s vows; then the pastimes of Kalki and the birth of his sons, grandsons, and others;
and indeed, the arrival of hosts of gods and Gandharvas is narrated here.
Then, the departure of Viṣṇu to Vaikuṇṭha and the advent of Kalki are described here; after recounting the appropriate auspicious stories and the departure of Śuka,
the hymn to the Gaṅgā, which is esteemed by the sages, is proclaimed here in this Purāṇa.
It brings joy to the worlds, is ancient, and possesses five characteristics;

it bestows the perfection of all ritual residues (kalkas), consists of six thousand verses with an additional hundred, is the essence of the true meaning of all scriptures, and is enchanting to the ear. ||27-28||
The Kalki Purāṇa is proclaimed as the bestower of the four goals of life;
it emerged from the mouth of Hari at the end of the dissolution and has spread throughout the world.
Oh, it was narrated by Vyāsa on this earth in the form of a twice-born brahmin!

Those who, with devotion, here in this world listen to and recite this most wonderful power of the Blessed Viṣṇu Kalki— the stainless essence of the Purāṇas, overflowing with the spirit of Śrī Viṣṇu— in an assembly of the virtuous, in a sacred field, or in a hermitage by a holy ford;

Having respectfully given a cow, a horse, an elephant, a noble elephant, and gold to a twice-born man, and having honored him according to the rules with garments, ornaments, and other articles, they were indeed liberated as the most excellent ones;
having heard the injunction, the brāhmaṇa who had mastered the Vedas performed it according to the rule.
A Kṣatriya becomes a sovereign, a Vaiśya becomes wealthy, and a Śūdra becomes great.
One desiring a son obtains a son; one desiring wealth obtains wealth;
and one desiring knowledge obtains knowledge through both recitation and hearing.
Having thus recited this meritorious narrative that causes the hair to stand on end, the sage Lomaharṣaṇaja,
out of devotion, departed to wander among sacred fords, after having addressed the sages.
Śaunaka, the knower of dharma, together with the sages, took leave of Sūta.
Having meditated upon Hari in the holy forest, he attained Brahman along with the ṛṣis.
I bow down to that Sūta, the best of sages, the disciple of Vyāsa, who was born from the hair-pit of [Brahmā], who knows all the Purāṇas, and who is firm in his vows. ||35-36||
Having examined all the scriptures and having reflected upon them again and again, this alone has been well-established: Nārāyaṇa is to be meditated upon at all times.
This is so in the Veda, in the Rāmāyaṇa, in the Purāṇas, and likewise in the Mahābhārata.
Hari is sung of everywhere— in the beginning, in the end, and in the middle.
His body is like a water-laden cloud, he has the wind as his sole vehicle,
he holds a sword in his hand, and he is the sole protector of all the worlds.
May that king in the form of Kalki—the destroyer of the forest of the Kali age and the proclaimer of truth and dharma—bestow welfare upon you.
(39) Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the third part of the *Śrī Kalki Purāṇa*, the *Anubhāgavata* within the *Bhaviṣya*. (21)
